s:
Sun Ltd. finalises its accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026; the Board approves them on 20 May 2026. Between these dates:
1. A debtor owing ₹80 lakh at 31 March is declared insolvent on 15 April; its business had been failing since January.
2. Floods on 10 April destroy stock worth ₹1.2 crore.
3. The Board recommends a final dividend on 20 May.
4. A court case pending on 31 March is decided against the company on 5 May, fixing the damages.
Under AS 4, which events require ADJUSTMENT of the 2025-26 accounts?
o: 1 and 4 only
4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
w: Adjusting events give more evidence about conditions that existed at the balance sheet date: the debtor's failing business (1) and the lawsuit already pending (4). The flood (2) is a new condition after the date: disclose if material, don't adjust. A dividend proposed after the date is not a liability at the balance sheet date; it is only disclosed (3).

s: A company changes the estimated useful life of its machines from 10 to 6 years on the basis of a technical report. The Accounts Manager wants to recompute depreciation of the past 4 years and show the shortfall as a prior period item. Which is correct under AS 5?
o: The revision is a change in accounting policy and must be applied retrospectively with restatement
The shortfall must be adjusted directly against General Reserve without passing through Profit and Loss
The revision is a change in accounting estimate and is applied prospectively over the remaining revised life
The shortfall is a prior period item and must be shown separately in the current Profit and Loss Account
w: Useful life and residual value are estimates. Revising them is a change in accounting estimate: the effect goes to the current and future periods (prospective). Prior period items arise only from errors or omissions in earlier years' accounts, which is not the case here.

s: Which of the following correctly lists the situations in which AS 5 permits a change in accounting policy?
o: When required by statute, by an accounting standard, or when it results in a more appropriate presentation of financial statements
Whenever the Board considers that profit for the year will improve, provided the change is disclosed in the notes
Only when the statutory auditor certifies that the existing policy has become inconsistent with income-tax law
When required by statute only; accounting standards and better presentation are not valid grounds for a change
w: AS 5 allows a change in accounting policy only if (a) a statute requires it, (b) an accounting standard requires it, or (c) it gives a more appropriate presentation. Improving profit is never a ground. The impact of a material change must be disclosed.

s: Build-Right Ltd. has a fixed-price contract: price ₹200 crore, total estimated cost ₹160 crore, cost incurred till year-end ₹48 crore. The outcome can be estimated reliably and stage of completion is measured by cost incurred. What contract revenue and profit should be recognised for the year under AS 7?
o: Revenue ₹200 crore and profit ₹40 crore
Revenue ₹60 crore and profit ₹40 crore
Revenue ₹48 crore and profit nil until completion
Revenue ₹60 crore and profit ₹12 crore
w: Stage of completion = 48/160 = 30%. Revenue = 30% × 200 = ₹60 crore; cost = ₹48 crore; profit = ₹12 crore (= 30% of total expected profit of ₹40 crore). Waiting for completion is the old completed-contract method, which AS 7 does not allow when the outcome is reliable.

s: In the same type of contract, estimated total cost is revised to ₹215 crore against a contract price of ₹200 crore when the work is only 20% complete. What does AS 7 require?
o: The entire expected loss of ₹15 crore is recognised as an expense immediately
Only 20% of the expected loss, i.e. ₹3 crore, is recognised this year
No loss is recognised until the contract is completed and the final bill is raised
The expected loss is shown as a contingent liability in the notes
w: When it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, AS 7 requires the expected loss to be recognised as an expense immediately, whatever the stage of completion. This follows prudence.

s:
GreenTech Ltd. receives three grants during 2025-26:
1. ₹2 crore towards the cost of an effluent-treatment plant (life 10 years).
2. ₹50 lakh towards the cost of land for the plant, with no further conditions.
3. A State subsidy of ₹5 crore computed as 15% of total investment, not linked to any asset and not repayable.
Which treatment under AS 12 is correct?
o: 1: credit to P&L in the year received; 2: deduct from land; 3: other income
1: deduct from asset cost or treat as deferred income; 2: capital reserve; 3: capital reserve (promoters' contribution type)
1: capital reserve; 2: deferred income over 10 years; 3: deduct from plant cost
All three are credited to Capital Reserve because they are capital receipts
w: Grants related to a depreciable asset: deduct from cost or show as deferred income over the asset's life. Grants for non-depreciable assets like land with no obligations: capital reserve. Grants in the nature of promoters' contribution (linked to total investment, not to a specific asset): capital reserve, as part of shareholders' funds.

s: Under AS 12, a company receives an asset free of cost from the Government as a grant. At what value is it recorded?
o: At replacement cost with credit to Capital Reserve
At a nominal value
At its fair market value with credit to P&L
It is not recorded at all as no cost is incurred
w: AS 12 requires a non-monetary asset given free of cost to be recorded at a nominal value (e.g. ₹1). Assets given at a concessional rate are recorded at acquisition cost.

s: A grant related to a depreciable asset becomes refundable because the company broke a condition. Under AS 12, how is the refund shown in the Profit and Loss Account?
o: As a normal operating expense under 'Other expenses'
As a prior period item
As an extraordinary item
As a change in accounting estimate
w: AS 12 states that a government grant that becomes refundable is treated as an extraordinary item.

s:
Pharma Ltd. spends on a new drug:
1. Laboratory research to discover new compounds – ₹4 crore
2. Pilot plant work after technical feasibility is established, with resources and a market identified – ₹6 crore
3. Fees for registering the patent – ₹20 lakh
4. Advertising in medical journals before launch – ₹1 crore
5. Training the sales force – ₹40 lakh
How much can be recognised as an intangible asset under AS 26?
o: ₹10.20 crore
₹6.20 crore
₹11.60 crore
₹6 crore
w: Research (₹4 crore) is always expensed. Development meeting all recognition criteria (₹6 crore) plus directly attributable patent registration fees (₹0.20 crore) are capitalised. Advertising and staff training are always expensed under AS 26. Total = ₹6.20 crore.

s:
Consider these statements on AS 26:
1. Internally generated brands and customer lists can be capitalised if their value can be measured by a valuer.
2. If the research phase cannot be separated from the development phase, the whole expenditure is treated as research.
3. There is a rebuttable presumption that the useful life of an intangible asset does not exceed 10 years from the date it is available for use.
4. Expenditure on an intangible item that was once expensed can later be reinstated as an asset.
Which are correct?
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
w: Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists are never recognised (1 wrong). If phases can't be separated, all of it is research (2 correct). The 10-year rebuttable presumption applies (3 correct). Once expensed, an item cannot later be capitalised (4 wrong).

s: Which of the following is NOT a related party relationship requiring disclosure under AS 18?
o: A fellow subsidiary of the same holding company
A partnership firm in which the company's Managing Director is a partner
Two companies that have one director in common, with no other link
A relative of a Key Management Person who supplies goods to the company
w: AS 18 specifically states that two companies are not related merely because they have a director in common. A firm in which KMP has significant influence, fellow subsidiaries and relatives of KMP are related parties.

s: A bank gives an interest-free loan to its whole-time director's son and also lends to many customers. Regarding AS 18 disclosure, which statement is correct?
o: Only transactions resulting in profit or loss to the bank are disclosed, and interest-free loans are therefore excluded
Related-party transactions are disclosed even if no price is charged, but the bank need not disclose details that would breach its duty of confidentiality to ordinary customers
No disclosure is needed because no interest income arose from the loan, so no transaction value exists to report
Every loan to every customer must be disclosed individually, because a bank owes a duty of transparency to the public
w: AS 18 requires disclosure of related-party transactions whether or not a price is charged. It also exempts disclosures that would conflict with a statutory duty of confidentiality, which is relevant for banks' dealings with customers.

s: Under AS 2, which of these costs is INCLUDED in the cost of inventories of a manufacturer?
o: Administrative overheads of the head office not related to production
Fixed production overheads allocated on the basis of normal capacity
Abnormal wastage of materials due to a fire in the store
Selling and distribution costs of finished goods
w: AS 2 includes costs of purchase, costs of conversion (direct labour and systematically allocated fixed and variable production overheads, on normal capacity) and other costs to bring inventory to its present location and condition. Abnormal wastage, selling costs and unrelated admin overheads are excluded and expensed.

s: A trader holds an item of stock: cost ₹1,20,000; expected selling price ₹1,30,000; estimated selling expenses ₹16,000; replacement cost ₹1,10,000. At what value should it appear in the Balance Sheet under AS 2?
w: Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. NRV = selling price − costs to sell = 1,30,000 − 16,000 = 1,14,000. Lower of 1,20,000 and 1,14,000 = ₹1,14,000. Replacement cost is not the test for finished goods.

s: Which statement about AS 2 is NOT correct?
o: Work-in-progress under construction contracts is outside the scope of AS 2
Specific identification is used for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable
LIFO may be used if it is applied consistently from year to year
Inventory is written down to NRV on an item-by-item basis in normal cases
w: AS 2 allows FIFO or weighted average (and specific identification where items aren't interchangeable). LIFO is not permitted, even if applied consistently. Construction WIP is covered by AS 7.

s: Alpha Ltd. holds shares of Beta Ltd. bought as a long-term investment for ₹10 crore. Their market value fell to ₹9.6 crore due to a temporary market fall. Under AS 13, at what value are they shown?
o: ₹9.6 crore, because investments are always shown at market value
₹9.8 crore, being the average of cost and market value
₹10 crore, because only a permanent decline is provided for in long-term investments
₹9.6 crore, with ₹0.4 crore credited to revaluation reserve
w: Long-term investments are carried at cost; provision is made only for a decline that is other than temporary. Current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value.

s: A company borrows specifically to build a factory that will take 18 months to construct. Construction is halted for 3 months because of a labour strike. Under AS 16:
o: All borrowing costs till the factory is ready are capitalised, including the strike period
No borrowing cost can be capitalised as the factory is not a qualifying asset
Borrowing cost is capitalised only after the factory starts commercial production
Borrowing cost for the strike period is expensed because capitalisation is suspended during an extended interruption
w: A factory taking 18 months is a qualifying asset, so borrowing costs are capitalised. Capitalisation is suspended during extended periods when active development is interrupted (like a strike) and stops when the asset is substantially ready for use.

s: Under AS 28, an asset has carrying amount ₹50 lakh, net selling price ₹38 lakh and value in use ₹44 lakh. What is the impairment loss?
o: ₹12 lakh
Nil, because value in use is positive
₹6 lakh
₹9 lakh
w: Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price (38) and value in use (44) = ₹44 lakh. Impairment loss = 50 − 44 = ₹6 lakh.

s:
Consider the following under AS 29:
1. A provision is recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable and a reliable estimate can be made.
2. A contingent liability is disclosed in the notes unless the possibility of outflow is remote.
3. A contingent asset is recognised when its realisation is probable.
4. A contingent asset is ordinarily disclosed in the notes to accounts.
Which are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
w: AS 29: a provision needs all three conditions (1). Contingent liabilities are disclosed unless remote (2). A contingent asset is neither recognised nor disclosed in the financial statements; it is recognised only when realisation is virtually certain, and then it is no longer contingent (3 and 4 wrong).

s: An Indian subsidiary buys components from its UK parent at prices well above those charged to unrelated buyers, reducing Indian taxable profit. The tax officer adjusts income. Which concept and law apply?
o: Arm's Length Price under the transfer pricing provisions (Sections 92–92F) of the Income-tax Act
Fair value under Ind AS 113, applied by the Companies Act
Customs valuation, which automatically decides income-tax value
Group transfer price, which is binding because it follows internal group policy
w: Transactions between associated enterprises must be at arm's length price. Methods include CUP, resale price, cost plus, profit split and TNMM. A group's internal pricing policy does not bind the tax authorities.

s: Which statement about the Indian accounting framework is correct?
o: Ind AS are notified by RBI under the Banking Regulation Act and apply first to banks and NBFCs
Scheduled commercial banks still follow AS with RBI norms because RBI has deferred Ind AS for them until further notice
A company that adopts Ind AS voluntarily may revert to the old AS after three years with Board approval
All listed companies and all scheduled commercial banks moved to Ind AS together from 1 April 2016
w: Ind AS applied to companies in phases from 2016-17 (net worth ≥ ₹500 crore, then all listed and ≥ ₹250 crore). RBI deferred Ind AS for scheduled commercial banks until further notice. Once Ind AS is adopted, a company cannot revert. Ind AS are notified by the Central Government under the Companies Act.

s:
Which TWO features distinguish IFRS from US GAAP?
1. IFRS is principles-based; US GAAP is more rules-based.
2. IFRS permits LIFO; US GAAP prohibits it.
3. IFRS permits revaluation of property, plant and equipment; US GAAP does not.
4. Both prohibit reversal of impairment losses on all assets.
o: 1 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 2
2 and 4
w: IFRS is principles-based and allows PPE revaluation; US GAAP is rules-based and cost-only for PPE. It is US GAAP that permits LIFO (IFRS prohibits it). IFRS allows reversal of impairment (except goodwill); US GAAP does not.

s: Under AS 9, when is revenue from a sale of goods recognised?
o: When the seller has transferred the significant risks and rewards of ownership and no significant uncertainty exists about collection
When the goods are physically dispatched from the seller's warehouse, whatever the terms
When the buyer pays the price in full
When the sale invoice is raised, even if goods are sent on approval
w: AS 9 links revenue to transfer of significant risks and rewards with no significant uncertainty about consideration. Goods sent on approval are not sold until the buyer approves or the time for rejection lapses. Cash receipt alone does not decide it.

s: Under AS 11, a company has a foreign-currency trade payable of USD 10,000 recorded at ₹83 when the goods were bought. At year-end the rate is ₹85 and it is still unpaid. What is the treatment?
o: Keep the payable at ₹8,30,000 until it is paid, since it arose from a historical transaction
Restate the payable at ₹8,50,000 and debit the ₹20,000 exchange loss to Capital Reserve
Restate the payable at ₹8,50,000 and charge the ₹20,000 exchange loss to the Profit and Loss Account
Restate the payable at ₹8,50,000 and add the ₹20,000 loss to the cost of the goods purchased
w: A trade payable is a monetary item. AS 11 requires monetary items to be reported at the closing rate, with exchange differences recognised in P&L of the period.

s: Mr Raj, a sole proprietor, pays from the business bank account: (i) his personal life-insurance premium, (ii) school fees of his son, and (iii) the shop's electricity bill. The accountant debits all three to expenses, saying "the proprietor and the business are legally the same person". Which concept is violated and what is the correct treatment of (i) and (ii)?
o: Money measurement concept; (i) and (ii) are not recorded at all
Business entity concept; (i) and (ii) are debited to Drawings Account
Going concern concept; (i) and (ii) are debited to Capital Reserve
Matching concept; (i) and (ii) are shown as prepaid expenses
w: Accounting treats the business as separate from the owner even when the law does not (sole proprietorship). Personal payments are drawings, reducing the owner's capital. Only the shop's electricity is a business expense.

s: A company bought land for ₹2 crore five years ago. A valuer now says it is worth ₹3.5 crore. The CFO wants to show it at ₹3.5 crore "to reflect reality". Under traditional accounting (no revaluation policy), the land stays at ₹2 crore mainly because of:
o: The conservatism convention
The materiality convention
The money measurement concept
The historical cost concept
w: Assets are recorded at acquisition cost and not at current market value: the cost concept. Conservatism concerns anticipating losses, not ignoring gains on an asset. Revaluation is possible only as a deliberate policy under AS 10 / Ind AS 16.

s:
Which of the following is an application of the conservatism (prudence) convention?
1. Valuing closing stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
2. Creating a provision for doubtful debts.
3. Creating a provision for discount on creditors.
4. Ignoring an expected profit on a contract not yet executed.
o: 1 and 2 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
w: Prudence anticipates losses but not gains. Stock at lower of cost/NRV, provision for doubtful debts and ignoring unrealised profit apply it. A provision for discount on creditors anticipates a gain, so it is NOT made under conservatism.

s: Going concern assumption justifies which of the following?
o: Recording revenue only when the cash is actually received from customers
Treating the proprietor's withdrawals for personal use as drawings
Showing fixed assets at cost less depreciation rather than at their forced-sale value
Recording only those transactions that can be measured in terms of money
w: Because the business is expected to continue, assets are shown at cost less depreciation (used over their life), not at liquidation value. Prepaid expenses and long-term liabilities also rest on going concern.

s: A consulting firm on cash basis has, for March: fees earned but unpaid ₹3 lakh, April rent paid in March ₹50,000, March electricity unpaid ₹20,000. By how much does accrual-basis profit for March differ from cash-basis profit (assuming nothing else)?
o: Accrual profit is higher by ₹3.30 lakh
Accrual profit is higher by ₹3.70 lakh
Accrual profit is lower by ₹0.70 lakh
Accrual profit is higher by ₹2.30 lakh
w: Accrual adds unpaid fees (+3,00,000), removes April rent paid in March from March expense (+50,000), and adds unpaid March electricity (−20,000). Net: +3,30,000.

s: Which concept distinguishes the receipt of cash from the right to receive cash, and the payment of cash from the legal obligation to pay?
o: Accrual concept
Cost concept
Money measurement concept
Dual aspect concept
w: Under the accrual concept income is recorded when the right to receive arises (earned) and expense when the obligation arises (incurred), regardless of the timing of cash.

s: Under AS 1, which are the fundamental accounting assumptions whose observance need NOT be disclosed?
o: Prudence, substance over form and materiality
Consistency, materiality and full disclosure
Going concern, prudence and accrual
Going concern, consistency and accrual
w: AS 1 names going concern, consistency and accrual as fundamental assumptions. If followed, no disclosure is needed; if not followed, the fact must be disclosed. Prudence, substance over form and materiality guide the choice of policies.

s: A business has: Cash ₹40,000; Debtors ₹65,000; Stock ₹85,000; Machinery ₹2,10,000; Creditors ₹90,000; Bank loan ₹1,20,000; Outstanding wages ₹10,000; Prepaid rent ₹5,000. What is the owner's capital?
Opening capital ₹5,00,000; additional capital introduced ₹1,00,000; drawings ₹60,000; closing capital ₹6,90,000. What was the profit for the year?
w: Closing capital = Opening + additional capital + profit − drawings. 6,90,000 = 5,00,000 + 1,00,000 + P − 60,000 → P = 6,90,000 − 5,40,000 = ₹1,50,000.

s: Which transaction changes BOTH total assets and total liabilities but leaves capital unchanged?
o: Purchase of furniture for cash
Withdrawal of cash by the proprietor for personal use
Payment of salary in cash
Repayment of a bank loan by cheque
w: Loan repayment reduces bank (asset) and loan (liability) equally. Furniture for cash only swaps assets. Salary and drawings reduce assets and capital.

s: A company converts part of its equity share capital into a loan from the promoter. The effect on the accounting equation is:
o: No element of the equation changes, because no cash moves
Assets decrease and capital decreases, because equity is paid out
Assets and liabilities both increase, because the loan brings in fresh funds
Liabilities increase and capital decreases; total assets are unchanged
w: No cash moves, so assets are unchanged. Owners' funds fall and outside liabilities rise by the same amount.

s: The Finance Manager says: "Whenever the company earns a profit, its liabilities must go up." Which response is correct?
o: Profit first increases owners' equity through retained earnings; liabilities change only if a dividend is declared or debt is repaid later
Correct, because profit is always owed to shareholders and must be shown as a current liability
Correct, because a profit always results in higher trade creditors and outstanding expenses
Profit has no effect on the Balance Sheet at all; it affects only the Statement of Profit and Loss
w: Profit raises capital (reserves). Declaring a dividend creates a liability; using profit to repay a loan reduces liabilities; reinvesting it in assets changes asset mix. So there is no automatic increase in liabilities.

s: A stapler costing ₹350 that will last three years is charged to expenses in the year of purchase. Which convention justifies this?
o: Consistency
Conservatism
Materiality
Full disclosure
w: Materiality allows insignificant items to be treated in the simplest way. Capitalising and depreciating a ₹350 item would not change any user's decision.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Accounting is often called the 'language of business'.
2. Book-keeping covers recording, classifying, summarising and interpreting.
3. Accounting records only events that can be expressed in money.
4. A limitation of accounting is that it is based on historical cost and ignores price-level changes.
Which are correct?
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
w: Book-keeping is only the recording (and posting) stage. Analysis and interpretation are part of accounting, not book-keeping. The rest are correct.

s: Goods sent to a customer on approval on 28 March (cost ₹60,000, price ₹80,000) were recorded as sales; the customer had not approved by 31 March. Which concept is breached, and what is the correction?
o: Consistency; keep the sale as recorded but disclose the approval terms in notes
Revenue recognition (realisation); reverse the sale and include the goods at cost in closing stock
Going concern; show the debtor at ₹80,000 with a provision of ₹20,000 against it
Materiality; no correction is needed since the goods have already left the warehouse
w: Revenue is recognised only when risks and rewards pass. Goods on approval still belong to the seller until approved, so the sale is reversed and the goods are included in stock at cost (₹60,000), not at sale price.

s: A trainee classifies: Goodwill – Nominal; Outstanding Salary – Personal; Drawings – Personal; Discount Received – Real. How many are correct under the traditional classification?
o: Three
One
Two
All four
w: Goodwill is an intangible real account (wrong). Outstanding salary is a representative personal account (correct). Drawings is the proprietor's personal account (correct). Discount received is a nominal account, an income (wrong). So two are correct.

s: Which of these is a 'representative personal account'?
o: Prepaid Insurance Account
Furniture Account
Patents Account
Insurance Expense Account
w: Prepaid insurance represents the insurance company, which owes service for the unexpired period, so it is a representative personal account. Insurance expense is nominal; furniture and patents are real.

s:
Vertex Ltd. made these entries:
1. Purchased office furniture on credit – debited Purchases.
2. Paid outstanding electricity through bank – debited Outstanding Electricity.
3. Received cash from a debtor after allowing discount – debited Cash and Discount Allowed.
4. Bought machinery by issuing equity shares – debited Machinery.
Which evaluation is correct?
o: Only entry 1 is wrong; furniture is a fixed asset and must be debited to Furniture Account
Entries 1 and 3 are wrong, because discount allowed should be credited to the debtor only
Entries 2 and 4 are wrong, because no cash or bank is involved in entry 4
All four entries are correct under the traditional golden rules
w: Purchases Account is only for goods dealt in. Furniture (a capital asset) is debited to Furniture A/c. Paying an outstanding liability debits the liability; discount to a debtor is a loss (Dr Discount Allowed); asset received for shares debits the asset.

s: The proprietor withdraws goods costing ₹12,000 (sale price ₹15,000) for personal use. The correct entry is:
o: Drawings A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Sales A/c ₹15,000
Capital A/c Dr ₹12,000; To Stock A/c ₹12,000
Drawings A/c Dr ₹12,000; To Sales A/c ₹12,000
Drawings A/c Dr ₹12,000; To Purchases A/c ₹12,000
w: Goods taken by the owner are recorded at cost and reduce purchases (they were never sold). Debit Drawings (reduces capital), credit Purchases.

s: Under the imprest system of petty cash, the main cashier reimburses the petty cashier ₹4,750 spent during the week. Which account is debited in the main books when the reimbursement is made?
o: Petty Cash Account
Each expense account directly
Cash Account
Suspense Account
w: Under the imprest system the cash given to the petty cashier, both initially and as reimbursement, is debited to Petty Cash A/c (credit Cash/Bank). Individual expenses are posted from the petty cash book later.

s: Which of the following is recorded in the Purchases Day Book?
o: Machinery bought on credit
Stationery bought on credit for office use
Goods bought for cash
Goods bought on credit for resale
w: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods in which the business deals. Credit purchases of assets or office supplies go to the journal proper; cash purchases go to the cash book.

s: A business records a sales return of ₹4,000 as a purchase of ₹4,000. Which single rectifying entry corrects it (books not closed)?
o: Purchases A/c Dr ₹4,000; To Sales Returns A/c ₹4,000
Sales Returns A/c Dr ₹4,000; To Purchases A/c ₹4,000
Sales Returns A/c Dr ₹8,000; To Purchases A/c ₹8,000
Debtors A/c Dr ₹4,000; To Purchases A/c ₹4,000
w: Purchases was wrongly debited, so credit it to remove the debit. Sales Returns should have been debited, so debit it. The party's account side was the same in both cases (credited), so it needs no change.

s: Which entry is correct when goods costing ₹50,000 are destroyed by fire and the insurer admits a claim of ₹35,000?
o: Insurance Claim A/c Dr ₹35,000 and Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Purchases A/c ₹50,000
Insurance Company A/c Dr ₹50,000; To Purchases A/c ₹50,000
Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹50,000; To Stock A/c ₹50,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹35,000 and Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Sales A/c ₹50,000
w: Goods lost are removed from purchases at cost. The admitted claim is an amount receivable (insurance company / claim account), and the balance is a loss charged to P&L.

s: A debt of ₹20,000 written off as bad last year is recovered this year. The correct entry is:
o: Debtor's A/c Dr; To Bad Debts A/c
Cash A/c Dr; To Bad Debts A/c
Cash A/c Dr; To Debtor's Personal A/c
Cash A/c Dr; To Bad Debts Recovered A/c
w: The debtor's account was closed when the debt was written off. The recovery is an income/gain of the current year, credited to Bad Debts Recovered (a nominal account).

s: In a triple-column cash book, which statement is correct?
o: A contra entry is recorded only in the cash column and never in the bank column
Trade discount and cash discount are both recorded in the discount columns
The discount columns are not balanced; their totals are posted to Discount Allowed and Discount Received accounts
The discount columns are balanced like the cash and bank columns and the balances carried forward
w: Discount columns are memorandum columns: they are totalled, not balanced, and the totals are posted to the ledger. Trade discount is never recorded. A contra entry (cash deposited/withdrawn) affects both cash and bank columns.

s: Under the modern approach, which pair of accounts both normally carry a CREDIT balance?
o: Drawings and Capital introduced
Discount allowed and Net sales
Outstanding wages and Commission received
Prepaid rent and Trade creditors
w: Liabilities (outstanding wages) and incomes (commission received) have credit balances. Drawings, prepaid rent and discount allowed have debit balances.

s: Which of the following statements on double entry is correct?
o: Double entry ensures that all errors are automatically detected
Every transaction is recorded twice in the same account
Every transaction has one debit and one credit only, never more
Every transaction affects at least two accounts, with equal debit and credit amounts
w: Double entry means equal debits and credits for every transaction (a compound entry can have several accounts). It makes the trial balance agree but does not catch errors like omission, principle or compensating errors.

s:
Which of the following errors will cause the Trial Balance to disagree?
1. A credit sale of ₹4,500 recorded in the Sales Book as ₹5,400.
2. The Purchases Book total undercast by ₹1,000.
3. Repairs to building debited to Building Account.
4. Cash received from Ram ₹2,000 posted to the debit of Ram's account.
5. A credit purchase from Shyam completely omitted from the books.
o: 1, 2, 4 and 5 only
2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
w: Undercasting a subsidiary book (2) and posting to the wrong side (4) are one-sided errors. An error in the book of original entry (1) affects both sides equally; an error of principle (3) and complete omission (5) leave both sides balanced.

o: Credit side, ₹9,400
Debit side, ₹11,400
Credit side, ₹13,200
Debit side, ₹9,400
w: Credit excess: (a) +10,000; (b) Ravi credited 1,800 short → −1,800; (c) discount received credited 600 and discount allowed not debited 600 → credit +600, debit −600 → net 1,200. Total credit excess = 10,000 − 1,800 + 1,200 = 9,400, so suspense is debited ₹9,400. (d) does not affect the TB.

s: For the errors in the previous case [(a) sales book overcast ₹10,000; (b) Ravi's account posted ₹5,700 instead of ₹7,500; (c) discount allowed ₹600 posted to credit of discount received; (d) repairs ₹2,000 debited to Building], what is the effect of the rectification on net profit?
o: Net profit decreases by ₹9,400
Net profit decreases by ₹11,200
Net profit increases by ₹13,200
Net profit decreases by ₹13,200
w: (a) sales reduced by 10,000; (b) personal account only, no effect; (c) adds 600 expense and removes 600 income = −1,200; (d) 2,000 charged to repairs. Total = −13,200. Note that the profit effect differs from the suspense amount.

s: A machine bought on credit for ₹18,00,000 on 1 January 2026 was entered in the Purchases Day Book; the supplier was correctly credited. Depreciation is 10% p.a. SLM. If not rectified before the 31 March 2026 accounts are finalised:
o: Fixed assets overstated by ₹17,55,000, net profit understated by ₹18,00,000, Trial Balance agrees
Only the classification is wrong; profit and assets are unaffected
Fixed assets understated by ₹17,55,000, net profit understated by ₹17,55,000, Trial Balance agrees
Fixed assets understated by ₹18,00,000, net profit overstated by ₹18,00,000, Trial Balance disagrees
w: Purchases is overstated by ₹18,00,000 (profit understated) but 3 months' depreciation ₹45,000 was not charged (profit overstated by that). Net profit understated = ₹17,55,000. Machine net book value missing = 18,00,000 − 45,000 = ₹17,55,000. Both debit and credit were made, so the TB agrees: an error of principle.

s: A credit sale of goods (cost ₹3,20,000, price ₹4,80,000) was completely omitted from the Sales Day Book; stock records were updated correctly. Before rectification:
o: Net profit is unaffected because both sales and cost of sales are omitted
Gross profit and trade receivables are understated by ₹4,80,000 each, and the Trial Balance agrees
Closing stock is overstated by ₹4,80,000
Gross profit is understated by ₹1,60,000 and the Trial Balance disagrees
w: Stock records were updated (goods excluded from closing stock), so cost of sales already reflects the goods. Only the sale is missing: sales and debtors are both understated by ₹4,80,000. Complete omission affects neither side of the TB.

s:
Which of the following are errors of principle?
1. Purchase of office furniture debited to Purchases Account.
2. Annual maintenance expenditure capitalised.
3. Legal expenses for acquiring land debited to Land Account.
4. Freight on a new machine debited to Freight Outward Account.
5. Sale of an old typewriter credited to Sales Account.
o: 1, 2, 4 and 5 only
All five
1, 2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 5 only
w: 1, 2, 4 and 5 confuse capital and revenue items. Legal expenses to acquire land are part of land's cost, so debiting Land is correct (3).

s: ₹500 received from Mohan was posted to the debit of his account. The rectifying entry is:
o: Suspense A/c Dr ₹1,000; To Mohan ₹1,000
Mohan Dr ₹1,000; To Suspense A/c ₹1,000
Suspense A/c Dr ₹500; To Mohan ₹500
Cash A/c Dr ₹500; To Mohan ₹500
w: Mohan should have been credited ₹500 but was debited ₹500. Crediting him ₹1,000 cancels the wrong debit and records the correct credit. The other side goes to suspense because the original error was one-sided.

s: The Finance Executive says: "Every correction passed through the Suspense Account changes the company's profit." Which response is correct?
o: Incorrect, because the suspense account is used only while preparing the bank reconciliation statement
Correct, because every posting error ultimately flows into the Profit and Loss Account
Incorrect; corrections to personal or real accounts through suspense change only ledger balances, while those involving nominal accounts change profit
Correct, because the suspense account is opened only for errors in revenue items such as sales and expenses
w: Suspense absorbs one-sided errors of any account type. Correcting a debtor's or creditor's account through suspense has no P&L effect; correcting sales, purchases or expenses does.

s: A credit sale of ₹123 to Mr M was posted to his account as ₹321. This error will:
o: Not affect the Trial Balance, being an error of principle
Affect the Trial Balance and be a clerical error of commission
Not affect the Trial Balance, being an error of omission
Not affect the Trial Balance, being a compensating error
w: The sales book shows ₹123 (sales credited ₹123) but Mr M is debited ₹321. Debit side exceeds by ₹198, so the TB disagrees. Wrong amount posting is an error of commission.

s: An error found next year after the accounts were closed: wages of ₹15,000 paid for installing a new machine were debited to Wages Account. The rectifying entry in the new year is:
o: Machinery A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Wages A/c ₹15,000
Machinery A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c ₹15,000
Machinery A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Suspense A/c ₹15,000
Wages A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Machinery A/c ₹15,000
w: After closing, the Wages account (nominal) of last year has been closed to P&L. The correction to last year's profit goes through Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c (or as a prior period item). Machinery (real) is corrected directly.

s: Which statement about the Trial Balance is correct?
o: It is a statement, not an account; its agreement shows arithmetical accuracy but not freedom from all errors
It is an account in the general ledger that must always agree before the books are closed
It proves that the books of account are free from all errors once its two totals agree
It is prepared only after the final accounts are drawn up, to verify the Balance Sheet
w: A TB is a list (statement) of balances prepared before final accounts. Agreement shows only arithmetical accuracy: omissions, principle errors and compensating errors still remain.

s: Which pair contains one error that disturbs the Trial Balance and one that does not?
o: Wrong balancing of the Wages Account / Goods bought from Arun posted to Varun's account
Error of principle / Compensating error
Undercasting of the Sales Book / Overcasting of the Purchases Returns Book
Complete omission of a credit sale / Wrong amount in the Purchases Book
w: Wrong balancing affects one account, so the TB disagrees. Posting to the wrong personal account on the correct side does not affect the TB. The other pairs are both non-disturbing or both disturbing.

s: Closing stock appears inside the Trial Balance in which situation?
o: When closing stock has been adjusted through the Purchases Account before preparing the Trial Balance
Never, since closing stock is always an adjustment shown outside the Trial Balance
Always, since closing stock is an asset that must appear among the debit balances
Only when stock is valued at market price instead of at cost
w: Normally closing stock is an adjustment outside the TB, recorded in both the Trading A/c and the Balance Sheet. If it was already deducted from purchases (adjusted purchases), it appears in the TB and goes only to the Balance Sheet.

s: On 31 March, Nova Enterprises' cash book shows ₹24,80,000 (debit). Items found: outstanding cheques ₹4,20,000; a dishonoured cheque not recorded ₹1,10,000; bank charges ₹12,500; dividend credited directly ₹95,000; insurance premium paid under standing instruction ₹48,000. What is the adjusted cash-book balance to be shown in the Balance Sheet?
w: Only bank-originated items adjust the cash book: 24,80,000 − 1,10,000 − 12,500 + 95,000 − 48,000 = ₹23,04,500. Outstanding cheques are a timing difference shown only in the BRS. (Balance as per pass book would be 23,04,500 + 4,20,000 = ₹27,24,500.)

s: Cash book shows a debit balance of ₹40,000. Cheques issued but not presented ₹12,000; cheques deposited but not collected ₹8,000; bank charges ₹1,000 not recorded in the cash book; interest credited by bank ₹600. What is the balance as per pass book?
o: ₹43,600 credit
₹42,400 credit
₹45,600 credit
₹36,400 credit
w: 40,000 + 12,000 (unpresented, bank not yet reduced) − 8,000 (deposit not yet credited) − 1,000 (charges) + 600 (interest) = ₹43,600 (a credit balance in the pass book means money with the bank).

s: Cash book shows an overdraft of ₹80,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹15,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹22,000; bank charges ₹500 and interest on overdraft ₹2,500 debited by bank; a customer deposited ₹12,000 directly. What is the overdraft as per pass book?
w: Treat the overdraft as −80,000. Unpresented cheques +15,000 (bank hasn't paid yet), uncredited deposits −22,000, charges −500, interest −2,500, direct deposit +12,000 → −78,000, i.e. overdraft ₹78,000 per pass book.

s:
While preparing a BRS, which of these require a correcting entry in the cash book itself?
1. Cheque deposited ₹1,80,000 recorded in the cash book as ₹18,000.
2. Bank charges debited by the bank, not yet recorded.
3. A cheque issued that is still unpresented.
4. Interest credited by the bank, not entered in the cash book.
5. A cheque wrongly debited by the bank to our account (belongs to another customer).
o: 1, 2, 4 and 5 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
w: The firm's own error (1) and bank-originated items (2, 4) are corrected in the cash book. An unpresented cheque (3) is a timing difference. A bank's error (5) is shown in the BRS and the bank is asked to reverse it; our cash book is correct.

s: Balance as per cash book is ₹20,000 and as per pass book ₹28,000 (both favourable). If there is no other difference, which single item explains it?
o: Cheques of ₹8,000 deposited but not yet credited by the bank
A cheque of ₹8,000 deposited and dishonoured, not yet recorded in the cash book
Bank charges of ₹8,000 not yet recorded in the cash book
Cheques of ₹8,000 issued but not yet presented for payment
w: The pass book is higher by ₹8,000. Unpresented cheques have reduced the cash book but not yet the bank balance. The other three items would make the pass book lower than the cash book.

s: Starting from the balance as per pass book (credit ₹50,000), how should 'cheques deposited but not yet collected ₹6,000' be treated to arrive at the cash-book balance?
o: Ignored, as it is a timing difference
Added, giving ₹56,000
Deducted, giving ₹44,000 overdraft
Deducted, giving ₹44,000
w: The cash book already includes the deposit; the bank does not. So the cash book is higher: start at 50,000 and add 6,000 = ₹56,000.

s: Which balance of bank is shown in the Balance Sheet after preparing the BRS?
o: The cash-book balance after recording bank charges, direct credits and other omitted items (adjusted cash book)
The unadjusted cash-book balance, because the BRS is only a statement and needs no entries
The pass-book balance, because it is prepared independently by the bank and is therefore reliable
The average of the cash-book and pass-book balances, to spread the timing differences
w: After all bank-originated items and the firm's errors are entered, the adjusted cash book shows the true balance from the firm's side. Timing differences don't change the firm's true position.

s: Which statement about the pass book being a 'mirror image' of the cash book is correct?
o: An overdraft appears as a debit balance in the cash book and a credit balance in the pass book
A favourable cash-book balance appears as a debit balance in the pass book prepared by the bank
A debit in the cash book bank column appears as a credit in the pass book, but timing differences and errors make the balances differ
The pass book always shows exactly the same balance as the cash book on any given date
w: The customer's asset (debit in cash book) is the bank's liability (credit in pass book). Overdraft = credit in cash book, debit in pass book. Balances match only if no timing differences or errors exist.

s: A trainee argues: "Since the bank statement is correct, we should just copy its closing balance into the books and skip the BRS." Which is the strongest objection?
o: Bank balances are not shown in the Balance Sheet, so the closing balance has no use in the books
The bank statement is not admissible in court as evidence, so the firm's own records must prevail
A BRS is required only for overdraft accounts, where interest is charged on daily balances
The bank statement omits timing items and may itself contain errors; a BRS identifies these and protects against errors and fraud
w: The bank doesn't yet know about unpresented and uncleared cheques, and banks do make errors. Reconciliation is a key internal control against errors and frauds.

s: A cheque of ₹15,000 received from a debtor was recorded in the cash book and deposited, but the bank returned it dishonoured; this is not yet recorded. Starting from the cash-book balance, how is it treated?
o: Added to find the pass-book balance with no cash-book entry
Deducted to find the pass-book balance, and a cash-book entry 'Debtor Dr; To Bank' must be passed
Ignored because the debtor will pay later
Deducted in the BRS only, no cash-book entry because it is a timing difference
w: The bank has already reversed the credit, so its balance is lower. A dishonour is a real event: the debtor owes again, so the cash book must be corrected.

s: A machine costs ₹48 lakh plus ₹2 lakh installation; residual value ₹5 lakh; useful life 9 years; SLM. The company plans to sell it after 3 years. What is its carrying amount just before sale?
o: ₹35 lakh
₹33 lakh
₹36.50 lakh
₹38.50 lakh
w: Cost = 48 + 2 = ₹50 lakh. Annual depreciation = (50 − 5)/9 = ₹5 lakh. After 3 years: 50 − 15 = ₹35 lakh. Ignoring installation gives a wrong answer.

s: A machine costing ₹4,00,000 is depreciated at 20% p.a. under the WDV method. What is its book value at the end of Year 2?
A machine was bought for ₹5,00,000 on 1 October 2020; useful life 5 years; nil salvage; SLM; accounts close on 31 March. What is the total depreciation charged up to 31 March 2024?
w: Annual depreciation = 5,00,000/5 = 1,00,000. Period 1 Oct 2020 to 31 Mar 2024 = 3.5 years → ₹3,50,000.

s: Machinery costing ₹12,00,000 has an estimated residual value of ₹2,00,000 and a total production capacity of 1,00,000 units. In Year 1 it produced 18,000 units. Depreciation for Year 1 under the units-of-production method is:
w: Depreciable amount = 10,00,000. Per unit = ₹10. Year 1 = 18,000 × 10 = ₹1,80,000.

s: An asset costs ₹6,50,000, salvage value ₹50,000, life 5 years. Depreciation for Year 2 under the sum-of-the-years'-digits method is:
w: Sum of digits = 1+2+3+4+5 = 15. Year 2 uses the remaining life at the start of year 2, which is 4: 4/15 × 6,00,000 = ₹1,60,000.

s: A vehicle costing ₹2,40,000 was bought on 1 July 2024. Depreciation is 15% p.a. WDV, charged on a time basis; the year ends on 31 March. What is depreciation for FY 2025-26?
A machine bought on 1 April 2023 for ₹5,00,000 (WDV 20% p.a.) is sold on 30 September 2025 for ₹2,80,000. What is the profit or loss on sale?
o: Profit of ₹40,000
Profit of ₹8,000
Loss of ₹8,000
Loss of ₹40,000

s: Machinery cost ₹1.80 crore; useful life 10 years; residual value ₹20 lakh; SLM. After 5 years the residual value is revised to ₹8 lakh; remaining life unchanged. What is the annual depreciation from Year 6?
o: ₹16 lakh
₹20.80 lakh
₹18.40 lakh
₹17.20 lakh
w: Old charge = (180 − 20)/10 = 16 lakh; carrying amount after 5 years = 180 − 80 = 100 lakh. Revised (prospective): (100 − 8)/5 = ₹18.40 lakh. Past depreciation is not recomputed (change in estimate).

s: A transport company buys electric buses. Utilisation is highest in the early years, maintenance rises in later years, and management wants the charge to follow how benefits are consumed. Which method fits, and why?
o: Sinking fund method, because it sets aside cash so the buses can be replaced later
WDV, because it charges more in early years and less later, so depreciation plus repairs stays roughly even
Units of production, because the number of passengers carried decides the charge
SLM, because equal charges every year give the most accurate matching for vehicles
w: WDV front-loads depreciation, matching higher early benefits and offsetting rising later repair costs. Units-of-production fits only if usage (km/units) is the driver and can be estimated; the facts here point to WDV.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under WDV, the book value of an asset never becomes zero.
2. Under SLM with nil residual value, the book value becomes zero at the end of useful life.
3. Depreciation is a process of valuation of fixed assets at market price.
4. Depreciation provides cash for replacement of assets.
Which are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
w: WDV applies a % to a falling balance, so it never reaches zero (1). SLM with nil residual writes off fully (2). Depreciation allocates cost; it does not value assets at market (3 wrong). It is a non-cash charge and does not by itself create cash; a sinking fund investment does (4 wrong).

s: Two identical machines cost ₹25 lakh each. Machine A: SLM over 10 years (nil residual). Machine B: WDV at 20%. Carrying amounts at the end of Year 3?
o: A ₹15 lakh; B ₹12.8 lakh
A ₹17.5 lakh; B ₹12.8 lakh
A ₹17.5 lakh; B ₹15 lakh
Both ₹17.5 lakh
w: SLM: 2.5 lakh a year × 3 = 7.5 → 17.5 lakh. WDV: 25 × 0.8³ = 12.8 lakh. WDV writes off more in the early years.

s: Under Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013, the residual value of an asset is ordinarily:
o: Not less than 15% of the original cost, for all asset classes
Exactly 10% of the original cost in all cases, without exception
Nil, since Schedule II does not permit any residual value at all
Not more than 5% of the original cost, unless a higher value is justified and disclosed
w: Schedule II states that the residual value of an asset shall not ordinarily be more than 5% of its original cost. A different estimate needs justification and disclosure.

s:
A company creates a sinking fund to replace a machine after 5 years. Which statements are correct?
1. Annual instalments are invested outside the business so that cash is available on replacement.
2. Interest received on sinking-fund investments is credited to the Sinking Fund Account.
3. Once the fund is created, depreciation is no longer charged to Profit and Loss.
4. The sinking fund removes the need to replace the asset.
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
w: A sinking fund sets aside and invests a fixed amount each year; investment income is added to the fund. The annual amount is still charged to P&L as depreciation (3 wrong), and it only provides funds; it doesn't replace the asset (4 wrong).

s: Depreciation on a newly constructed factory should start from:
o: The date the factory is available for use, even if production has not begun
The date the first payment is made to the building contractor
The date commercial production actually starts in the factory
The beginning of the financial year following completion
w: Depreciation begins when the asset is available for use, i.e. in the location and condition needed to operate as intended (AS 10).

s: Which item is NOT depreciated?
o: Freehold land used for a factory
Factory building
A mine (through depletion)
Leasehold land with a 30-year lease
w: Freehold land has an unlimited useful life, so it is not depreciated. Leasehold land is written off over the lease period; buildings are depreciated; mines are depleted.

s: The WDV rate that reduces a ₹1,00,000 asset to a residual value of ₹10,000 in 5 years is closest to (given 0.1^(1/5) ≈ 0.631):

Neptune Cements Ltd. buys a kiln. Related costs: freight to site, installation, a 3-day trial run (output sold for ₹50,000), staff training on the kiln, and routine maintenance in the first month. Which costs are capitalised under AS 10?
o: Freight, installation, trial run, staff training and maintenance
Freight, installation and the trial-run cost net of ₹50,000 sale proceeds
Only the invoice price of the kiln
Freight and installation only; trial-run cost is always expensed
w: Directly attributable costs (delivery, installation, testing less net proceeds of test output) are capitalised. Staff training and routine maintenance are expensed.

s: Nova Petrochem spends ₹2.80 crore on a statutory major inspection of its turbine, done every 5 years. No part is replaced, but the turbine cannot legally run without it. The Accounts Manager wants to expense it because 'no new asset is bought'. Which treatment is right under AS 10?
o: Expense it fully in the current year as a repair, because no new part has been installed
Debit it directly to General Reserve because it is not a normal operating expense of the year
Capitalise the inspection cost as a component if recognition criteria are met, and derecognise any remaining cost of the previous inspection
Show it as deferred revenue expenditure and write it off equally over the next 5 years
w: AS 10 treats a major inspection that is a condition for continued operation as a component of the asset, capitalised when performed, with the remaining carrying amount of the previous inspection derecognised.

s: An amount of ₹5,000 is spent on replacing a small worn-out part of a machine in use, so that the machine keeps working at its existing capacity. This is:
o: Capital expenditure
Revenue expenditure
Deferred revenue expenditure
Capital loss
w: Replacing a small part only maintains the asset's existing condition; it neither increases capacity nor extends life. So it is charged to P&L as repairs.

s: Which of the following is a capital expenditure?
o: Wages paid to factory workers for producing goods for sale
Carriage paid on goods purchased for resale to customers
Annual white-washing and painting of the factory building
Wages paid to the company's own workers for installing a new machine
w: Installation wages are a directly attributable cost of bringing the machine into working condition, so they are added to its cost.

s: A firm buys a second-hand truck for ₹6 lakh and spends ₹80,000 on overhauling the engine before putting it on the road. Six months later it spends ₹12,000 on routine servicing. Correct treatment?
o: ₹80,000 capitalised; ₹12,000 expensed
₹80,000 expensed; ₹12,000 capitalised
Both capitalised
Both expensed
w: Repairs needed to make a second-hand asset usable at the time of purchase are part of its cost. Routine servicing after it is in use is revenue expenditure.

s: Which of the following is a revenue receipt?
o: Loan received from a bank
Insurance claim received for stock destroyed by fire
Sale proceeds of old machinery
Insurance claim received for a building destroyed by fire
w: A claim for stock replaces revenue-type assets, so it is a revenue receipt (shown in P&L). Proceeds from fixed assets, loans and claims on fixed assets are capital receipts.

s: A company capitalised ₹10 lakh of routine maintenance on its plant. Effect if not corrected?
o: Profit understated and assets overstated by ₹10 lakh, and the Trial Balance will disagree
Profit overstated by ₹10 lakh, and the Trial Balance will disagree by the same amount
No effect on profit, since the money was spent anyway and only its classification differs
Profit and fixed assets are both overstated by ₹10 lakh (less any depreciation on it), and the Trial Balance agrees
w: Treating revenue expenditure as capital is an error of principle: expenses fall (profit up) and the asset rises. Both sides were posted, so the TB agrees.

s: Under AS 10, which of these is NOT included in the cost of an item of PPE?
o: Import duty that cannot be refunded
Initial estimate of the cost of dismantling the asset at the end of its life
Professional fees of the engineer who designed the installation
Cost of advertising the new product the machine will make
w: Costs of introducing a new product or service, including advertising and promotion, are excluded. Non-refundable duties, decommissioning estimates and directly attributable professional fees are included.

s: GST of ₹1.8 lakh is paid on purchase of a machine of ₹10 lakh, and full input tax credit is available. Freight is ₹20,000. At what amount is the machine capitalised?
w: Refundable or creditable taxes (GST with ITC) are excluded from cost. Freight is included. Cost = 10,00,000 + 20,000 = ₹10,20,000.

s:
Consider the following:
1. Heavy advertising for launching a new product can be carried forward as deferred revenue expenditure under current accounting standards.
2. Interest on a loan taken to construct a factory, for the construction period, is capital expenditure.
3. Profit on sale of an old machine is a capital profit.
4. Replacement of a major component that extends the asset's life is capital expenditure.
Which are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 4 only
w: AS 26 requires advertising and promotion costs to be expensed when incurred, so they can't be carried forward (1 wrong). Borrowing cost on a qualifying asset during construction is capitalised (AS 16), profit on sale of a fixed asset is a capital profit, and replacing a major component that extends life is capitalised.

s: A bill was drawn on 23 November 2024 payable two months after date. 26 January is a public holiday. What is the due date?
o: 27 January 2025
25 January 2025
26 January 2025
24 January 2025
w: 23 Jan 2025 + 3 days of grace = 26 Jan 2025, a public holiday. Under Section 25 of the NI Act the bill is payable on the preceding business day, 25 January 2025.

s: A bill dated 31 January 2026 is payable one month after date. Its due date is:
o: 2 March 2026
4 March 2026
3 March 2026
28 February 2026
w: One calendar month from 31 Jan: February has no 31st, so take 28 Feb 2026. Add 3 days of grace = 3 March 2026.

s: Vertex Engineering drew a bill on 10 January 2026 payable 90 days after date. Ignoring holidays, the due date is:
o: 12 April 2026
13 April 2026
10 April 2026
11 April 2026
w: Exclude the date of drawing: Jan 11–31 = 21 days, Feb = 28 (total 49), Mar = 31 (total 80), plus 10 days of April = 90 → 10 April. Add 3 days of grace → 13 April 2026.

s: A bill payable 'two months after sight' is drawn on 20 February 2026 and accepted on 5 March 2026. Its due date is:
o: 23 April 2026
20 April 2026
w: For after-sight bills, time runs from the date of acceptance (sight): 5 March + 2 months = 5 May + 3 days of grace = 8 May 2026.

s: Three group companies face a cash crunch. X draws a bill on Y; Y accepts though no goods are sold; X discounts it with a bank and shares the proceeds with Y. The credit officer says 'Y legally accepted it, so it is a genuine trade bill.' Which is correct?
o: It is void for want of consideration and cannot be enforced by anyone, including the discounting bank
It automatically becomes a demand bill, because no goods were supplied and so no credit period exists
It is an accommodation bill: enforceable by a holder in due course, but with no trade behind it and higher credit risk
It is a genuine trade bill, because acceptance by the drawee is conclusive proof of an underlying sale
w: An accommodation bill is drawn and accepted without consideration to raise funds. It can be enforced by a holder in due course for value, but there is no self-liquidating trade transaction behind it. Banks are advised not to discount accommodation bills.

s: Horizon Traders discounted a ₹1,00,000, 90-day bill receivable with its bank at 12% p.a. with 60 days to run. Which entry does Horizon pass?
o: Bank A/c Dr ₹98,027; Discount A/c Dr ₹1,973; To Bills Receivable A/c ₹1,00,000
Bank A/c Dr ₹97,041; Discount A/c Dr ₹2,959; To Sales A/c ₹1,00,000
Bank A/c Dr ₹1,00,000; To Bills Receivable A/c ₹1,00,000
Bills Receivable A/c Dr ₹1,00,000; To Bank A/c ₹98,027; To Discount A/c ₹1,973
w: Discount = 1,00,000 × 12% × 60/365 = ₹1,973 (rounded). Bank receives ₹98,027. The bill (asset) is replaced by cash; discount is a finance cost. Sales were recorded when the goods were sold.

s: A bill receivable that had been discounted with the bank is dishonoured on maturity; the bank pays noting charges of ₹100. In the drawer's books the entry is:
o: Drawee's A/c Dr (bill amount + ₹100); To Bank A/c
Bills Receivable A/c Dr; To Bank A/c
Drawee's A/c Dr; To Bills Receivable A/c
Bank A/c Dr; To Drawee's A/c
w: The bill is no longer in the drawer's B/R account (it was discounted). The bank recovers the amount plus noting charges from the drawer, and the drawer in turn charges the drawee.

s: The acceptor of a ₹50,000 bill pays it one month before maturity, and the holder allows a rebate of ₹500. In the holder's books the entry is:
o: Cash Dr ₹49,500; To Bills Receivable ₹49,500
Bills Payable Dr ₹50,000; To Cash ₹49,500; To Rebate ₹500
Cash Dr ₹49,500; Rebate on Bills Dr ₹500; To Bills Receivable ₹50,000
Cash Dr ₹50,000; To Bills Receivable ₹49,500; To Rebate ₹500
w: This is retiring a bill. The holder allows a rebate (expense to him); the acceptor records the rebate as income.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A promissory note contains an unconditional promise; a bill contains an unconditional order.
2. A bill must be accepted by the drawee before it binds him; a promissory note needs no acceptance.
3. A cheque is entitled to three days of grace.
4. A promissory note can be made payable to bearer on demand by any trader.
Which are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
w: Cheques are always payable on demand, with no grace days (3 wrong). Section 31 of the RBI Act bars anyone other than RBI (and the Government in specified cases) from issuing promissory notes payable to bearer on demand (4 wrong).

s: When a bill of exchange is sent to the bank for collection, the drawer passes:
o: Bills Sent for Collection A/c Dr; To Bills Receivable A/c
Bank A/c Dr; To Bills Receivable A/c (as if already collected)
No entry at all until the bank actually collects the amount
Bills Receivable A/c Dr; To Bank A/c (on handing over)
w: The bill moves from 'in hand' to 'with bank for collection'. When the bank collects: Bank A/c Dr; To Bills Sent for Collection A/c.

s: Which of the following is correct about noting of a dishonoured bill?
o: It is done by a notary public, and noting charges paid by the holder are ultimately recoverable from the drawee
It is done by the bank, and the noting charges are always borne by the collecting bank
It is compulsory for every dishonoured cheque before a complaint can be filed
It is done by the drawer himself, and the noting charges are a loss to the drawer
w: A notary public records the dishonour (noting); a protest is the formal certificate. Noting charges are paid by the holder and charged to the party liable.

s: A bank finds that five unrelated borrowers submitted invoices from suppliers that do not exist on GSTN, funds were withdrawn within 48 hours, and stock statements were identical across industries; concurrent audit flagged nothing. The Board appoints a forensic auditor. Which approach best establishes a coordinated fraud?
o: Compare each account's interest yield with industry averages and quantify the revenue leakage
Trace end-use of funds, verify supplier existence, examine digital evidence and rebuild the transaction trail before fixing responsibility
Review branch profitability, staff appraisal ratings and whether sanctions exceeded delegated powers
Recompute drawing power from stock statements and increase provisioning under IRAC norms
w: A forensic audit gathers evidence that can be used in legal proceedings: money trail, document genuineness, digital trail, and links between parties. Provisioning or profitability reviews don't prove fraud.

s: Which statement about concurrent audit in banks is correct?
o: It is a statutory audit whose auditors need RBI approval under Section 30 of the BR Act
It is conducted only once a year, after the balance sheet date, by the central auditors
It is an inspection carried out by RBI officials under Section 35 of the BR Act
It examines transactions at or close to the time they take place and is a part of the bank's internal audit system
w: Concurrent audit is a continuous, early-warning check that forms part of internal audit. Statutory auditors (Sec 30) give the year-end opinion; RBI inspects under Sec 35.

s: The Long Form Audit Report (LFAR) in banks is submitted by:
o: Concurrent auditors, to the branch manager every month
Internal auditors, to the Audit Committee of the Board only
Statutory auditors, in addition to their audit report on the accounts
RBI inspectors, to the bank's Board after inspection
w: LFAR is prepared by statutory central and branch auditors in RBI-prescribed format, covering advances, deposits, internal controls and other areas, alongside the main audit report.

s: Under RBI's 2021 guidelines on appointment of statutory auditors of banks, an audit firm can be appointed for:
o: A continuous period of five years, followed by a cooling-off period of two years
One year at a time, renewable indefinitely as long as RBI approves each year
A continuous period of three years, after which it is not eligible for re-appointment for six years
Ten years, subject to fresh RBI approval and a performance review every year
w: RBI's April 2021 guidelines fix the tenure of SCAs/SAs at three continuous years, subject to satisfying eligibility norms each year, followed by a cooling-off period of six years.

s:
Match the legal provisions of the Banking Regulation Act:
P. Form of balance sheet and P&L of banks
Q. Audit of banks; approval of auditors
R. Inspection by RBI
o: P – Section 35; Q – Section 30; R – Section 29
P – Section 29; Q – Section 30; R – Section 35
P – Section 29; Q – Section 35; R – Section 30
P – Section 30; Q – Section 29; R – Section 35
w: Sec 29 requires accounts in the Third Schedule forms; Sec 30 deals with audit and RBI approval of auditors; Sec 35 empowers RBI to inspect banks.

s: What is the primary feature of Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA)?
o: The frequency and depth of audit of each unit depend on its assessed risk, not a uniform calendar
Only branches showing losses or rising NPAs are audited during the year
Every branch is audited every month regardless of its size or business profile
Audit is replaced by quarterly self-certification of controls by branch managers
w: RBIA allocates audit resources to high-risk branches and activities (business risk and control risk), as guided by RBI since 2002.

s: Regarding inter-branch accounts in banks, which statement is correct?
o: Banks must make 100% provision for net debit balances in inter-branch accounts outstanding for more than one year
Unreconciled credit balances must be taken to income after six months of being outstanding
Inter-branch accounts need to be reconciled only at the year-end, before the statutory audit
Unreconciled debit entries carry no risk as both branches belong to the same bank
w: Long-pending debits in inter-branch accounts can conceal frauds or losses. RBI requires full provision for net debit balances outstanding beyond one year; credit balances are not taken to income.

s: In bank treasury, why are front office, mid office and back office kept separate?
o: To give each office the power to approve and settle its own deals without delay
To allow the back office to take trading positions whenever the dealers are absent
To ensure internal control: dealers deal, the mid office monitors risk and limits, and the back office independently confirms, settles and accounts
Because RBI requires the three offices to be located in different cities for safety
w: Separation of duties prevents one person both dealing and settling or recording; that segregation is a key control against fraud.

s: In bank accounting, a 'composite voucher' is used when:
o: Cash is deposited by a single customer into his own savings account
One debit or credit is matched by several entries, so a single voucher records multiple accounts
The voucher has to be signed by two officers under maker–checker
The day book does not balance and a difference has to be carried
w: A composite (transfer) voucher records a transaction affecting several accounts in one voucher, e.g. salary credit to many staff accounts from one debit.

s: Which of the following is NOT a typical back-office function in a bank?
o: Settlement of NEFT, RTGS and clearing
Preparing MIS and regulatory returns
Reconciliation of nostro and inter-branch accounts
Meeting walk-in customers to sell new products
w: Selling to customers is a front-office function. Reconciliation, settlement, accounting and reporting are back-office functions.

s: Opening stock ₹17,000; purchases ₹52,000; wages ₹8,000; carriage inward ₹2,000; sales ₹1,10,000; returns inward ₹5,000; carriage outward ₹3,000; closing stock ₹20,000. What is the gross profit?
w: COGS = 17,000 + 52,000 + 8,000 + 2,000 − 20,000 = 59,000. Net sales = 1,10,000 − 5,000 = 1,05,000. GP = 46,000. Carriage outward is a selling expense (P&L), not in COGS.

s: Net sales ₹18 crore; GP ratio 25% on sales; opening stock ₹2.10 crore; net purchases ₹11.80 crore; carriage inward ₹40 lakh. What is the closing stock?
o: ₹1.50 crore
₹0.40 crore
₹0.80 crore
₹1.20 crore
w: COGS = 75% of 18 = 13.50. Goods available = 2.10 + 11.80 + 0.40 = 14.30. Closing stock = 14.30 − 13.50 = ₹0.80 crore.

s: Goods costing ₹32 lakh (price ₹40 lakh) were sent on approval on 28 March and recorded as sales; the customer had neither approved nor rejected them by 31 March. The correct treatment is:
o: Keep the sale but create a provision of ₹8 lakh for the unrealised profit margin
Keep the sale, because the goods physically left the warehouse before 31 March
Reverse the sale and include the goods in closing stock at ₹40 lakh (sale price)
Reverse the ₹40 lakh sale and include the goods in closing stock at ₹32 lakh (cost)
w: Risks and rewards have not passed, so it is not a sale. The goods are still the seller's stock, valued at cost (or NRV if lower), not at sale price.

s: Which of the following appears on the DEBIT side of the Trading Account?
o: Carriage outward on goods sold
Carriage inward on raw materials
Discount allowed to customers
Salaries of office staff
w: Direct expenses that bring goods to saleable condition and location (carriage inward, wages, factory power) go to Trading. The others are indirect expenses for the P&L.

s: Debtors ₹1,00,000; further bad debts ₹2,000; provision for doubtful debts to be 5% of debtors; existing provision ₹3,000; bad debts already in the trial balance ₹1,500. What is the total charge to the P&L for bad and doubtful debts?
w: New provision = 5% × (1,00,000 − 2,000) = 4,900. Charge = 1,500 + 2,000 + 4,900 − 3,000 = ₹5,400. Forgetting the old provision gives 8,400.

s: Which item is NOT debited to a partnership firm's Profit & Loss Appropriation Account?
o: Amount transferred to General Reserve
Interest on partners' capital
Interest on a loan advanced by a partner to the firm
Salary payable to a working partner
w: Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit (debited to the P&L A/c), payable even if there is a loss. The others are appropriations of profit.

s: At year-end Delta Ltd. has outstanding salary, prepaid insurance, interest accrued but not due on investments, and depreciation on plant. The accountant wants to adjust only depreciation because the others involve no cash this year. Which is correct?
o: Adjustments are optional if the trial balance has already agreed
Only depreciation needs adjustment, because the others involve no immediate cash flow
Only outstanding salary needs adjustment, because it is a legal liability to employees
All four need adjustment entries under the accrual basis, whatever the timing of cash
w: Accrual accounting records income and expenses in the period they relate to. Outstanding and prepaid expenses and accrued income are all adjusted at year-end, not just depreciation.

s: Rent of ₹60,000 is paid for 15 months from 1 January 2025; the year ends 31 March 2025. How much rent is charged to the P&L for the year and how much is prepaid?
o: ₹60,000 to P&L; nil prepaid
₹48,000 to P&L; ₹12,000 prepaid
₹12,000 to P&L; ₹48,000 prepaid
₹36,000 to P&L; ₹24,000 prepaid
w: Monthly rent = 60,000/15 = 4,000. Jan–Mar = 3 months = ₹12,000 expense. The remaining 12 months (₹48,000) is a prepaid expense (current asset).

s: A firm has opening cash of ₹50,000, cash receipts from sales ₹2,50,000, cash expenses ₹1,80,000 and drawings ₹30,000. Closing cash is:
Stock costing ₹1,00,000 was destroyed by fire; the insurer admitted a claim of ₹70,000. How is this shown in the final accounts?
o: Only ₹30,000 is debited to the Trading A/c and nothing else is recorded
Closing stock is increased by ₹70,000 and the loss is ignored
₹1,00,000 is debited to the P&L A/c and ₹70,000 credited to Capital
Trading A/c Cr ₹1,00,000; P&L Dr ₹30,000; claim ₹70,000 as an asset
w: The goods are removed from the Trading A/c (credited at cost), the uninsured part is a loss in the P&L, and the admitted claim is a current asset until received.

s: GP is 25% on sales. What is the equivalent mark-up on cost?
w: If sales are 100, GP 25, cost 75: 25/75 = 33⅓% on cost. (A 25% mark-up on cost would be 20% on sales.)

s: Galaxy Ltd. offered 2,40,000 shares; applications were received for 3,60,000. Applications for 40,000 shares were rejected and the rest got pro-rata allotment. Mr Arjun applied for 18,000 shares. How many does he get?
o: 12,000 shares
14,400 shares
15,000 shares
13,500 shares
w: Accepted applications = 3,60,000 − 40,000 = 3,20,000 for 2,40,000 shares → 3 : 4. 18,000 × 3/4 = 13,500. Using all 3,60,000 (ratio 2/3) gives 12,000, the trap.

s: In the same allotment (application money ₹4 per share), how much excess application money from Mr Arjun is available to adjust against allotment?
w: He paid 18,000 × ₹4 = 72,000 but needed only 13,500 × ₹4 = 54,000 on application. The excess ₹18,000 is adjusted towards allotment money due.

s: 1,000 equity shares of ₹10 issued at a premium of ₹2 (payable on allotment). Application ₹3, allotment ₹5 (incl. premium), final call ₹4. A shareholder paid only the application money and the shares were forfeited after the final call. The forfeiture entry credits Share Forfeiture with:
o: ₹3,000, after debiting Share Capital ₹3,000 only
₹3,000, after debiting Share Capital ₹10,000 and Securities Premium ₹2,000
₹3,000, after debiting Share Capital ₹12,000
₹5,000, after debiting Share Capital ₹10,000 only
w: Share Capital is debited with the called-up ₹10,000; Securities Premium ₹2,000 is debited because the premium was never received; allotment (₹5,000) and call (₹4,000) unpaid are credited; Share Forfeiture gets the amount received, ₹3,000.

s: Those 1,000 forfeited shares (forfeiture balance ₹3,000) are reissued as fully paid at ₹8 each. What is transferred to Capital Reserve?
o: Nil
w: Discount on reissue = ₹2 × 1,000 = ₹2,000, met from the forfeiture account. The balance ₹1,000 is a capital profit, transferred to Capital Reserve.

s: Zenstar Ltd. forfeited shares of ₹10 each (issued at ₹12) after the holder paid application and allotment (including the premium) but not the final call. Which treatment is correct?
o: Share Capital is debited only with the amount actually received from the holder
Share Capital is debited with the called-up amount; Securities Premium is not touched
Securities Premium is always debited on forfeiture whether or not it was received
Calls in arrears never appear in a forfeiture entry
w: Premium already received stays in Securities Premium. Share Capital is debited with the called-up value; unpaid calls are credited; the amount received goes to Share Forfeiture.

s:
Delta Infrastructure has 10% cumulative preference capital of ₹15 crore; no dividend was paid for two years due to losses. Profits are now adequate. Which statements are correct?
1. Preference holders automatically become equity holders after two years of unpaid dividend.
2. Arrears must ordinarily be paid before any equity dividend.
3. Arrears represent accumulated contractual preference rights.
4. Non-payment reduces the paid-up preference capital.
o: 1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
w: Cumulative dividend accumulates and ranks ahead of equity dividend. Non-payment for 2 years gives preference holders voting rights on all resolutions, not conversion to equity; capital is unaffected.

s:
For which purposes can Securities Premium be used under Section 52?
1. Writing off preliminary expenses.
2. Paying cash dividend.
3. Issuing fully paid bonus shares.
4. Writing off commission paid on issue of shares.
5. Buy-back of the company's own shares.
o: All five
1, 3, 4 and 5 only
2, 3 and 5 only
1, 2, 3 and 4 only
w: Sec 52 lists bonus issue, preliminary expenses, issue expenses/commission/discount, premium on redemption, and buy-back (Sec 68). It cannot be used for cash dividends.

s:
InnovateX issues equity shares to its Chief Scientist in exchange for a patented technology instead of cash. Which statements are correct?
1. Existing shareholders' percentage may be diluted.
2. The issue brings fresh cash into the company.
3. The shares are issued for intellectual property (sweat equity).
4. Such issues can help retain skilled employees.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
w: Sweat equity is issued for know-how or IPR, so no cash comes in. It increases the number of shares (dilution) and is used to reward and retain talent.

s: Which statement on preference shares under the Companies Act, 2013 is NOT correct?
o: Preference shares must normally be redeemed within 20 years of issue
A company may issue irredeemable preference shares with Board approval
Preference holders can vote on all resolutions if their dividend remains unpaid for two years or more
Preference shares carry preferential rights as to dividend and repayment of capital
w: Sec 55 prohibits irredeemable preference shares. Maximum tenure is 20 years (30 for infrastructure).

s: Galaxy Ltd. has authorised capital ₹20 crore, issued capital of 1.5 crore shares of ₹10, some calls unpaid and some shares forfeited but not reissued. A trainee wants to cut 'issued capital' because of forfeiture. Which is correct?
o: Issued capital automatically falls once any shares are forfeited by the Board
Authorised capital always equals paid-up capital at the year-end
Forfeiture affects only the Securities Premium Account and nothing else
Paid-up capital falls on forfeiture; issued capital does not change merely because of it
w: Paid-up = called-up less arrears (forfeited amounts move to Share Forfeiture). Authorised is the MoA ceiling; issued is what was offered.

s: The maximum amount of share capital a company is authorised to issue, as stated in its Memorandum of Association, is called:
o: Authorised (nominal) capital
Issued capital
Subscribed capital
Called-up capital
w: Authorised capital is the ceiling in the MoA; issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital cannot exceed it.

s: The Food Corporation of India is an example of a:
o: Private company limited by shares
Section 8 non-profit company
Statutory corporation created by a special Act of Parliament
Government company registered under the Companies Act, 2013
w: FCI was set up under the Food Corporations Act, 1964, a special statute, like LIC (LIC Act 1956).

s: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company becomes a subsidiary of another when the other company:
o: Holds at least 20% of its voting power
Supplies more than half of its raw materials
Has at least one common director on its Board
Controls its board composition or more than half of its total voting power
w: Sec 2(87): control of board composition or more than half the total voting power (alone or with subsidiaries). 20% is the associate (significant influence) test.
