s: Equity shares with differential voting rights (DVR) can be issued up to what limit under the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules?
o: 50% of authorised capital
26% of total post-issue paid-up equity share capital
74% of total post-issue paid-up equity share capital
10% of net worth
w: The 2019 amendment raised the DVR limit from 26% to 74% of total post-issue paid-up equity capital (including DVRs).

s: A public issue is 'over-subscribed' when:
o: Applications received exceed the number of shares offered
The shares are listed at a premium on the first day
The issue price is above the face value of the shares
Applications received are less than the minimum subscription
w: Over-subscription means demand exceeds the issue size; the company may reject some, allot fully to some, or allot pro-rata.

s:
Sigma Ltd. (share capital ₹25 crore, securities premium ₹18 crore, general reserve ₹40 crore, cash ₹3 crore) plans fully paid bonus shares instead of a cash dividend. Which statements are correct?
1. Proportionate ownership remains unchanged.
2. Liquidity improves because bonus shares bring in cash.
3. Paid-up capital rises without any increase in total shareholders' funds.
4. EPS may fall immediately if profits remain the same.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
w: Bonus capitalises reserves: no cash comes in, total equity is unchanged, every holder gets shares in proportion, and the larger share count dilutes EPS.

s: A listed company makes a rights issue of 1 share for every 4 held at ₹180; the market price before the issue is ₹260. What is the theoretical ex-rights price and the value of one right per existing share?
o: TERP ₹244; value of right ₹64 per existing share
TERP ₹260; rights have no value because the price is unchanged
TERP ₹244; value of right ₹16 per existing share
TERP ₹220; value of right ₹40 per existing share
w: TERP = (4 × 260 + 180)/5 = 1,220/5 = 244. Value per new share = 244 − 180 = 64; as 4 existing shares give one right, value per existing share = 64/4 = ₹16.

s: Mr Arjun holds 8,000 shares; the company makes a 1-for-4 rights issue at ₹180 when the market price is ₹260. He neither subscribes nor renounces his rights. What is the most likely consequence?
o: His ownership percentage falls and he loses the value of the rights he let lapse
He loses all voting rights on his existing shares
His wealth necessarily rises because prices always go up after a rights issue
His existing shares become invalid until he exercises the rights
w: Others subscribe, so his percentage falls; and the market price falls towards TERP (₹244) while he gets nothing for his entitlement. Renouncing (selling) the rights would have preserved value.

s: ABC Technologies: PAT ₹48 crore; 2 crore equity shares all year; ₹20 crore convertible debentures (post-tax interest ₹1.2 crore a year) converted into 20 lakh shares on 1 October. What are basic and diluted EPS?
o: Basic ₹22.86; Diluted ₹22.86
Basic ₹21.82; Diluted ₹22.09
Basic ₹24.00; Diluted ₹21.82
Basic ₹22.86; Diluted ₹22.09
w: Weighted shares = 2 + 0.2 × 6/12 = 2.1 crore; basic = 48/2.1 = 22.86. Diluted treats the debentures as converted from the start: earnings 48 + 0.6 (half-year interest saved) = 48.6; shares 2.2 crore → 22.09.

s: Vardhman Chemicals buys machinery for ₹1.20 crore; books use SLM over 10 years and tax uses WDV at 40%; tax rate 30%. What deferred tax arises at the end of year 1?
o: No deferred tax, as it is a permanent difference
Deferred tax asset of ₹10.8 lakh
Deferred tax liability of ₹10.8 lakh
Deferred tax liability of ₹36 lakh
w: Book depreciation 12 lakh; tax depreciation 48 lakh; timing difference 36 lakh makes taxable profit lower now → DTL = 36 × 30% = ₹10.8 lakh, reversing in later years.

s: Orion Industries: accounting profit before tax ₹96 crore; taxable profit ₹82 crore, the difference being entirely due to higher tax depreciation; tax rate 30%. What is the total tax expense in the P&L?
o: ₹33.0 crore (current ₹28.8 + deferred ₹4.2)
₹28.8 crore (current tax ₹24.6 crore + deferred tax ₹4.2 crore)
₹24.6 crore, being current tax only
₹20.4 crore (current ₹24.6 − deferred ₹4.2)
w: Current tax = 82 × 30% = 24.6. Timing difference 14 → DTL 4.2. Total = 28.8 = 96 × 30%, matching tax to book profit.

s: Which of the following gives rise to a deferred tax ASSET under AS 22?
o: Bonus provided in the books but allowed for tax only when paid next year
Dividend income that is exempt from tax
A penalty paid for violating a law, which is never allowed for tax
Tax depreciation exceeding book depreciation in the early years
w: Disallowed now, allowed later → taxable profit higher now → DTA. Higher tax depreciation creates a DTL. Penalties and exempt income are permanent differences: no deferred tax.

s:
Which statements about deferred tax are correct?
1. Current tax is based on taxable profit.
2. Deferred tax arises because depreciation differences are timing differences that reverse.
3. Deferred tax is recognised on permanent differences.
4. A DTA on carried-forward business losses needs virtual certainty supported by convincing evidence.
o: 2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
w: Permanent differences never reverse, so no deferred tax (3 wrong). Unabsorbed depreciation and carried-forward losses need virtual certainty (AS 22).

s: TechNova grants 2,50,000 options vesting after 3 years; exercise price ₹220, market price at grant ₹310. HR says no entry is needed until exercise. Which is correct?
o: Option value is expensed over the 3-year vesting period, with a credit to equity
ESOP expense is recognised only if the company declares a dividend
No entry is needed until the options are exercised and cash is received
The ₹90 difference is recorded immediately as goodwill
w: Share-based payments are employee cost for services received over the vesting period; the credit goes to 'Employee Stock Options Outstanding' within equity.

s: Under Section 63 of the Companies Act, 2013, fully paid bonus shares may be issued out of:
o: Capital reserve arising on revaluation of fixed assets only
Revaluation reserve, free reserves and securities premium
Profits of the current year that have not yet been audited
Free reserves, securities premium account and capital redemption reserve
w: Bonus shares cannot be issued out of reserves created by revaluation of assets. Free reserves, securities premium and CRR are permitted sources.

s: Which reserve can a company use to declare dividend?
o: Capital Redemption Reserve
Revaluation Reserve
General Reserve (a free reserve)
Securities Premium Account
w: Dividend can come from current/past profits after depreciation or free reserves. Revaluation reserve, CRR and securities premium are not free reserves.

s: While preparing Nova Industries' Schedule III balance sheet, which classification is correct?
o: Trade receivables are shown without any ageing information
A security deposit recoverable after four years is shown under current assets
Short-term and long-term borrowings are clubbed under non-current liabilities
Current maturities of long-term debt are shown under short-term borrowings in current liabilities
w: Since the 2021 amendment, current maturities of long-term borrowings appear under short-term borrowings. Deposits recoverable after 12 months are non-current; receivables and payables need ageing.

s: As per Section 2(40) of the Companies Act, which document is NOT part of a company's 'financial statements'?
o: Cash Flow Statement
Notes to accounts
Directors' Report
Statement of Profit and Loss
w: Financial statements = balance sheet, P&L, cash flow statement, statement of changes in equity and explanatory notes. The Directors' Report and Auditor's Report accompany them but are not part of them.

s:
Which items are included under 'Employee Benefits Expense' in the Statement of Profit and Loss?
1. Wages and salaries.
2. Contribution to provident and other funds.
3. Share-based payment (ESOP) expense.
4. Staff welfare expenses.
o: 1 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 4 only
w: Schedule III lists all four under employee benefits expense.

s: If a company converts part of its equity into a loan from shareholders, the balance sheet shows:
o: A decrease in shareholders' funds and an increase in borrowings, with total assets unchanged
No change in any component, since it is only a reclassification within equity
An increase in both assets and shareholders' funds
A decrease in cash and in shareholders' funds
w: Equity moves to debt; no cash moves, so total assets stay the same.

s: During the year Delta Ltd. (a manufacturer) had: cash from customers, purchase of plant, sale of old machinery, dividend received on investments and issue of equity shares. A trainee puts the sale of old machinery under operating activities because it generated cash. Correct classification?
o: Investing activity
Financing activity
Extraordinary activity shown separately below financing
Operating activity
w: Purchase or sale of long-term assets is investing. Classification depends on the nature of the transaction, not merely on cash movement.

s: NPBT ₹12 crore; depreciation ₹1.8 crore; profit on sale of machinery ₹0.75 crore; increase in trade receivables ₹1.5 crore; increase in trade payables ₹0.9 crore. Cash generated from operations (indirect method) is:
o: ₹13.95 crore
₹15.45 crore
₹12.45 crore
₹10.95 crore
w: 12 + 1.8 − 0.75 − 1.5 + 0.9 = ₹12.45 crore. Depreciation added (non-cash), profit on sale removed (investing), increase in receivables deducted, increase in payables added.

s: For a NON-financial company, how are 'interest paid on long-term borrowings' and 'dividend received on investments' classified under AS 3?
o: Interest paid – investing; dividend received – operating
Interest paid – operating; dividend received – financing
Interest paid – financing; dividend received – investing
Both – operating
w: For non-financial enterprises, interest and dividends paid are financing cash flows (cost of funds); interest and dividends received are investing (returns on investments).

s: For a commercial BANK, interest paid on deposits and interest received on advances are classified as:
o: Investing activities
Financing activities
Operating activities
Financing and investing activities respectively
w: For financial enterprises, borrowing and lending are the main revenue-producing activities, so interest paid and received are operating cash flows.

s:
Which of these transactions will NOT appear in the cash flow statement but should be disclosed?
1. Purchase of land by issuing equity shares to the seller.
2. Issue of bonus shares.
3. Conversion of debentures into equity shares.
4. Purchase of machinery for cash.
o: 2 and 3 only
4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
w: Non-cash investing and financing transactions are excluded from the statement and disclosed elsewhere. A cash purchase of machinery is an investing outflow.

s: A company bought new machinery for ₹2,00,000 and sold an old machine (book value ₹40,000) for ₹50,000. The net cash flow from investing activities is:
o: Inflow of ₹50,000
Outflow of ₹1,50,000
Outflow of ₹1,60,000
Outflow of ₹2,00,000
w: Investing shows actual proceeds: −2,00,000 + 50,000 = −1,50,000. The ₹10,000 profit is deducted from operating activities under the indirect method.

s: Under the indirect method, which adjustment is correct?
o: Profit on sale of an investment is added to net profit
A decrease in inventory is added to net profit
An increase in trade receivables is added to net profit
A decrease in trade payables is added to net profit
w: Lower inventory releases cash (add). Higher receivables tie up cash (deduct), lower payables use cash (deduct), and profit on sale of investments is investing (deduct).

s: Which statement on cash equivalents under AS 3 is correct?
o: They generally mature within three months of acquisition, and their components must be disclosed
Equity shares of listed companies are treated as cash equivalents because they are liquid
Cash equivalents need not be reconciled with balance sheet items
Any fixed deposit, whatever its maturity, is a cash equivalent
w: Cash equivalents carry insignificant risk of change in value; equity investments are excluded. The enterprise discloses the components and reconciles them with the balance sheet.

s: Which companies are exempt from preparing a cash flow statement under the Companies Act, 2013?
o: All private companies
All unlisted companies
Companies whose turnover is below ₹500 crore
One Person Companies, small companies and dormant companies
w: Sec 2(40) proviso: the financial statements of an OPC, a small company and a dormant company may exclude the cash flow statement.

s: ABC Bank sanctioned a ₹12 crore term loan; it has been in the Doubtful category for two years (D2). Realisable value of security is ₹7 crore. What is the required provision under IRAC norms?
o: ₹7.8 crore
₹4.6 crore
₹12 crore
₹5 crore
w: Unsecured portion ₹5 crore → 100% = 5.0. Secured portion ₹7 crore in D2 → 40% = 2.8. Total ₹7.8 crore.

s: Under the Third Schedule, 'Bills Purchased and Discounted' by a bank are shown under:
o: Advances (Schedule 9)
Investments (Schedule 8)
Other Assets (Schedule 11)
Contingent Liabilities (Schedule 12)
w: Bills purchased and discounted are a form of credit to customers, so they appear as the first item of Advances.

s: Under which head does a bank show 'Acceptances, endorsements and other obligations' (e.g. LCs, bills accepted on behalf of customers)?
o: Borrowings (Schedule 4)
Deposits (Schedule 3)
Contingent liabilities (Schedule 12)
Other liabilities and provisions (Schedule 5)
w: The bank becomes liable only if the customer fails, so these are contingent liabilities, not actual liabilities.

s: A bank has given a festival advance (interest-free) and a housing loan (interest-bearing) to its staff. As per RBI's instructions, they are shown as:
o: Housing loan under Advances; festival advance under Other Assets
Housing loan under Fixed Assets; festival advance under Other Assets
Both under Advances
Both under Other Assets
w: All interest-bearing staff loans go into Advances (Schedule 9); non-interest-bearing staff advances go into Other Assets (Schedule 11).

s: In a bank's P&L, items such as 'Rent, taxes and lighting' and 'Printing and stationery' are shown under:
o: Provisions and contingencies
Operating expenses (Schedule 16)
Interest expended (Schedule 15)
Other income (Schedule 14), net of recoveries
w: Schedule 16 Operating Expenses covers employee costs, rent, taxes and lighting, printing and stationery, advertisement, depreciation, directors' and auditors' fees, law charges, postage, repairs, insurance and others.

s: Before declaring a dividend, a scheduled commercial bank must transfer to the statutory reserve:
o: No transfer is required if CRAR exceeds 9%
At least 50% of net profit as per the Companies Act
Exactly 10% of net profit as per Section 17 of the BR Act
At least 25% of net profit, as RBI requires (the BR Act says 20%)
w: Section 17(1) requires at least 20%; RBI has directed scheduled commercial banks to transfer at least 25% of net profit.

s: In a bank's financial statements, Schedule 18 generally contains:
o: Notes to accounts
Significant accounting policies
Contingent liabilities
Interest earned
w: Schedule 17 = significant accounting policies; Schedule 18 = notes to accounts (Basel III, NPAs, maturity pattern, exposures and other RBI-required disclosures).

s: A loan becomes NPA on 31 December. Interest of ₹2 lakh for October–December had been credited to income but not realised. The bank should:
o: Reverse the unrealised ₹2 lakh and stop accruing interest to income
Keep the ₹2 lakh but stop accrual from January
Transfer the ₹2 lakh to the statutory reserve
Keep the ₹2 lakh in income and also accrue interest for January–March
w: Income on NPAs is recognised only on realisation. Interest already taken to income but not realised when the account becomes NPA must be reversed.

s: Which item is shown under 'Interest earned' (Schedule 13)?
o: Income on investments in government securities
Commission on letters of credit
Dividend received from a subsidiary
Profit on sale of investments
w: Schedule 13: interest/discount on advances and bills, income on investments, interest on balances with RBI and other inter-bank funds. Commission, profit on sale of investments and dividends from subsidiaries are Other Income (Schedule 14).

s: Refinance obtained by a bank from NABARD against agricultural loans is shown:
o: Under Deposits from other institutions
As a contingent liability in Schedule 12
Under Borrowings, with the advances shown gross
As a deduction from the related Advances
w: RBI's instructions: refinance is shown under 'Borrowings' and advances are shown at the gross amount.

s: Which of the following is shown below the balance sheet total of a bank rather than as a contingent liability?
o: Guarantees given on behalf of constituents
Bills for collection
Liability on partly paid investments
Outstanding forward exchange contracts
w: Bills for collection are shown as a memorandum item below the balance sheet; the bank acts only as an agent and has no liability.

s: A hydroelectric station uses an old device that continuously measures temperature, pressure and voltage, with output as continuously varying signals. A trainee calls it a digital computer because numbers are shown. It is actually:
o: An analog computer, because it processes continuously varying physical quantities
A digital computer, because every computer processes binary data
A mainframe computer, because it runs continuously without stopping
A hybrid computer, because all engineering devices are hybrid
w: Analog computers work on continuous physical quantities; digital computers on discrete binary data; hybrids combine both.

s: In the core banking system of a large bank:
o: There is no central server; each branch works offline and uploads data monthly
Each branch connects through the network to a central server at the bank's data centre
Each branch has its own database server connected directly to every other branch
Two central servers are kept at each branch for redundancy
w: CBS centralises the database at the data centre (with a DR site); branches access it online, enabling anywhere banking.

s: Which is a fundamental difference between manual and computerised accounting?
o: Computerised accounting eliminates the need for vouchers and source documents
Posting, balancing and statements are automatic once data is entered
Manual accounting cannot follow the double-entry system
Computerised accounting automatically detects errors of principle
w: Software automates everything after data entry. Source documents are still needed, and errors of principle or wrong entries are not detected.

s: The main benefit of online (real-time) processing over batch processing in banking is that:
o: It eliminates the need for data backups
Transactions are grouped and processed at the end of the day at lower cost
Each transaction updates the database immediately, so balances are always current
It needs no network connectivity at the branches
w: Real-time processing posts each transaction at once, which supports ATMs, internet banking and any-branch banking. Batch processing accumulates transactions for later processing.

s: A fintech markets itself as a 'Neo Bank' offering instant accounts, virtual debit cards and API payments. Can it independently accept public deposits, lend from them and maintain CRR/SLR?
o: No; but they may issue currency through digital wallets instead
No; they work through partner licensed banks, which hold deposits and do regulated functions
Yes; neo banks get a banking licence automatically after three years of operation
Yes; neo banks function exactly like scheduled commercial banks
w: Indian neo banks are technology platforms without their own banking licence; the partner bank holds deposits, lends and maintains CRR/SLR.

s: Which statement about computerised accounting is NOT correct?
o: It guarantees that financial statements are free from all errors
It provides an audit trail of entries and changes
It needs regular data backups and access controls
It enables reports for any period to be generated instantly
w: Wrong data entry or errors of principle still flow into the statements: 'garbage in, garbage out'. The other statements are correct.

s: The three core objectives of information security in a bank's CBS are:
o: Encryption, firewalls and passwords
Authorisation, accounting and auditing
Confidentiality, integrity and availability
Speed, cost and accuracy
w: The CIA triad. Encryption, firewalls and passwords are controls used to achieve these objectives.

s: Five professionals want limited liability, a separate legal identity, perpetual succession and the ability to own property in the firm's name, without issuing share capital. One says an ordinary partnership already gives all this. Which is correct?
o: An ordinary partnership and an LLP have identical legal characteristics under Indian law
An LLP must first issue share capital and list it before it can commence business
An LLP cannot own property in its own name, so they should form a company
An LLP gives these features; an ordinary partnership has unlimited liability and no separate legal entity
w: Under the LLP Act 2008, an LLP is a body corporate with perpetual succession and limited liability; no share capital is needed. A partnership firm under the 1932 Act has unlimited, joint and several liability.

s: Omega Ltd. has PAT ₹180 crore, negative free cash flow of ₹25 crore, debt-equity 2.8 : 1 and large loan instalments due in six months. Investors press for last year's 45% payout. The CFO advises against it. Which reasoning supports the CFO?
o: Dividends must balance profit with liquidity, debt obligations and future funding needs; accounting profit is not cash
Dividends depend only on accounting profit, so the 45% payout should be maintained this year as well
Once a dividend rate is declared, a profitable company can never reduce it without shareholders' consent
Companies are legally required to pay at least the previous year's dividend once profits are earned
w: Profit may not be available as cash. With negative FCF, high leverage and near-term repayments, conserving cash protects solvency and lenders' covenants.

s: Which statement about the agency problem is NOT correct?
o: It arises because managers (agents) may not always act in shareholders' (principals') interest
It can be completely eliminated by appointing professional managers
Linking managers' pay to share performance can reduce it
Monitoring costs such as audit are a type of agency cost
w: Professional managers are themselves agents; the problem can be reduced by incentives, monitoring and governance, but not eliminated.

s: Shakti Engineering's CSR committee considers: (1) toilets in government schools, (2) a foreign holiday for top distributors, (3) contribution to an approved disaster-relief fund, (4) skill training for unemployed youth. Which qualify as CSR?
o: 2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
4 only
w: Schedule VII covers education and sanitation, disaster relief and livelihood/skill development. A distributors' holiday benefits the business, so it is marketing, not CSR.

s: Vedic Systems Ltd. has net profit of ₹8 crore last year, turnover ₹650 crore and net worth ₹300 crore. Its average net profit for the last three years is ₹6 crore. Which is correct under Section 135?
o: CSR does not apply because turnover is below ₹1,000 crore and net worth is below ₹500 crore
CSR applies because net profit exceeds ₹5 crore; minimum spend is ₹12 lakh (2% of ₹6 crore)
CSR applies and the minimum spend is ₹16 lakh (2% of last year's ₹8 crore)
CSR applies only if all three criteria are met together, so it does not apply here
w: Any one criterion triggers CSR. The spend is 2% of the AVERAGE net profit of the three immediately preceding years: 2% × 6 crore = ₹12 lakh.

s: A company has unspent CSR money relating to an ongoing project at the year-end. Under the Companies Act, it must:
o: Pay it to the Government within 7 days as a penalty for non-spending
Transfer it to an 'Unspent CSR Account' in a scheduled bank within 30 days of the year-end and spend it within 3 years
Credit it back to the Profit and Loss Account as income of the next year
Transfer it to General Reserve and disclose it in the Directors' Report
w: Sec 135(6): unspent amount for an ongoing project goes to the Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of the year-end and must be spent within three years; unspent sums not tied to ongoing projects go to a Schedule VII fund within six months.

s: Members of a Hindu Undivided Family who acquire a right in ancestral property by birth are called:
o: Kartas
Designated partners
Beneficiaries
Coparceners
w: Coparceners have a birthright in coparcenary property (daughters included since 2005). The Karta manages the HUF.

s: Which is the most widely accepted objective of financial management, and why?
o: Sales maximisation, because it raises market share
Profit maximisation, because profit is easy to measure and verify
Dividend maximisation, because shareholders prefer cash every year
Wealth maximisation, because it considers time value of money, risk and long-term value
w: Profit maximisation ignores the timing and risk of returns and is vague. Wealth (share value) maximisation captures both.

s:
Which statements are correct?
1. A private company can have a maximum of 200 members.
2. A One Person Company can be formed only by a natural person who is an Indian citizen.
3. A partnership firm has a legal identity separate from its partners.
4. An LLP must have at least two designated partners, one of whom is resident in India.
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
w: A partnership firm is not a separate legal entity (3 wrong). The others are correct under the Companies Act 2013 and LLP Act 2008.

s: The three core decisions of financial management are:
o: Production, marketing and HR decisions
Budgeting, auditing and taxation decisions
Investment, financing and dividend decisions
Pricing, credit and inventory decisions
w: Where to invest (capital budgeting and working capital), how to finance (capital structure) and how much to distribute (dividend).

s: Nova Engineering has current assets of ₹18 crore, a current ratio of 2 : 1 and a quick ratio of 1.25 : 1. There are no prepaid expenses. What is its inventory?
o: ₹6.75 crore
₹4.50 crore
₹7.20 crore
₹9.00 crore
w: CL = 18 ÷ 2 = ₹9 crore. Quick assets = 1.25 × 9 = ₹11.25 crore. Inventory = CA − quick assets = 18 − 11.25 = ₹6.75 crore.

s: A firm's working capital is ₹6 lakh and its current ratio is 2.5 : 1. What are its current assets?
o: ₹8.4 lakh
₹15 lakh
₹4 lakh
₹10 lakh
w: CA − CL = 6 and CA = 2.5 CL → 1.5 CL = 6 → CL = 4 and CA = 10. (4 lakh is CL, the trap.)

s: Opening debtors ₹2,40,000; closing debtors ₹3,60,000; cash sales ₹5,00,000; total sales ₹20,00,000; year of 365 days. What is the average collection period?
o: 60.8 days
54.75 days
73 days
87.6 days
w: Credit sales = 20,00,000 − 5,00,000 = 15,00,000. Average debtors = (2,40,000 + 3,60,000)/2 = 3,00,000. DTR = 5 times. Collection period = 365/5 = 73 days. Using total sales gives 54.75 days (wrong).

s: A firm has credit sales of ₹10,00,000 and average accounts receivable of ₹1,60,000. Taking 365 days, the average collection period is closest to:
o: 58 days
63 days
6.25 days
44 days
w: DTR = 10,00,000/1,60,000 = 6.25 times. Collection period = 365/6.25 = 58.4 days.

s: Sales are ₹30 lakh with a gross profit of 25% on sales. Opening stock is ₹2.5 lakh and closing stock ₹3.5 lakh. What is the inventory turnover ratio?
o: 8.57 times
10 times
7.5 times
6.43 times
w: COGS = 30 − 25% of 30 = 22.5 lakh. Average stock = (2.5 + 3.5)/2 = 3 lakh. ITR = 22.5/3 = 7.5 times. Using sales (30/3 = 10) is the common mistake.

s: A borrower's PAT is ₹30 lakh, depreciation ₹10 lakh, interest on term loan ₹8 lakh and the term-loan instalment due ₹20 lakh. What is the DSCR?
w: DSCR = (PAT + Depreciation + Interest on TL) ÷ (Interest on TL + Instalment) = (30 + 10 + 8) ÷ (8 + 20) = 48/28 = 1.71. Forgetting to add back interest gives 40/28 = 1.43.

s: For a term-lending banker, which ratio is the most important for judging repayment capacity?
o: Current ratio
Inventory turnover ratio
Gross profit ratio
Debt Service Coverage Ratio
w: Term loans are repaid from cash accruals over years. DSCR shows how many times instalment plus interest is covered by accruals. Current ratio is a working-capital banker's tool.

s: Company X: long-term debt ₹180 crore, shareholders' funds ₹90 crore, interest coverage 6.5 times. Company Y: debt ₹120 crore, funds ₹160 crore, interest coverage 3.2 times. The credit officer prefers Y only because its debt-equity is lower. Which view is sound?
o: Y is always safer, because a lower debt-equity ratio by itself guarantees lower credit risk for the lender
Debt-equity must be read with repayment capacity: X is more leveraged (2 : 1) but covers interest far better than Y (0.75 : 1)
The two ratios measure the same aspect of strength, so X's higher interest coverage can be safely ignored
X should be rejected outright, because any debt-equity above 1 : 1 is unacceptable
w: Debt-equity shows structure (X 2:1, Y 0.75:1); interest coverage and DSCR show ability to service debt. A lending decision weighs both along with cash flows and profitability.

s: A company issues bonus shares in the ratio 2 : 1 by capitalising general reserve. Its debt-equity ratio will:
o: Remain unchanged, because total shareholders' funds do not change
Increase, because the number of equity shares increases
Decrease, because share capital increases threefold
Become zero, because reserves are fully capitalised
w: Bonus issue only transfers reserves to share capital; net worth (equity) stays the same, so D/E is unchanged. EPS and book value per share fall.

s: Current assets ₹4 lakh and current liabilities ₹2 lakh. The firm pays ₹1 lakh to creditors in cash. The new current ratio is:
w: CA = 3, CL = 1 → 3 : 1. When CR is above 1, paying off a current liability raises the ratio. (If CR were below 1, it would fall.)

s: FY 2025: current ratio 2.10, quick ratio 1.28, inventory holding 52 days. FY 2026: current ratio 2.08, quick ratio 0.82, inventory holding 96 days. The borrower says liquidity hasn't changed. Your conclusion:
o: Liquidity has weakened: funds are increasingly locked in slow-moving stock, which the stable current ratio hides
Inventory has no impact on liquidity because it is part of current assets anyway
Liquidity is satisfactory because the current ratio is still above the 2 : 1 benchmark
Quick ratio is irrelevant whenever the current ratio exceeds 2 : 1, so no further analysis is needed
w: Same current ratio but a sharply lower quick ratio and nearly doubled holding period show that inventory is rising as a share of current assets; liquid assets have fallen.

s: EBIT ₹24 crore, interest ₹4 crore, lease rentals ₹2 crore, principal repayment ₹5 crore. Using the simplified formula (EBIT + Lease rentals) ÷ (Interest + Lease rentals + Principal), the fixed-charge coverage ratio is about:
o: 2.36 times
6.00 times
2.18 times
4.33 times
w: (24 + 2) ÷ (4 + 2 + 5) = 26/11 = 2.36. Interest coverage alone (24/4 = 6) overstates comfort because it ignores lease and principal commitments.

s:
Company X: market price ₹480, DPS ₹18. Company Y: market price ₹360, DPS ₹12. Which statements are correct?
1. X's dividend yield is 3.75%.
2. Y's dividend yield is 3.33%.
3. Dividend yield relates dividend to the current market price.
4. A higher DPS always means a higher dividend yield.
o: 1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3 only
w: 18/480 = 3.75%; 12/360 = 3.33%. Yield depends on both DPS and price, so a higher DPS doesn't always mean a higher yield.

s: PAT ₹12 lakh; preference dividend ₹2 lakh; 5 lakh equity shares; market price ₹30. What are EPS and P/E?
o: EPS ₹2; P/E 6.67 times
EPS ₹2; P/E 15 times
EPS ₹2.40; P/E 15 times
EPS ₹2.40; P/E 12.5 times
w: EPS = (12 − 2)/5 = ₹2. P/E = 30/2 = 15. Not deducting preference dividend gives 2.40.

s: Which financial statements are needed to compute Return on Investment (ROCE)?
o: Only the Profit and Loss Account, since return is a profit figure
Only the Balance Sheet, since investment is a balance sheet figure
Only the Cash Flow Statement, since return means cash generated
Both the Profit and Loss Account (for EBIT) and the Balance Sheet (for capital employed)
w: ROI = EBIT ÷ capital employed: the numerator comes from the P&L and the denominator from the Balance Sheet.

s: Which is an essential condition for a meaningful comparison of ratios between two firms or periods?
o: The firms or periods must follow comparable accounting policies and similar bases
Ratios must be calculated by the same analyst for both firms
Only firms listed on the same stock exchange can be compared
Both firms must have exactly the same sales turnover every year
w: Different depreciation or inventory methods, period lengths or classifications distort ratios. Comparable policies and bases matter, not identical size.

s: The Credit Manager boasts that debtors turnover improved from 5 to 8 times. The CRO is not convinced credit management improved. Why?
o: A higher debtors turnover always shows weaker collection efficiency, so the CRO is right to worry
Debtors turnover has no link with working-capital management, so the change is irrelevant here
Ratio analysis is meaningful only for banking companies and not for manufacturing borrowers like this one
The ratio must be read with credit policy, customer mix, seasonality and sales trends; for example, tighter credit may have cut sales
w: A ratio in isolation can mislead; a jump may come from lower credit sales, factoring of receivables, or a seasonal year-end, not better collection.

s: In bank credit appraisal, redeemable preference shares with a residual maturity of 8 years are treated, while computing debt-equity, as:
o: Ignored altogether
Current liabilities
Equity, since they are share capital
Debt (term liability)
w: Banks treat redeemable preference shares maturing within 12 years as term debt; those redeemable after 12 years are treated as quasi-equity.

s: Net sales ₹50 lakh; COGS ₹35 lakh; operating expenses ₹7.5 lakh. What are the operating ratio and the operating profit ratio?
w: Operating ratio = (35 + 7.5)/50 = 85%. Operating profit ratio = 100 − 85 = 15%.

s:
Which pair of transactions REDUCES the current ratio when it is currently 1.8 : 1?
1. Purchase of stock on credit.
2. Payment of a current liability in cash.
3. Purchase of machinery for cash.
4. Issue of equity shares for cash.
o: 3 and 4
2 and 4
1 and 3
1 and 2
w: With CR above 1, adding equal amounts to CA and CL (1) lowers it; paying a current liability (2) raises it; spending cash on a fixed asset (3) lowers CA; issuing shares (4) raises CA.

s: A customer deposits ₹24,000 for 9 months at 8% p.a. simple interest. What interest does he earn?
What is the future value of ₹10,000 after one year at 12% p.a. compounded quarterly?
Loan offers: Bank A 12% p.a. compounded annually; Bank B 11.70% p.a. compounded monthly. Which is cheaper and why?
o: Bank B, because monthly compounding benefits the borrower through smaller payments
Bank A, because Bank B's effective annual rate is about 12.35%
Bank B, because its quoted nominal rate is 0.30% lower than Bank A's
Both cost exactly the same, because the difference in compounding is negligible
w: EAR(B) = (1 + 0.117/12)^12 − 1 ≈ 12.35% > 12%. Compounding frequency raises the true cost, so nominal rates can't be compared directly.

s: Mr Raj invests ₹50,000 at the END of each year for 20 years at 8% compounded annually. The maturity value is closest to:
w: FV of ordinary annuity = 50,000 × [(1.08)^20 − 1]/0.08 = 50,000 × 45.762 = ₹22,88,098. (24,71,146 would be an annuity due; 10,00,000 ignores interest.)

s: ₹10,000 is invested every year for 5 years at 8%. The future value is ₹58,666 if each payment is at the year-end. If each payment is made at the BEGINNING of the year instead, the future value is:
w: Annuity due = ordinary annuity × (1 + r) = 58,666 × 1.08 = ₹63,359. Each payment earns interest for one extra year.

s: A company can buy a production line for ₹47.50 lakh or lease it for ₹12 lakh payable at the end of each year for 5 years. Cost of capital 10%; PVAF (10%, 5) = 3.7908. The Finance Manager rejects the lease because total payments are ₹60 lakh. The correct decision is:
o: Buy, because time value of money does not apply to the purchase of fixed assets
Indifferent, because both options cost the same once spread over 5 years
Lease, because the present value of lease payments (about ₹45.49 lakh) is below ₹47.50 lakh
Buy, because total lease payments of ₹60 lakh exceed the purchase price
w: PV of lease = 12 × 3.7908 = ₹45.49 lakh < ₹47.50 lakh, so leasing is cheaper in today's money.

s: A ₹10 lakh loan at 9% p.a. is repayable in 60 equal monthly instalments. The EMI is closest to:
In the first EMI of ₹20,758 on a ₹10 lakh loan at 9% p.a. (monthly reducing balance), how much goes towards principal?
w: Interest for month 1 = 10,00,000 × 0.75% = ₹7,500; principal = 20,758 − 7,500 = ₹13,258. The principal share rises every month as the balance falls.

s: The population of a city is 10 lakh and grows at 5% p.a. compounded. What is it after 3 years?
A bank lends ₹1,00,000 for one year at 10% but deducts the interest upfront (front-end/discounted). What is the effective rate for the borrower?
w: Borrower gets ₹90,000 and repays ₹1,00,000: 10,000/90,000 = 11.11%. Collecting interest in advance raises the effective cost.

s: Using the Rule of 72, at what annual compound rate will money double in about 6 years?
o: About 12%
About 6%
About 16.7%
About 8%
w: Rate ≈ 72 ÷ 6 = 12%. Check: 1.12^6 = 1.97. Simple interest would need 16.7%.

s:
Which statements about annuities are correct?
1. In an ordinary annuity, payments are made at the end of each period.
2. Rent paid in advance at the start of each month is an annuity due.
3. The present value of an annuity due is lower than that of an ordinary annuity with the same payments and rate.
4. The present value of a perpetuity is the periodic payment divided by the rate.
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
w: An annuity due receives each payment one period earlier, so its PV is HIGHER (× (1 + r)). The rest are correct.

s: ₹8 lakh is invested for 4 years at 9% compounded annually (1.09⁴ = 1.4116). Another option pays 10% simple interest. Which is correct?
o: Compound option ≈ ₹11.60 lakh, higher than the simple-interest option's ₹11.29 lakh
Compound option ≈ ₹11.29 lakh, higher than the simple-interest option's ₹11.20 lakh
Compound option ≈ ₹11.29 lakh, lower than the simple-interest option's ₹11.60 lakh
Both give exactly ₹11.20 lakh after 4 years
w: 8 × 1.4116 = 11.29 lakh; 8 + 8 × 0.10 × 4 = 11.20 lakh. Compounding at 9% beats 10% simple over 4 years.

s: What is the present value of ₹1,00,000 receivable after 3 years at 10% compound?
w: PV = 1,00,000/1.1^3 = 1,00,000/1.331 = ₹75,131. 70,000 deducts simple interest; 1,33,100 is the future value of 1 lakh.

s: A borrower compares two term loans of ₹48 lakh for 5 years. Bank A: 9.00%, EMI ₹99,640, no fee. Bank B: 8.60%, EMI ₹98,890, processing fee ₹1,20,000. Total EMI saving with Bank B over 60 months is ₹45,000. What should guide the choice?
o: Processing fee is a one-time cost and should be ignored in comparing loans
Lowest EMI, so Bank B should be chosen because it saves ₹750 every month
Interest rate alone, so Bank B should be chosen because 8.60% is less than 9.00%
Effective all-in cost: Bank B's upfront fee of ₹1.2 lakh exceeds its EMI saving, so Bank A is cheaper
w: B saves (99,640 − 98,890) × 60 = ₹45,000 in EMIs but charges ₹1,20,000 upfront (paid today, so worth even more). The effective cost of B is higher.

s: Two bonds of the same company: Bond A (8% coupon, 4 years) and Bond B (12% coupon, 4 years). Market yields jump from 8% to 11%. Which statement is correct?
o: Bond B falls more, because higher-coupon bonds always carry more interest-rate risk
Bond B's price rises, because investors prefer higher coupons when rates rise
Bond A falls by about 9.3% and Bond B by about 9.0%; the lower-coupon bond is more sensitive
Both fall by exactly the same percentage, because maturity is identical
w: A: 1,000 → 906.93 (−9.31%). B: 1,132.49 → 1,031.02 (−8.96%). For the same maturity, the lower coupon puts more value in the distant redemption, so its price is more sensitive.

s:
A pension fund holds three 7% G-secs maturing in 3, 8 and 18 years. RBI is expected to raise rates. Which statements are correct?
1. The 18-year bond should show the largest percentage fall.
2. The 3-year bond carries the highest interest-rate risk because it matures first.
3. Longer maturity generally means greater price sensitivity.
4. Since coupons are equal, maturity does not affect volatility.
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
w: Bond theorem: for a given yield change, longer maturity → bigger % change. The short bond has the least rate risk; maturity matters even with equal coupons.

s: A ₹1,000 bond carries a 9% annual coupon and matures in 5 years at par. If the market yield is 10%, its price is closest to:
When the current market yield is LOWER than a bond's coupon rate, the bond trades at:
o: A premium to its face value
Its redemption value plus accrued interest only
A discount to its face value
Exactly its face value
w: Investors pay more than par for a coupon above the going yield. Price falls back to par as maturity nears (pull to par).

s: A bond of face value ₹1,000 with a 15% coupon is quoted at ₹1,500. Its current yield is:
w: Current yield = annual coupon ÷ market price = 150 ÷ 1,500 = 10%.

s: An 8% bond (face ₹1,000, redeemable at par in 6 years) is bought at ₹920. Using the approximation formula, its YTM is about:
w: Approx YTM = [80 + (1,000 − 920)/6] ÷ [(1,000 + 920)/2] = (80 + 13.33)/960 = 9.72%. 8.70% is the current yield (80/920). For a discount bond: YTM > CY > coupon.

s:
Bond X (9% coupon) is bought at ₹960 and Bond Y (9% coupon) at ₹1,050; both mature at par in 5 years. Which statements are correct?
1. X's YTM is higher than 9%.
2. Y's YTM is lower than 9%.
3. The gap between purchase price and redemption value affects YTM.
4. Coupon rate and YTM are always equal.
o: 1 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
w: Buying below par adds a capital gain (YTM > coupon); buying above par adds a capital loss (YTM < coupon). They are equal only when bought at par.

s: A trainee says the current yield of a bond bought at ₹920 is the total return if held to maturity. What is wrong?
o: Nothing is wrong: current yield and YTM are always identical for any bond held to maturity
Current yield considers only coupon versus price; YTM also includes the gain on redemption and the time value of money
YTM ignores the redemption value and uses only the coupon received during the holding period
Current yield applies only to Government securities and not to corporate bonds
w: CY = 80/920 = 8.70% captures income only; the ₹80 gain on redemption at par and its timing are captured only in YTM.

s:
A treasury portfolio has Bond A (MD 2.6), Bond B (MD 4.8) and Bond C (MD 7.2). Rates are expected to rise. Which statements are correct?
1. Bond C has the highest interest-rate risk.
2. Modified duration approximates the % price change for a 1% change in yield.
3. If yields rise 1%, Bond A will fall more than Bond C.
4. Managers usually shorten portfolio duration when they expect rates to rise.
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
w: %ΔP ≈ −MD × Δy, so C (7.2) falls about 7.2% and A about 2.6% for a 1% rise. Shortening duration reduces losses when rates rise.

s: A bond has a modified duration of 4.8. If its yield rises by 50 basis points, its price will change by approximately:
Which of the following is NOT a property of bond duration?
o: The higher the yield, the lower the duration
The higher the coupon rate, the lower the duration
A coupon bond's duration is always greater than its maturity
A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity
w: A coupon bond pays cash before maturity, so its weighted-average time (duration) is less than maturity. The others are standard properties.

s: For a 3-year bond with a 10% annual coupon priced at par (yield 10%), the Macaulay duration and modified duration are about:
o: 3.00 years and 2.73
2.74 years and 3.01
2.49 years and 2.74
2.74 years and 2.49

s:
Which statements on bond theorems are correct?
1. Bond prices move inversely to market yields.
2. For a given change in yield, the price rise when yields fall exceeds the price fall when yields rise by the same amount.
3. Price sensitivity increases with maturity, but at a decreasing rate.
4. Higher-coupon bonds show larger percentage price changes than lower-coupon bonds of the same maturity.
o: 1 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
w: Statement 4 reverses theorem 5: lower-coupon bonds are more sensitive. The convexity property (2) and decreasing-rate sensitivity (3) are part of Malkiel's theorems.

s: A company issues a bond that gives the ISSUER the right to redeem it before maturity. Such a bond is called a:
o: Perpetual bond
Callable bond
Puttable bond
Convertible bond
w: Callable = issuer's option to redeem early (typically when rates fall). Puttable = investor's option to sell back. Convertible = option to convert into equity.

s: Which of the following is NOT an asset-backed security?
o: A mortgage-backed security
A pass-through certificate on credit-card receivables
A plain dated Government of India security
A security backed by a pool of auto loans
w: ABS are created by securitising pools of loans or receivables. A G-sec is a direct sovereign obligation with no pool of assets behind it.

s: The price of a zero-coupon bond of face value ₹1,000 maturing in 5 years, at a yield of 8%, is closest to:
w: Price = 1,000/1.08^5 = 1,000/1.4693 = ₹680.58. Its duration equals 5 years.

s: An exporter will receive USD 5,00,000. The bank's quote is USD/INR 83.25 / 83.33. A new officer suggests applying the selling rate because foreign currency is involved. Which is correct?
o: The exporter sells USD to the bank, so the bank's buying rate of 83.25 applies
The mid-rate of 83.29 must be applied to all customer deals
The buying rate applies only to cash transactions; for remittances the selling rate applies
The selling rate of 83.33 applies whenever foreign currency is involved
w: Quotes are from the bank's side: bid (lower) is what the bank pays to buy USD. An exporter brings USD in, so the bank buys at 83.25.

s: An importer must remit USD 5,00,000 immediately. Spot USD/INR is 83.48 / 83.56. What rupee amount will be debited?
w: The importer buys USD from the bank at the bank's selling rate, 83.56: 5,00,000 × 83.56 = ₹4,17,80,000.

s: Spot USD/INR 83.42 / 83.48; 3-month forward margin +18 / +22 paise. An exporter will receive and an importer will pay USD in 3 months. What forward rates apply?
o: Exporter 83.66; importer 83.64
Exporter 83.24; importer 83.26
Exporter 83.60; importer 83.70
Both 83.65, the forward mid-rate
w: Ascending margins mean the USD is at a premium, so add: buying 83.42 + 0.18 = 83.60 (exporter); selling 83.48 + 0.22 = 83.70 (importer).

s: A 3-month forward quote shows margins of 25/20 paise against spot 83.10/83.16. What is the forward selling rate?
w: Descending margins mean a discount, so subtract: selling = 83.16 − 0.20 = 82.96 (buying = 83.10 − 0.25 = 82.85).

s: Spot USD/INR is 83.00 and the 3-month forward rate is 83.60. The annualised forward premium is about:
Spot USD/INR is 83.00, 3-month rupee interest 7% p.a. and USD interest 5% p.a. By interest rate parity, the 3-month forward rate is about:
o: 83.00, as forward and spot rates are always equal
83.41, with the USD at a forward premium
82.59, with the USD at a forward discount
84.66, with the USD at a forward premium
w: F = 83 × (1 + 0.07/4)/(1 + 0.05/4) = 83 × 1.0175/1.0125 = 83.41. The currency with lower interest (USD) trades at a forward premium.

s: USD/INR 83.20/83.30 and GBP/USD 1.2600/1.2610. What is the GBP/INR quote?

Which statements about the Indian forex market are correct?
1. India follows the direct method of quotation.
2. A spot transaction is settled on the second working day after the deal date.
3. The bill buying rate is higher than the TT buying rate.
4. FEDAI frames rules for interbank forex dealing.
o: 2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
w: Direct quotes since 1993; spot = T+2; FEDAI sets dealing rules. Bill buying is LOWER than TT buying because the bank pays out before it is reimbursed.

s: An Indian exporter books a forward contract to sell USD 10,000 at ₹83.00. On maturity, spot is ₹84.20. What is the effect?
o: He receives ₹8,30,000 as contracted, forgoing a ₹12,000 gain he would have made at spot
He can cancel the contract free of cost and sell at the spot rate
He receives ₹8,42,000 because forward contracts settle at the spot rate on maturity
He receives ₹8,30,000 and the bank also pays him the ₹12,000 difference
w: A forward contract fixes the rate: he must deliver at 83.00, getting ₹8,30,000. The hedge removed both downside risk and upside gain.

s: 'Nostro account' of an Indian bank means:
o: The Indian bank's rupee account with the Reserve Bank of India
The Indian bank's account maintained with a foreign bank abroad, in foreign currency
An account of one foreign bank with another foreign bank
A foreign bank's rupee account maintained with the Indian bank
w: Nostro = 'ours with you' (in foreign currency, abroad). Vostro = 'yours with us' (in INR, in India). Loro = a third party's account.

s: A fund manager evaluates: A (β 0.80, expected return 12%), B (β 1.10, 16%), C (β 1.60, 18%). Risk-free rate 6%, market return 14%. Which has the highest positive alpha?
o: Company A, with alpha of +0.4%
Company C, with alpha of +2.0% because its return is highest
Company B, with alpha of +1.2%
All three have identical alpha because all lie on the security market line
w: Required = 6 + β × 8: A 12.4 (α −0.4), B 14.8 (α +1.2), C 18.8 (α −0.8). Only B earns more than CAPM requires.

s: Risk-free rate 6.5%, market return 13%, beta 1.2. The cost of equity under CAPM is:
A share's last dividend was ₹4, dividends grow at 6% a year, and the share price is ₹53. The cost of equity (Gordon model) is:
10% debentures of face value ₹100 are issued at ₹95 and are redeemable at par after 5 years. Tax rate 30%. The approximate after-tax cost of debt is:
Capital structure: equity 50% (cost 15%), preference 10% (cost 11%), debt 40% (pre-tax cost 10%), tax 25%. The WACC is:
Two mutually exclusive projects return 13% (A) and 15% (B); WACC is 12%; B carries much higher business risk. The CEO wants to accept both. Which observation is most appropriate?
o: WACC is only a minimum hurdle for average risk; project-specific risk and cash-flow certainty must also be weighed
WACC is relevant only for projects financed by debt, so it cannot decide equity-funded projects
Project A must be rejected because its return is lower than Project B's, whatever the risk difference
Every project earning more than WACC must be accepted, whatever its risk or the other options available
w: Mutually exclusive projects can't both be accepted, and a much riskier project needs a risk-adjusted hurdle above the firm's WACC.

s: Which of the following is NOT an internal factor affecting a firm's WACC?
o: The firm's investment policy
The prevailing level of interest rates in the economy
The firm's capital-structure policy
The firm's dividend policy
w: Interest rates, tax rates and the market risk premium are external factors the firm cannot control. Capital-structure, dividend and investment policies are internal.

s: Vertex needs ₹150 crore. Option I: all equity. Option II: ₹75 crore equity + ₹75 crore debt at 9%. EBIT is expected to grow strongly. The Finance Director says Option II may raise shareholders' returns despite more risk. This reflects:
o: Operating leverage from fixed operating costs
Working-capital leverage from short-term creditors
Financial leverage from fixed-cost debt (trading on equity)
Dividend leverage from paying out all profits
w: When return on capital exceeds the cost of debt, debt magnifies EPS: financial leverage. It also magnifies the fall in EPS if EBIT falls.

s: Contribution ₹80 lakh, EBIT ₹50 lakh, interest ₹10 lakh. If sales rise by 10%, EPS will rise by about:
Which capital-structure approach holds that firm value and WACC are independent of the debt-equity mix, because the cost of equity rises to offset cheaper debt?
o: Pecking order theory
Net Operating Income approach
Net Income approach
Traditional approach
w: NOI (and MM without taxes): the benefit of cheap debt is exactly offset by a rising Ke, so WACC stays constant. NI says debt lowers WACC; the traditional view says an optimum exists.

s: Under Modigliani–Miller with corporate taxes, an unlevered firm is worth ₹100 crore. An identical firm has ₹40 crore of debt; tax rate 30%. The levered firm's value is:
o: ₹140 crore
₹100 crore
₹88 crore
₹112 crore
w: VL = VU + tD = 100 + 0.30 × 40 = ₹112 crore. The interest tax shield adds value.

s:
Which statements about CAPM are correct?
1. Beta measures systematic (non-diversifiable) risk.
2. (Rm − Rf) is the market risk premium.
3. A security with positive alpha plots above the security market line.
4. CAPM rewards investors for unsystematic (firm-specific) risk.
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
w: Unsystematic risk can be diversified away, so CAPM gives no reward for it. The other three statements are correct.

s: Why is debt normally the cheapest source of long-term finance for a profitable company?
o: Interest is tax-deductible and debt holders take less risk than shareholders, so they accept a lower return
Debt carries no obligation to pay interest in years when the company makes losses
Interest is paid out of profit after tax, so it reduces the tax liability available on equity dividends
Debt holders get voting rights in the company that compensate them for a lower return
w: Fixed claim, priority in repayment and the tax shield (Kd × (1 − t)) make debt cheaper. Interest must be paid even in losses, which is the risk to the firm.

s: A project costs ₹10 lakh and yields ₹3 lakh a year for 5 years. Cost of capital 10% (PVAF = 3.7908). Its NPV and PI are:
o: NPV ₹5 lakh; PI 1.50
NPV −₹1.37 lakh; PI 0.86
NPV ₹1.37 lakh; PI 0.88
NPV ₹1.37 lakh; PI 1.14
w: PV of inflows = 3 × 3.7908 = 11.37. NPV = 11.37 − 10 = 1.37; PI = 11.37/10 = 1.137. ₹5 lakh is the undiscounted surplus.

s: For the same project (outlay ₹10 lakh, ₹3 lakh a year for 5 years), the IRR lies:
o: Between 15% and 16% (about 15.2%)
Below 10%, because NPV at 10% is small
Exactly at 30%, the inflow-to-outlay ratio
Between 10% and 11%, close to the cost of capital
w: IRR is where PVAF = 10/3 = 3.333. PVAF(15%, 5) = 3.352 and PVAF(16%, 5) = 3.274, so IRR ≈ 15.2%. A positive NPV at 10% already tells you IRR > 10%.

s: A project costing ₹5 lakh generates inflows of ₹1.5 lakh, ₹2 lakh, ₹2.5 lakh and ₹1 lakh in years 1–4. Its payback period is:
o: 3 years
2.5 years
2.6 years
2.86 years
w: After 2 years: 3.5 recovered; 1.5 more needed out of 2.5 in year 3 → 0.6 year. Payback = 2.6 years.

s: An asset costs ₹10 lakh, has no salvage value and a 5-year life (SLM). It yields cash inflows of ₹3 lakh a year before depreciation; ignore tax. What is the ARR on average investment?
w: Annual profit = 3 − depreciation 2 = ₹1 lakh. Average investment = 10/2 = ₹5 lakh. ARR = 1/5 = 20%. Using cash flow instead of profit (3/5 = 60%) is the trap.

s: Projects P and Q are mutually exclusive. P: NPV ₹12 lakh, IRR 18%. Q: NPV ₹15 lakh, IRR 16%. Cost of capital 12%. Which should be chosen?
o: Q, because NPV directly measures the addition to shareholders' wealth
P, because a higher IRR always means the better project
Both, because both have positive NPV and IRR above 12%
Neither, because the two methods give conflicting signals
w: When NPV and IRR rank mutually exclusive projects differently, NPV prevails: it measures absolute value added and assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital.

s: In estimating cash flows of a new plant, which item should be EXCLUDED?
o: ₹5 lakh already spent on a feasibility study last year
Rent the company will forgo by using its own vacant building
Tax saved because of depreciation on the plant
Additional working capital needed at the start
w: Sunk costs can't be recovered whatever the decision, so they are ignored. Opportunity costs, working capital and the depreciation tax shield are relevant.

s:
Which statements are correct?
1. NPV and IRR give the same accept/reject decision for an independent conventional project.
2. IRR assumes intermediate cash flows are reinvested at the IRR.
3. The payback method considers all cash flows over the project's life.
4. A project with PI greater than 1 has positive NPV.
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
w: Payback ignores cash flows after the payback date (and time value). The others are correct.

s: While appraising a term loan for a new project, the banker's primary test of repayment capacity is:
o: Current ratio of the promoter's existing business
Gross profit ratio of the first year of operations
Market value of the collateral offered
Debt Service Coverage Ratio based on projected cash accruals
w: Term loans are repaid out of cash accruals over several years; DSCR measures this. Security is a fallback, not the source of repayment.

s: A bank gives a guarantee to a machinery supplier that the buyer will pay the instalments of the price over 5 years. This facility is a:
o: Letter of credit for import of raw materials
Deferred Payment Guarantee, a non-fund facility with credit risk like a term loan
Cash credit facility secured by hypothecation of machinery
Bank guarantee for performance, with no credit risk to the bank
w: Under a DPG the bank guarantees deferred instalments to the supplier. No funds move upfront, but if the buyer defaults the bank pays, so it is appraised like a term loan.

s: In project finance (non-recourse), the lender relies mainly on:
o: The cash flows of the project itself, generally housed in a special purpose vehicle
The personal guarantees and net worth of the sponsors, enforced if the project fails
Government budget support for the sector concerned, through viability-gap funding
The sponsor company's consolidated balance sheet and its other businesses
w: Project finance is repaid from the project's own revenues; lenders have no (or limited) recourse to the sponsors.

s: Zen Motors takes a 7-year lease of an identified factory; it gets the right to use and direct the asset, but legal title stays with the lessor. The executive wants to book rentals as rent expense. Under Ind AS 116 the lessee should generally:
o: Capitalise the asset only if ownership will transfer to it at the end of the lease
Expense the rentals as rent, because legal ownership never passes to the lessee
Recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability, unless the short-term or low-value exemption applies
Disclose the lease only as a contingent liability in the notes until it expires
w: Ind AS 116 removed the operating/finance split for lessees: control of an identified asset for a period leads to an ROU asset and a lease liability. Exemptions: leases of 12 months or less and low-value assets.

s: An airline hires an aircraft along with the lessor's crew, maintenance and insurance for the peak season. This is a:
o: Sale and leaseback
Leveraged lease
Wet lease
Dry lease
w: A wet lease (ACMI) includes aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance from the lessor. In a dry lease the lessee arranges crew and maintenance.

s: Which feature is most closely associated with a finance lease?
o: The aircraft is supplied together with crew and insurance by the lessor
The lease term is short and rentals recover only a small part of the asset's cost
Substantially all risks and rewards of ownership pass to the lessee over a non-cancellable term covering most of the asset's life
The lessor bears obsolescence risk and maintains the asset, and the lease can be cancelled at short notice
w: A finance lease is in substance a financing arrangement: full pay-out, non-cancellable, lessee bears risks. The other descriptions fit an operating or wet lease.

s: A company can buy a warehouse for ₹24.50 lakh or lease it for ₹10 lakh at the end of each year for 3 years. Required return 12%; PVAF (12%, 3) = 2.4018. Which is preferable?
o: Lease, because the PV of rentals (about ₹24.02 lakh) is lower than the purchase price
Buy, because time value of money does not apply when acquiring fixed assets
They are financially identical, because the rentals are fixed in amount
Buy, because total rentals of ₹30 lakh exceed the purchase price of ₹24.50 lakh
w: PV = 10 × 2.4018 = ₹24.02 lakh < ₹24.50 lakh. Comparing undiscounted totals (₹30 lakh) is the trap.

s: If the same lease rentals of ₹10 lakh for 3 years at 12% were payable at the BEGINNING of each year, their present value would be about:
o: ₹30.00 lakh
₹26.90 lakh
₹24.02 lakh
₹21.45 lakh
w: Annuity due PV = 2.4018 × 1.12 × 10 = ₹26.90 lakh; now buying (₹24.50 lakh) becomes cheaper.

s: A company sells its office building to a leasing company and immediately takes it back on lease. This is called:
o: Cross-border lease
Leveraged lease
Hire purchase
Sale and leaseback
w: Sale and leaseback releases funds locked in the asset while the seller keeps using it.

s:
Which statements are correct?
1. In a leveraged lease, a lender finances a large part of the asset's cost.
2. In an operating lease, the lessor generally bears the risk of obsolescence.
3. In hire purchase, ownership stays permanently with the hire vendor.
4. There is no separate Act in India governing leasing; general contract law applies.
o: 1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
w: In hire purchase, ownership passes to the hirer on payment of the last instalment (3 wrong). Leasing is a contract of bailment under the Indian Contract Act.

s: Under Ind AS 116, which leases may a lessee keep off the balance sheet by choosing the recognition exemption?
o: Leases of 12 months or less and leases of low-value assets
Leases where rentals are paid in advance
All leases where legal ownership does not pass at the end
All leases of land and buildings
w: Only short-term (≤12 months) and low-value asset leases can be expensed on a straight-line basis; others create an ROU asset and lease liability.

s: In which case will the working-capital requirement be HIGHER?
o: A restaurant that sells only for cash and buys on 30 days' credit
An electricity utility that bills customers monthly in advance
A heavy engineering firm with a long production cycle that sells on long credit
A firm whose suppliers give longer credit than it allows its own customers
w: A longer operating cycle (long production plus long debtor period) ties up more funds. Cash sales and generous supplier credit reduce WC needs.

s: Raw-material holding 40 days, WIP 15 days, finished goods 25 days, debtors 50 days, creditors 45 days. What is the net operating cycle?
o: 175 days
130 days
85 days
60 days
w: Gross cycle = 40 + 15 + 25 + 50 = 130 days; net = 130 − 45 = 85 days.

s: A firm has current assets of ₹400 lakh and current liabilities (other than bank borrowings) of ₹100 lakh. Under Tandon Method II, what is the maximum permissible bank finance?
o: ₹225 lakh
₹250 lakh
₹200 lakh
₹300 lakh
w: Method II: MPBF = 75% of CA − other CL = 300 − 100 = ₹200 lakh. (Method I: 75% of WCG = 0.75 × 300 = ₹225 lakh.)

s: A small enterprise projects annual turnover of ₹3.2 crore. Under the Nayak Committee turnover method, its working-capital requirement and the minimum bank finance are:
o: Requirement ₹64 lakh; bank finance ₹48 lakh, with the borrower bringing ₹16 lakh
Requirement ₹80 lakh; bank finance ₹64 lakh, with the borrower bringing ₹16 lakh
Requirement ₹80 lakh; bank finance ₹80 lakh with no margin
Requirement ₹96 lakh; bank finance ₹80 lakh, with the borrower bringing ₹16 lakh
w: WC need = 25% of 3.2 crore = ₹80 lakh. Bank finance = 20% of turnover = ₹64 lakh; margin = 5% = ₹16 lakh.

s: Which of the following CANNOT issue Commercial Paper in India?
o: A housing finance company registered with the regulator
An all-India financial institution such as EXIM Bank
A listed manufacturing company with a good credit rating
A scheduled commercial bank, which raises such funds through Certificates of Deposit instead
w: CP is for companies, NBFCs/HFCs, AIFIs and eligible body corporates. Banks raise short-term money through CDs.

s:
Which statements about Commercial Paper are correct?
1. It is an unsecured promissory note issued at a discount.
2. Its tenor ranges from 7 days to 1 year.
3. It is issued in multiples of ₹1 lakh in physical form.
4. Issuers need a credit rating.
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
w: CP is issued in ₹5 lakh denominations and only in dematerialised form (3 wrong).

s: Which is an INTERNAL source of finance?
o: Retained earnings
Trade credit from suppliers
Commercial paper
Cash credit from a bank
w: Retained earnings (and depreciation provisions) are generated inside the firm. The rest come from outsiders.

s:
Which statements comparing factoring and forfaiting are correct?
1. Factoring suits ongoing open-account sales; forfaiting suits one-off export receivables backed by bills or LC.
2. Factoring is normally medium- to long-term; forfaiting is short-term.
3. Factoring may be with or without recourse; forfaiting is without recourse.
4. Forfaiting usually provides 100% finance of the receivable value.
o: 1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
w: Factoring is short-term (up to about 180 days); forfaiting is medium-term (often 1–5 years), so statement 2 is reversed.

s: Under RBI's loan system for delivery of bank credit, for a borrower with aggregate fund-based working-capital limits of ₹200 crore, from April 2019 at least what portion must be drawn as a working-capital loan?
w: For aggregate limits of ₹150 crore and above, the minimum loan component was 40% from 1 October 2018 and 60% from 1 April 2019; the rest may be cash credit.

s: Net working capital represents:
o: Fixed assets less long-term liabilities, i.e. the firm's long-term surplus
Total current assets, also known as gross working capital of the firm
The excess of current assets over current liabilities, i.e. the part of current assets financed by long-term funds
The part of current liabilities that is financed by bank borrowings
w: Net WC = CA − CL. It is the borrower's long-term contribution (margin) to working capital. Gross WC = total current assets.

s: Which statement about exchange-traded derivatives (ETDs) is TRUE?
o: They are standardised contracts where the clearing corporation becomes the counterparty, so counterparty risk is minimal
They are regulated in India by RBI, while OTC derivatives are regulated by SEBI
They are customised to each client's amount and date and settled bilaterally at maturity
They are not subject to any margins or daily mark-to-market settlement by the exchange
w: ETDs are standardised and margined daily with the clearing house as central counterparty. ETDs are regulated by SEBI; OTC interest-rate and forex derivatives by RBI.

s:
Which statements are correct?
1. The buyer of a call option has the right but not the obligation to buy the underlying.
2. The writer of an option receives the premium and takes on the obligation.
3. A European option can be exercised on any day up to expiry.
4. In an interest rate swap, the notional principal is exchanged at the start and the end.
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
w: A European option can be exercised only on expiry (American any time). IRS exchanges only interest flows on a notional amount; principal is exchanged in a currency swap.

s: Compared with a currency futures contract, a forex forward contract:
o: Is guaranteed by a clearing corporation and freely tradable
Gives the holder a right but no obligation to exchange currency
Is customised and carries counterparty risk, with no daily mark-to-market
Is standardised and traded on a stock exchange with daily margins
w: Forwards are OTC, bilateral and customised, settled at maturity, with default risk. Futures are exchange-traded, standardised and margined.

s: A company borrows at a floating rate and fears rates will rise. Which derivative converts its floating-rate liability into a fixed-rate one?
o: An interest rate swap in which it pays floating and receives fixed
Buying a put option on foreign currency
Selling a forward rate agreement for the same period
An interest rate swap in which it pays fixed and receives floating
w: Paying fixed / receiving floating offsets its floating payments, leaving a fixed cost. Selling an FRA would benefit from falling rates, the opposite of what it needs.

s: A '3 × 6 FRA' means a forward rate agreement:
o: With a 3% fixed rate payable against a 6% floating rate on the notional
That is traded on the stock exchange in standard lots of 3 and 6 contracts
That fixes the interest rate for a 3-month period starting 3 months from today, settling only the rate difference
Under which principal is exchanged after 3 months and repaid after 6 months
w: The FRA covers the period from month 3 to month 6. Only the difference between the agreed and the reference rate on the notional amount is settled.

s: The maximum loss for the BUYER of an option is:
o: The full notional value of the underlying
Unlimited
The strike price
The premium paid
w: The buyer can simply let the option lapse, losing only the premium. The writer of a call faces potentially unlimited loss.

s: Which user enters derivatives to lock in a riskless profit from price differences between two markets?
o: Speculator
Arbitrageur
Hedger
Market regulator
w: Arbitrageurs exploit mispricing across markets without risk; hedgers reduce existing risk; speculators take risk hoping to profit.

s: Section 80U of the Income-tax Act (1961) relates to deduction in respect of:
o: Royalty on patents
Interest on deposits received by senior citizens
A resident individual who is himself a person with disability
Royalty income of authors of certain books
w: 80U = assessee with disability (₹75,000; ₹1,25,000 if severe). 80QQB = authors' royalty; 80RRB = patent royalty; 80TTB = seniors' deposit interest.

s: Dr Mehra receives a salary from a private hospital, fees from his evening clinic and interest on fixed deposits. He wants to show everything under 'Business or Profession'. Which is correct?
o: All income under 'Salaries' because his main income is salary
All income under PGBP because it arises from his medical expertise
Salary under Salaries, clinic under PGBP, FD interest under Other sources
He may choose any head, provided he applies it consistently
w: Each income is taxed under the head matching its source; the assessee has no choice. Employer–employee income is salary; independent practice is profession; interest is other sources.

s: Ms Kavya has salary, DA, HRA and savings-bank interest. She wants the standard deduction to be allowed against her savings-bank interest too. Which is correct?
o: Standard deduction applies to income under every head
Standard deduction is available only to Government employees
Standard deduction is available only if HRA exemption is not claimed
Standard deduction is available only against income under the head 'Salaries'
w: Standard deduction (₹75,000 new regime / ₹50,000 old) is a deduction from salary or pension income only. Savings interest may get 80TTA (old regime).

s: Mr Arvind pays LIC premium, employee's PF contribution, tuition fees for two children, a medical insurance premium and a donation to an approved relief fund. His consultant puts all of them under Section 80C. Which is correct?
o: LIC, PF and tuition fees under 80C; medical insurance 80D; donation 80G
Only the LIC premium qualifies under 80C; the rest get no deduction
Medical insurance premium is deductible only as a business expense
All five qualify under 80C, subject to the ₹1.5 lakh limit
w: 80C covers LIC, PF, PPF, tuition fees and similar. Health insurance has its own section, 80D; donations are under 80G.

s: A 66-year-old resident earns interest of ₹70,000 on fixed deposits and ₹8,000 on her savings account (old regime). What deduction can she claim for this interest?
o: ₹78,000 under Section 80TTB
₹10,000 under Section 80TTA
₹58,000 under Sections 80TTA and 80TTB together
₹50,000 under Section 80TTB
w: Senior citizens get 80TTB on interest from all deposits (savings, FD, RD) up to ₹50,000; 80TTA is then not available. 80TTA (₹10,000, savings only) is for non-seniors.

s: Which statement about Section 80D is correct?
o: Premium must be paid other than in cash, except preventive check-up up to ₹5,000
The deduction is part of the ₹1.5 lakh limit of Section 80C
Premium paid in cash is fully deductible
The deduction is available only for the taxpayer's own policy, not for parents
w: 80D is separate from 80C. It covers self/family and parents, but payments must be non-cash, except preventive check-up up to ₹5,000.

s: Under Section 2(31) of the Income-tax Act, which of the following is NOT separately listed as a 'person'?
o: A firm
A branch of a company
A Hindu Undivided Family
An artificial juridical person
w: Persons: individual, HUF, company, firm, AOP/BOI, local authority, artificial juridical person. A branch is part of the company, not a separate person.

s: A registered charitable trust applies only 78% of its income to its objects and accumulates the rest without following the prescribed conditions. A trustee says registration alone guarantees full exemption. Which is correct?
o: Registration under Section 12AB alone guarantees complete exemption of all income
Rental income of a charitable trust is always taxable
Exemption also needs at least 85% of income applied; registration alone is not enough
Educational trusts are exempt only if they receive Government grants
w: Sec 11 requires application of at least 85% of income (15% free accumulation; more only via Form 10 for specific purposes). Registration is necessary but not sufficient.

s: Prime Metals sells goods on which TCS applies under the Income-tax Act. The buyer argues that since GST is charged on the invoice, TCS should not be collected. Which is correct?
o: TCS can be collected only by Government departments
TCS and GST are under separate laws and must be examined independently
TCS applies only to export transactions
Once GST is charged, no TCS can apply on the same invoice
w: The two are separate statutes with separate obligations; one doesn't override the other.

s: From 1 April 2025, a bank need not deduct TDS on deposit interest paid to a senior citizen if the year's interest does not exceed:
w: Budget 2025 raised the Sec 194A threshold for banks to ₹50,000 (general) and ₹1,00,000 for senior citizens.

s: A depositor without PAN earns interest above the TDS threshold. At what rate will TDS be deducted?
o: 20%, under Section 206AA
30%, the maximum marginal rate
Nil, because PAN is not available
10%, the normal rate under Section 194A
w: Without PAN, TDS is at the higher of the applicable rate or 20% (206AA). Form 15G/15H also needs a valid PAN.

s:
Which statements about the Income-tax Act 2025 are correct?
1. It came into force on 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act.
2. It replaces 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with a single 'tax year'.
3. It abolished the deduction for life-insurance premium and PPF.
4. Section 80C of the old Act now appears as Section 123.
o: 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
w: The new Act mainly simplifies and renumbers: 80C-type deductions continue (as Sec 123) with the same ₹1.5 lakh limit under the old regime.

s: Under Section 80QQB and Section 80RRB, the maximum deduction for authors' royalty and patent royalty respectively is:
o: ₹3 lakh each
₹1.5 lakh each
₹3 lakh and ₹1.5 lakh
No limit for either
w: Both 80QQB (authors of certain books) and 80RRB (patentees) allow up to ₹3 lakh of royalty income.

s: ABC Constructions buys: (1) steel to construct its factory building, (2) office laptops, (3) a motor car for the MD, (4) raw materials used in taxable supplies. The executive wants ITC on all because GST was paid. ITC is available on:
o: Raw materials only
Steel, laptops and raw materials, but not the car
Office laptops and raw materials only
All four, since GST was paid on every purchase
w: Sec 17(5) blocks ITC on goods and services used to construct immovable property on own account (other than plant and machinery) and on motor vehicles for transport of persons. Laptops and raw materials used in business are eligible.

s: Aarav Handicrafts (Rajasthan only) has taxable intra-State supplies of ₹31 lakh, exempt supplies of ₹6 lakh and sale of old office furniture of ₹3 lakh. The owner says registration is not needed because taxable turnover is below the threshold. Which is correct?
o: Test aggregate turnover, which includes exempt supplies and the furniture sale
Registration becomes compulsory only when an inter-State supply is made
Sale of office furniture automatically makes registration compulsory
Registration depends only on taxable turnover, so it is not required
w: Aggregate turnover covers taxable, exempt, export and inter-State supplies of the same PAN. Here it is about ₹40 lakh, right at the goods threshold, so it must be tested on aggregate turnover.

s: A supplier invoiced ₹12,00,000 plus GST; goods worth ₹1,50,000 were later returned, so both value and GST must be reduced. Which document should be issued?
o: Debit note
Revised tax invoice
Payment voucher
Credit note
w: A credit note (Sec 34) reduces taxable value or tax charged in an earlier invoice; a debit note increases it.

s: Mr Rajesh removes goods for delivery on 15 July, they are delivered on 16 July, the invoice is issued on 18 July and payment is received on 28 July. What is the time of supply?
o: 18 July
28 July
15 July
16 July
w: For goods, time of supply = earlier of the invoice date or the last date by which the invoice should have been issued (at or before removal). The invoice was due by 15 July, so 15 July.

s: An invoice is issued on 16 June 2024 but supply of goods is completed on 13 July 2024. When is GSTR-3B for this liability due (monthly filer)?
o: 13 August 2024
20 July 2024
20 August 2024
16 July 2024
w: Time of supply = earlier of invoice (16 June) and supply → June. June's GSTR-3B (summary return with payment) is due by the 20th of the next month: 20 July 2024.

s: Which return is used by a registered taxpayer to give a summary of outward and inward supplies, claim ITC and pay tax?
o: GSTR-2B
GSTR-1
GSTR-9
GSTR-3B
w: GSTR-3B is the summary return with tax payment. GSTR-1 gives invoice-wise outward supplies; GSTR-2B is an auto-generated ITC statement; GSTR-9 is the annual return.

s: Under GST, interest at 18% per annum is chargeable mainly for:
o: Issuing a credit note after the due date
Delay in filing GSTR-1
Delay in payment of tax after the due date
Delay in obtaining registration when turnover crosses the threshold
w: Section 50 levies interest at 18% p.a. on tax paid late (for the period of delay). Late filing of returns attracts late fees, not this interest.

s: TCS (Tax Collected at Source) under GST is collected by:
o: The e-commerce operator on supplies made through its platform
The bank through which the GST payment is made
The supplier from every customer on all taxable sales
Government departments when paying their contractors
