w: Longer-maturity bonds generally show greater price sensitivity (higher percentage decline) to a given rise in interest rates because their cash flows are more heavily weighted towards the distant future, so Bond R (18 years) would decline the most — matching Statements 1 and 3 — while Statement 2 is wrong (shorter maturity means lower, not higher, rate risk) and Statement 4 is wrong (maturity does affect volatility even with identical coupons).

s:
A manufacturing company reports:
• Sales : ₹15 crore
• Variable Cost Ratio : 60%
• Fixed Cost : ₹4.20 crore Management proposes reducing selling price by 8% to increase market share. Before approving the proposal, the CFO recommends evaluating the Margin of Safety. Why is Margin of Safety particularly relevant?
o: It estimates recoverable amount under impairment testing.
It measures the extent by which actual sales exceed break-even sales, indicating the cushion available before losses begin.
It determines annual depreciation under marginal costing.
It measures inventory obsolescence.
w: Margin of Safety measures the excess of actual (or budgeted) sales over the break-even sales level, indicating how much sales can fall before the business starts incurring losses — it is a cushion/buffer concept in Cost-Volume- Profit analysis, unrelated to depreciation or impairment.

s:
On 31 March 2026, Nova Enterprises reported the following:
• Cash Book Balance : ₹24.80 lakh
Additional Information:
• Outstanding cheques : ₹4.20 lakh
• Dishonoured cheque not yet recorded : ₹1.10 lakh
• Bank charges debited : ₹12,500
• Dividend directly credited by bank : ₹95,000
• Insurance premium paid by bank under standing instruction : ₹48,000
The trainee accountant proposes including all five items only in the Bank Reconciliation Statement without passing any adjustment entries. Which statement is technically correct?
o: No adjustment is required until the bank issues revised statements.
Dishonoured cheque, bank charges, direct dividend credit and standing instruction require Cash Book adjustments, while outstanding cheques remain timing differences.
All five items are timing differences.
Only bank charges require adjustment.
w: A dishonoured cheque, bank charges debited by the bank, a dividend directly credited by the bank, and payments made under a standing instruction are all transactions that the bank has recorded but the depositor has not yet entered in the Cash Book, so they require correcting entries in the Cash Book itself — unlike an outstanding (unpresented) cheque, which is a simple timing difference that will clear itself and needs no Cash Book correction.

s:
Galaxy Ltd. invited applications for 1,20,000 equity shares. Applications were received for 1,80,000 shares. The company:
• Rejected applications for 20,000 shares.
• Made pro-rata allotment to the remaining applicants.
• Adjusted excess application money against allotment. Mr. Sharma applied for 9,000 shares. Ignoring fractional adjustments, how many shares should he receive?
o: 6,000 shares
8,000 shares
9,000 shares
6,750 shares
w: Valid applications = 1,80,000 − 20,000 = 1,60,000 for 1,20,000 shares → ratio 3 : 4. Mr Sharma gets 9,000 × 3/4 = 6,750 shares.
note: The coaching key (9,000) is wrong; options corrected so the right answer, 6,750, is present.

s: Zenstar Ltd. issued equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2. A shareholder paid application and allotment money but failed to pay the final call. The Board forfeited the shares after complying with all legal requirements. The Accounts Executive passed the forfeiture entry without considering the distinction between called-up capital and amount actually received. Which statement is correct?
o: Share Capital should always be debited only for the amount received.
Share Capital is debited for the called-up amount, while Share Forfeiture represents the amount actually received towards share capital.
Securities Premium is always debited during forfeiture.
Calls in Arrears never appear in forfeiture accounting.
w: On forfeiture, Share Capital Account is debited with the full called- up amount (since the shareholder is being removed from that liability), while the amount that had actually been received from the shareholder before forfeiture is transferred to a Share Forfeiture Account, to be dealt with on reissue.

s:
The Treasury Department receives the following quotation:
• Spot USD/INR : 83.42 / 83.48
• Three-Month Forward Margin : +18 / +22 paise Two customers approach simultaneously:
• Exporter receiving USD after three months.
• Importer paying USD after three months. A probationary officer suggests quoting the same forward rate to both customers. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Forward margins apply only to export transactions.
Importers always transact at spot rates.
Both customers should receive the same forward rate.
Exporter should receive the bank's forward buying rate, while importer should be quoted the forward selling rate.
w: In foreign exchange dealing, an exporter who is bringing in foreign currency is selling it to the bank, so the exporter is quoted the bank's buying rate; conversely, an importer who needs foreign currency to make a payment is buying from the bank, so the importer is quoted the bank's selling rate — the two customers are not quoted identical rates.

s:
During audit, the following transactions were identified:
1. Purchase of office furniture debited to Purchases Account.
2. Annual maintenance expenditure capitalised.
3. Legal expenses for acquiring land debited to Land Account.
4. Freight incurred for bringing machinery to the factory debited to Freight Outward Account.
Which of the above represent Errors of Principle?
o: 1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
All four
2 and 3 only
w: An Error of Principle occurs when a transaction is recorded by violating a fundamental accounting principle (such as treating a capital item as revenue, or vice versa) even though the double entry itself balances; applying that definition to the transactions in the scenario, Transactions 1, 2 and 4 are identified as principle errors, while Transaction 3 is not.

s:
At the end of the financial year, Delta Manufacturing Ltd. reports:
• Outstanding Salary
• Prepaid Insurance
• Interest Accrued but not Due
• Depreciation on Plant
The Accounts Officer proposes passing adjustment entries only for depreciation because the remaining items involve no immediate cash flow. Which statement is correct?
o: Outstanding expenses, prepaid expenses, accrued liabilities and depreciation all require adjustment under the accrual basis of accounting.
Only depreciation requires adjustment.
Cash transactions alone determine annual profit.
Adjustment entries are optional if the Trial Balance agrees.
w: Under the accrual basis of accounting, expenses and revenues must be recognised in the period to which they relate rather than when cash changes hands; this requires year-end adjustment entries for outstanding expenses, prepaid expenses, accrued liabilities and depreciation, not just one of these items alone.

s:
Vertex Manufacturing Ltd. entered into the following transactions:
1. Purchased machinery through bank.
2. Paid installation wages.
3. Purchased lubricants for routine servicing.
4. Received insurance claim for damage to machinery.
5. Exchanged an old machine for a new one.
The Accounts Executive debited Machinery Account in every transaction involving machinery. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Whenever bank is involved, the Golden Rules become irrelevant.
Installation wages should always be charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.
Only expenditure creating or enhancing future economic benefits should be capitalised; routine servicing should be charged to revenue.
Every payment relating to machinery should be capitalised.
w: Applying the Golden Rules, only expenditure that creates a new asset or genuinely enhances/extends the future economic benefit of an existing asset (like machinery) should be capitalised; routine servicing and maintenance costs that merely keep the asset in its normal working condition are revenue expenditure and must be charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

s:
ABC Manufacturing Ltd. intends to acquire an automated production line. Two alternatives are available:
Alternative I
• Immediate purchase price: ₹47,50,000
Alternative II
• Annual payment: ₹12,00,000 at the end of each year for 5 years
Additional Information:
• Cost of Capital = 10% p.a.
• PVAF (10%, 5 years) = 3.7908
The Finance Manager recommends rejecting Alternative II because total lease payments amount to ₹60 lakh, which exceeds the purchase price. Which conclusion is financially justified?
o: Lease should be accepted because the present value of lease payments is lower than the immediate purchase price.
Lease should be rejected because total cash payments exceed the purchase price.
Both alternatives are financially identical because annual payments are fixed.
Present Value analysis is irrelevant since machinery is a fixed asset.
w: Comparing the present value of the lease payments (discounted at the applicable cost of capital) against the immediate purchase price shows that leasing works out cheaper in present-value terms, so leasing is the financially preferable option despite the higher nominal total of the lease payments over the years.

s:
Mr. Arvind incurs the following expenditures during the financial year:
• LIC Premium
• Employee's Contribution to EPF
• Tuition Fees for two children
• Medical Insurance Premium
• Donation to an approved relief fund His consultant proposes claiming all deductions under Section 80C. Which statement is technically correct?
o: LIC, EPF and eligible tuition fees may qualify under Section 80C, whereas medical insurance and eligible donations fall under separate deduction provisions.
Every item qualifies under Section 80C.
Only LIC Premium qualifies.
Medical Insurance Premium is allowable only as a business expenditure.
w: Section 80C (overall ₹1.5 lakh) covers LIC premium, employee's PF contribution and tuition fees for up to two children. Medical insurance premium is under Section 80D; donations to approved funds under Section 80G.

s:
A manufacturing company reports:
Particular | Amount per Unit Selling Price | ₹920 Variable Cost | ₹610 Fixed Cost (Allocated) | ₹180 A foreign customer places a one-time order at ₹700 per unit.
Additional Information:
• Adequate idle capacity exists.
• Domestic sales remain unaffected.
• No additional fixed cost is incurred.
The Marketing Director recommends rejecting the order because the selling price is below total cost. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Reject because every order must recover total cost.
Accept every export order irrespective of contribution.
Accept the order because it generates positive contribution and improves overall profitability.
Contribution automatically becomes negative whenever price is below total cost.
w: Since idle capacity exists and domestic sales remain unaffected, the export order at ₹700 (above the ₹610 variable cost) generates a positive contribution of ₹90 per unit towards existing fixed costs, improving overall profitability even though the price is below full (absorption) cost — the correct marginal-costing decision is to accept it.

s:
• Authorised Share Capital : ₹20 crore
• Issued Share Capital : 1.50 crore equity shares
• Calls unpaid on certain shares
• Some shares forfeited but not yet reissued
A trainee accountant proposes reducing Issued Capital because forfeiture has taken place. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Paid-up Capital reflects amounts actually paid after adjusting calls unpaid and forfeiture, whereas Issued Capital does not automatically change merely because shares are forfeited.
Forfeiture affects only Securities Premium.
Issued Capital automatically reduces after forfeiture.
Authorised Capital always equals Paid-up Capital.
w: Forfeiture reduces paid-up capital (the forfeited amount is shown separately as Share Forfeiture until reissue). Issued capital is the nominal value of shares issued and authorised capital is the ceiling in the MoA; neither changes just because of forfeiture.

s:
Orion Industries Ltd. reports:
• Accounting Profit before Tax : ₹96 crore
• Taxable Profit : ₹82 crore
The difference arises primarily because depreciation under the Income-tax Act exceeds depreciation charged in the financial statements. The Finance Executive proposes recognising tax only on taxable income. Which accounting treatment is correct?
o: Recognise only Current Tax.
Recognise tax only after assessment is completed.
Recognise tax only on accounting profit.
Recognise Current Tax based on taxable income and Deferred Tax for temporary differences expected to reverse in future.
w: Under AS 22, an entity must recognise Current Tax based on taxable income computed as per tax law for the year, and separately recognise Deferred Tax to account for temporary differences between accounting income and taxable income that are expected to reverse in future periods — both need to be accounted for, not current tax alone.

s:
A hydroelectric power station uses an old computing device that continuously measures:
• Temperature
• Pressure
• Voltage fluctuations
The output is represented by continuously varying signals instead of binary digits. A trainee argues that since numerical values are processed, the machine must be a digital computer. Which statement is correct?
o: It is a digital computer because every computer processes binary data.
It is a hybrid computer because all engineering devices are hybrid.
Analog computers are used only in banking operations.
The machine is an analog computer because it processes continuously varying physical quantities.
w: A machine that processes continuously varying physical quantities (such as voltage, temperature, or pressure) rather than discrete binary data is classified as an analog computer, as distinguished from digital computers (which process data in binary form) and hybrid computers (which combine both analog and digital processing).

s:
A registered charitable trust earns income from:
• Donations
• Educational fees
• Bank Interest
• Rental Income Only 78% of the income is applied towards charitable purposes during the year, while the balance is accumulated without complying with the prescribed statutory conditions. One trustee argues that registration alone ensures complete tax exemption. Which statement is correct?
o: Educational trusts are exempt only when receiving Government grants.
Exemption depends upon satisfying statutory conditions relating to application and accumulation of income in addition to registration.
Rental income of charitable trusts is always taxable.
Registration alone guarantees exemption.
w: Mere registration under the Income-tax Act does not automatically guarantee tax exemption for a trust; the trust must also continue to satisfy statutory conditions relating to the application of income for charitable/religious purposes and permissible accumulation limits in order to retain its exemption each year.

s:
ABC India Pvt. Ltd. purchases specialised components from its overseas parent company. The Transfer Pricing Officer observes:
• Purchase prices are substantially above comparable uncontrolled prices.
• Indian taxable profits are significantly reduced.
• Pricing follows internal group policy.
Which principle forms the basis of Transfer Pricing adjustment?
o: Group companies are free to determine any transfer price.
Customs valuation automatically determines Income-tax valuation.
Transactions between associated enterprises should ordinarily satisfy the Arm's Length Principle.
Transfer Pricing provisions apply only to domestic transactions.
w: Under transfer pricing regulations, transactions between associated (related) enterprises must generally be priced as if they were between unrelated parties, i.e., they must satisfy the Arm's Length Principle, to prevent profit shifting through artificially set prices between group entities.

s:
following independent transactions occurred:
1. Purchased office furniture on credit.
2. Paid outstanding electricity charges through bank.
3. Received cash from a debtor after allowing discount.
4. Purchased machinery by issuing equity shares.
A trainee proposes:
• Debit Purchases Account in Transaction 1.
• Debit Outstanding Electricity Account in Transaction 2.
• Debit Discount Allowed Account in Transaction 3.
• Debit Machinery Account in Transaction
4.
Which evaluation is technically correct?
o: Transaction 1 is incorrect because furniture is a capital asset, whereas Transactions 2, 3 and 4 are correctly analysed.
All four journal treatments are incorrect.
Only Transactions 2, 3 and 4 are correctly analysed.
Transactions 1 and 2 are correct.
w: Furniture is a capital (fixed) asset, so purchasing furniture should be debited to a Furniture (asset) account, not treated as a revenue/expense item as done in Transaction 1 — making that entry incorrect — while Transactions 2, 3 and 4 apply the standard debit/credit rules correctly.

s:
Two listed companies report:
Particular | Company X | Company Y Market Price | ₹480 | ₹360 Dividend per Share | ₹18 | ₹12
The analyst makes the following observations:
1. Company X has a Dividend Yield of 3.75%.
2. Company Y has a Dividend Yield of 3.33%.
3. Dividend Yield measures dividend relative to current market price.
4. Higher Dividend per Share always implies higher Dividend Yield.
Which combination is correct?
o: Statements 1 and 4 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
All four statements
w: Dividend Yield = Dividend per Share ÷ Market Price per Share; based on the figures given, Company X's yield works out to 3.75% and Company Y's to 3.33% (Statements 1 and 2), consistent with the definition that Dividend Yield measures dividend relative to current market price (Statement 3) — but a higher DPS does not automatically mean a higher yield (Statement 4 is wrong) since market price also matters.

s:
ABC Manufacturing Ltd. plans to purchase a CNC machine costing ₹48 lakh. Two banks offer the following loans:
Particulars | Bank A | Bank B
Loan Amount | ₹48 lakh | ₹48 lakh
Interest Rate | 9.00% | 8.60%
Tenure | 5 Years | 5 Years
EMI | ₹99,640 | ₹98,890
Processing Fee | Nil | ₹1,20,000
The Finance Manager recommends Bank B solely because its EMI is lower. The CFO disagrees.
Which financial principle should primarily guide the decision?
o: Effective borrowing cost should be compared after considering interest, processing charges and total financing cost.
EMI comparison is meaningful only when interest rates are identical.
Lowest EMI should always be preferred.
Processing fees are irrelevant because they are one-time expenses.
w: Bank B's lower EMI saves (99,640 − 98,890) × 60 = ₹45,000 over 5 years, but its ₹1,20,000 processing fee is paid upfront. The effective cost of borrowing (all-in cost / IRR of the cash flows) is what must be compared, not EMI alone.

s:
A fintech company launches a digital banking platform offering:
• Instant account opening
• Virtual debit cards
• API-based payments
• Cash flow dashboards
• Automated expense management
The company markets itself as a Neo Bank. A customer believes that it can independently:
• Accept public deposits.
• Maintain CRR and SLR.
• Lend from customer deposits.
Which statement is technically correct?
o: Neo Banks generally operate in partnership with licensed banks and do not independently hold banking licences for accepting public deposits.
Neo Banks may issue currency notes through digital wallets.
Neo Banks automatically receive a banking licence after three years.
Neo Banks function exactly like scheduled commercial banks.
w: Most Neo Banks in India do not hold an independent banking licence of their own; instead, they operate as technology platforms in partnership with RBI-licensed banks, which continue to hold the deposits and carry out the regulated banking functions, while the Neo Bank provides the digital front-end and customer experience.

s:
ABC Bank Ltd. reports the following:
• Cash with RBI
• Government Securities
• Bills Purchased & Discounted
• Premises
• Customer Deposits
• Borrowings from RBI The trainee accountant classifies Bills Purchased & Discounted under Investments because the bank expects to receive money on maturity.
The Chief Manager disagrees. Under the Banking Regulation framework, Bills Purchased & Discounted are generally classified under:
o: Contingent Liabilities
Other Assets
Advances
Investments
w: Bills Purchased and Discounted by a bank represent credit extended to customers against bills of exchange and are therefore classified under 'Advances' in the bank's Balance Sheet, similar to other forms of lending, rather than under Investments, Other Assets, or Contingent Liabilities.

s: Mr. Rakesh invests ₹8,00,000 in a cumulative deposit carrying 9% p.a. compounded annually for 4 years. Another investment offers 10% simple interest. (Use 1.09⁴ = 1.4116) Ignoring taxation, which statement is correct?
o: Compound investment matures to approximately ₹11.29 lakh, which is lower than the maturity value under simple interest.
Both investments produce identical maturity values.
Compound interest becomes beneficial only after five years.
Compound investment matures to approximately ₹11.29 lakh, which is higher than the maturity value under simple interest.

s:
A company proposes to lease a warehouse.
Lease terms:
• ₹10 lakh payable at the end of each year for 3 years.
Alternative:
• Immediate purchase for ₹24.50 lakh.
Additional Information:
• Required Rate of Return = 12%
• PVAF (12%, 3 years) = 2.4018
Which option is financially preferable?
o: Time Value of Money is irrelevant since payments are fixed.
Both alternatives are financially identical because total lease payments are ₹30 lakh.
Purchase because future payments should never be discounted.
Lease because the present value of lease payments is lower than the purchase price.
w: Comparing the present value of the lease payments (discounted at the applicable cost of capital) against the immediate purchase cost shows the present value of leasing to be lower, making the lease option financially preferable despite requiring smaller periodic outflows over several years rather than one large payment today.

s:
An importer approaches ABC Bank to remit USD 5,00,000 immediately. The bank receives the following quotation: USD/INR Spot : ₹83.48 / ₹83.56
The trainee proposes applying the buying rate because the transaction takes place today. The Treasury Manager disagrees. Which explanation is technically correct?
o: Buying and selling rates become identical in spot transactions.
Buying rate applies because the transaction is a spot transaction.
Spot transactions always use the average of buying and selling rates.
Since the importer purchases foreign currency from the bank, the spot selling rate should be applied.
w: Since the importer needs to buy foreign currency from the bank to make payment to an overseas supplier, the bank applies its spot selling rate for foreign currency to that transaction — the buying rate would apply only if the customer were selling foreign currency to the bank.

s: A machine costing ₹3,00,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum under the Written Down Value Method. The company proposes selling the machine after three complete years. Ignoring taxation, the Written Down Value immediately before sale is closest to:
w: Under the Written Down Value Method, depreciation is charged each year at a fixed percentage on the asset's reducing book value (not on original cost); applying the applicable rate over the relevant years as per the figures given results in a closing book value of ₹1,53,600.

s:
The following transactions occurred during July:
1. Sale from Jaipur to Kota.
2. Sale from Jaipur to Ahmedabad.
3. Import of machinery from Japan.
4. Taxable service provided within Rajasthan.
In which of the above transactions is IGST levied?
o: 2, 3 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
w: Intra-State supply (Jaipur→Kota, service within Rajasthan) attracts CGST + SGST. Inter-State supply (Jaipur→Ahmedabad) and imports attract IGST. So IGST applies to 2 and 3.
note: Recalled question was incomplete; reframed to the point it tests (IGST = inter-State supply and imports).

s:
Precision Fabricators Ltd. manufactures customised pressure vessels. Each customer order differs in:
• Design
• Material
• Engineering hours
• Testing procedures
The Production Head recommends adopting Process Costing because it simplifies accounting. The Cost Accountant disagrees. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Process Costing is preferable because similar raw materials are used.
Marginal Costing eliminates the need for job-wise costing.
Standard Costing replaces Job Costing.
Job Costing provides meaningful cost information where each customer order is unique.
w: Job Costing is used where products or services are produced against specific, distinguishable customer orders that differ from one another (unlike continuous, identical output under Process Costing), making it the appropriate method for tracking costs of unique, order-specific work.

s:
Nova Engineering Ltd. reports:
• Current Assets = ₹18 crore
• Current Ratio = 2 : 1
• Quick Ratio = 1.25 : 1 Assuming there are no prepaid expenses, the inventory is closest to:
o: ₹4.50 crore
₹5.25 crore
₹6.75 crore
₹7.20 crore
w: Quick Ratio = (Current Assets − Inventory) ÷ Current Liabilities; rearranging this formula using the quick ratio, current ratio (or current assets/liabilities) and other data given in the question allows Inventory to be derived, working out to ₹6.75 crore as per the source's figures.

s:
ABC Bank's Treasury Department manages a ₹500 crore bond portfolio. The Investment Committee anticipates an increase in RBI policy rates over the next six months. The following bonds are under consideration:
Bond | Coupon | Maturity | Modified Duration
A | 7.5% | 3 Years | 2.6
B | 8.0% | 6 Years | 4.8
C | 8.5% | 10 Years | 7.2
The Head of Treasury makes the following observations:
1. Bond C carries the highest interest-rate risk.
2. Modified Duration estimates the approximate percentage change in bond price for a small change in market yield.
3. If market yield rises by 1%, Bond A is expected to decline more than Bond C.
4. Portfolio managers generally reduce portfolio duration when they expect interest rates to rise. Which combination is correct?
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
All four statements
Statements 1, 2 and 4 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
w: Modified Duration measures the approximate percentage change in a bond's price for a small change in yield (Statement 2); the bond with the highest duration (Bond C, 7.2) carries the highest interest-rate risk, so a rising- yield scenario would hurt it the most, not Bond A (contradicting Statement 3), and prudent portfolio managers typically shorten duration ahead of expected rate rises (Statement 4) — matching Statements 1, 2 and 4 only.

s: A manufacturing company plans to replace an imported boiler after six years. It invests ₹25 lakh today in a debt instrument yielding 9% p.a. compounded annually. (Use 1.09⁶ = 1.6771) The Finance Executive estimates the maturity amount at ₹42 lakh. Which amount is closest to the actual Future Value?
o: ₹52.10 lakh
₹45.80 lakh
₹41.93 lakh
₹33.50 lakh

s:
Omega Ltd. purchased machinery and follows:
• Straight Line Method for financial reporting.
• Written Down Value Method under Income-tax provisions.
The Accounts Executive makes the following observations:
1. Current Tax should be based on taxable profit.
2. Deferred Tax arises because depreciation differences are temporary and reverse over time.
3. Deferred Tax represents a permanent difference.
4. Deferred Tax should not be recognised unless additional tax is currently payable.
Which combination is correct?
o: Statements 1, 3 and 4 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
All four statements
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only
w: Current tax is on taxable profit (1). Different depreciation methods create a timing (temporary) difference that reverses over the asset's life, so deferred tax is recognised (2). It is not a permanent difference (3 wrong) and does not depend on extra tax being payable now (4 wrong).

s:
A borrower receives two loan offers:
Bank A
• 12% p.a. compounded annually Bank B
• 11.70% p.a. compounded monthly
The borrower immediately concludes that Bank B is cheaper because its quoted annual rate is lower. The Finance Consultant advises comparing the Effective Annual Rate (EAR). Which statement best justifies this advice?
o: EAR incorporates the impact of compounding frequency and therefore permits meaningful comparison of borrowing costs.
Nominal rates are legally binding whereas EAR is only an accounting estimate.
Compounding frequency affects investments but not loans.
EAR applies only to fixed deposits.
w: EAR = (1 + r/m)^m − 1. Bank B: (1 + 0.117/12)¹² − 1 ≈ 12.35%, which is higher than Bank A's 12%. So Bank B is actually costlier, although its quoted rate is lower.

s:
Galaxy Ltd. invited applications for 2,40,000 equity shares. Applications were received for 3,60,000 shares. The company:
• Rejected applications for 40,000 shares.
• Made pro-rata allotment to the remaining applicants. Mr. Arjun applied for 18,000 shares. Ignoring fractional adjustments, how many shares should ordinarily be allotted to him?
o: 14,400 shares
15,000 shares
12,000 shares
13,500 shares
w: Under pro-rata allotment, shares are allotted to applicants in the ratio that the total shares offered bears to the total shares applied for; applying that ratio to the specific applicant's application in the question results in an allotment of 13,500 shares as per the source's figures.

s:
Alpha Engineering Ltd. manufactures:
• Steel Pipes through continuous production.
• Modular Kitchens as per customer specifications.
• Industrial Fasteners in production batches.
The Finance Director recommends adopting one costing method for all products. The Cost Auditor disagrees. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
o: Use Process Costing for steel pipes, Job Costing for modular kitchens and Batch Costing for industrial fasteners.
Apply Process Costing uniformly.
Apply Standard Costing for every manufacturing environment.
Adopt Marginal Costing for statutory inventory valuation.
w: The most appropriate costing method depends on the nature of production: continuous, identical-output processes (like steel pipe manufacturing) suit Process Costing; distinct, customer-specific projects (like modular kitchens) suit Job Costing; and standardised products made in defined lots (like fasteners) suit Batch Costing — a single uniform method would not fit all three production types equally well.

s:
A Chartered Accountant identifies the following Accounting Standards:
• Government Grants
• Cash Flow Statements
• Intangible Assets
• Property, Plant and Equipment
The Managing Director asks: Which Accounting Standard primarily governs recognition and measurement of tangible fixed assets, and which governs classification of cash flows?
o: AS 26 and AS 12
AS 10 and AS 3
AS 3 and AS 26
AS 12 and AS 26
w: AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment) governs the recognition, measurement and capitalisation of fixed assets, while AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements) governs the classification and presentation of cash flows — together these are the two standards that best match the business situations typically presented in such integrated scenarios.

s:
A transport company purchases 500 electric buses. The technical report concludes:
• Highest utilisation during initial years.
• Maintenance expenditure increases in later years.
• Economic benefits are consumed more rapidly in early years.
Which depreciation method best reflects this pattern?
o: Inventory Method
Straight Line Method
Revaluation Method
Written Down Value Method
w: The Written Down Value Method charges a higher depreciation amount in the earlier years of an asset's life (when its economic benefit/usage is typically higher, as with transport vehicles that see heavier wear early on) and progressively lower amounts later, aligning the depreciation charge more closely with the actual pattern of the asset's consumption of economic benefits.

s:
Two identical machines costing ₹25 lakh each are purchased on the same date.
• Machine A –- Straight Line Method
• Machine B –- Written Down Value Method \@20% At the end of the third year, the CFO compares their carrying amounts.
Which statement is generally correct?
o: Machine B is likely to have the lower carrying amount because WDV recognises higher depreciation during earlier years.
Comparison is impossible because different methods are used.
Machine A will necessarily have the lower carrying amount.
Both machines must have identical carrying amounts.
w: WDV at 20%: 25 × 0.8³ = ₹12.8 lakh after 3 years. SLM gives a lower book value only if life is short (e.g. life under about 6 years). For normal lives WDV writes off more in early years, so Machine B is likely to have the lower carrying amount.

s:
An investor considers purchasing a corporate bond:
• Face Value : ₹1,000
• Coupon Rate : 8%
• Market Price : ₹920
• Remaining Maturity : 6 Years
• Redemption at Par
A trainee analyst calculates the Current Yield and concludes that it represents the total return expected if the bond is held until maturity. The Senior Investment Manager disagrees. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Current Yield applies only to Government Securities.
Current Yield and Yield to Maturity are always identical.
Yield to Maturity ignores redemption value.
Current Yield measures annual coupon income relative to market price, whereas Yield to Maturity also considers capital gain/loss and the time value of money.
w: Current Yield is simply the annual coupon (interest) payment divided by the bond's current market price, capturing only income return, whereas Yield to Maturity is a more complete measure that also factors in any capital gain or loss on redemption and the time value of money over the bond's remaining life, so the two figures generally differ except when a bond trades exactly at par.

s:
Omega Manufacturing Ltd. purchased an automated robotic arm for ₹2.40 crore. The company estimated:
• Useful Life: 8 years
• Residual Value: Nil
The Finance Controller remarks: "At the end of the useful life, the carrying amount of the asset should become zero." The Cost Accountant disagrees and argues that this outcome depends upon the depreciation method adopted. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Under the Straight Line Method with nil residual value, the carrying amount can reduce to zero at the end of the useful life.
Residual value has no relevance in determining depreciation.
Depreciation methods cannot reduce the carrying amount below the original residual value.
Under the Written Down Value Method, every depreciable asset necessarily reaches zero carrying amount.
w: Under the Straight Line Method, if the residual (salvage) value is taken as nil, equal depreciation is charged each year over the useful life so that the asset's carrying amount is fully written down to zero by the end of that period — unlike the Written Down Value Method, which mathematically never reduces the carrying amount to exactly zero.

s: A company plans to establish a technology upgradation fund. It proposes to invest ₹18 lakh today in a financial instrument yielding 11% p.a. compounded annually. The investment will remain untouched for 5 years. (Given: 1.11⁵ = 1.6851) The Finance Executive estimates the maturity amount at ₹30.33 lakh. The CFO believes the estimate is incorrect. Ignoring taxes, the Future Value is closest to:
o: ₹34.80 lakh
₹28.25 lakh
₹30.33 lakh
₹32.15 lakh
w: FV = 18 lakh × 1.11⁵ = 18 × 1.6851 = ₹30.33 lakh, so the estimate is correct.

s:
A fund manager is evaluating three listed companies.
Company | Beta | Expected Return
A | 0.80 | 12%
B | 1.10 | 16%
C | 1.60 | 18%
Additional Information:
• Risk-free Rate = 6%
• Expected Market Return = 14%
The manager wants to invest in the company generating the highest positive Alpha. Which investment should be preferred?
o: Company A
All three companies generate identical Alpha.
Company B
Company C
w: Alpha (α) = Actual Return − [Rf + β × (Rm − Rf)], using Risk-free Rate = 6% and Market Return = 14%. Applying this to the three companies' beta and expected return figures given, Company B is identified as generating the highest positive Alpha and should therefore be preferred by the fund manager over Companies A and C.

s:
Nova Industries Ltd. received the following during FY 2025-26:
1. Cash received from customers.
2. Proceeds from sale of machinery.
3. Dividend received on long-term investments.
4. Proceeds from issue of equity shares.
5. Refund of income tax relating to operating activities.
A trainee classifies all five receipts under Operating Activities because they increase cash balance. Which statement best explains the error?
o: Every cash receipt is an Operating Activity.
Cash Flow Statements recognise only revenue receipts.
Sale proceeds of fixed assets are disclosed only in the Balance Sheet.
Classification depends upon the underlying nature of the transaction. Cash flows may belong to Operating, Investing or Financing Activities under AS 3.
w: AS 3 requires that each cash inflow or outflow be classified according to the actual underlying nature of the transaction that generated it — an inflow could belong to Operating, Investing or Financing Activities depending on its source — rather than assuming that every cash receipt is automatically an operating inflow.

s: industrial pumps. The Production Director recommends implementing Standard Costing for performance evaluation. The Marketing Director recommends Marginal Costing while deciding whether to accept a special export order. The Managing Director believes that adopting one system eliminates the need for the other. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Marginal Costing is compulsory for statutory financial reporting.
Both systems always produce identical product costs.
Standard Costing completely replaces Marginal Costing.
Standard Costing and Marginal Costing serve different managerial purposes and may be used simultaneously.
w: Standard Costing (which focuses on setting cost benchmarks and analysing variances for cost control) and Marginal Costing (which focuses on separating fixed and variable costs for decision-making) serve different managerial purposes and are not mutually exclusive — a company can use both systems concurrently for different objectives.

s: Vertex Engineering Ltd. drew a bill of exchange on 10 January 2026, payable 90 days after date. The Accounts Officer records the maturity date as exactly 90 days after the bill date. The Internal Auditor objects. Ignoring public holidays, which statement is correct?
o: Three days of grace are generally added while determining the maturity date of a time bill.
Days of grace apply only to demand bills.
Time bills mature exactly after the specified period.
Days of grace are applicable only when specifically mentioned in the bill.
w: Traditionally, three additional days (known as 'days of grace') are added beyond the tenure specified in a time bill of exchange while computing its legal due/maturity date, a convention recognised under the Negotiable Instruments Act, unlike demand bills which are payable on presentation.

s:
A company entered into the following transactions:
• Sale to a wholly owned subsidiary.
• Purchase from an unrelated listed company.
• Interest-free loan to the Managing Director.
• Rent paid to a partnership firm in which a director is a partner.
The Finance Manager proposes disclosing only the transaction with the subsidiary. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Transactions with related parties covered under AS 18 require disclosure in accordance with the Standard.
Related Party Disclosure is necessary only when profit arises.
Only cash transactions require disclosure.
Only subsidiary transactions require disclosure.
w: AS 18 requires an enterprise to disclose material transactions it has entered into with related parties (not just subsidiaries, and irrespective of whether the transactions were in cash or resulted in profit), so that users of financial statements can assess the impact such relationships may have had on the reporting entity.

s:
A consulting firm follows the Cash Basis of accounting. During March:
• Consultancy fees earned remain outstanding.
• Office rent for next month is paid in advance.
• Electricity expense relating to March remains unpaid.
The auditor recommends adopting the Accrual Basis. Which explanation is most appropriate?
o: Cash Basis cannot recognise fixed assets.
Cash Basis is prohibited for every business entity.
Accrual accounting recognises income and expenses in the period to which they relate, resulting in a more faithful measurement of profit.
Accrual accounting records only credit transactions.
w: Accrual accounting recognises income when earned and expenses when incurred, matching them to the period to which they actually relate regardless of when cash is received or paid, which gives a more faithful and complete picture of an entity's true financial performance than the Cash Basis, which recognises transactions only when cash moves.

s:
While preparing the Bank Reconciliation Statement, the accountant discovers:
• A cheque deposited was recorded in the Cash Book as ₹18,000 instead of ₹1,80,000.
• Bank charges debited by the bank have not been recorded.
• A cheque issued remains unpresented.
• Interest credited by the bank has not been entered in the Cash Book.
The junior accountant proposes treating all four items merely as reconciling items. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Only the posting error requires correction.
Posting error, bank charges and bank interest require correction in the Cash Book, whereas the unpresented cheque represents a timing difference.
All four items should remain only in the Bank Reconciliation Statement.
Bank Reconciliation Statement cannot be prepared until every error is corrected.
w: A posting error, bank charges debited by the bank, and interest charged/credited by the bank are all items where the depositor's Cash Book needs to be corrected to reflect the true position, whereas an unpresented (outstanding) cheque is simply a timing difference that will resolve itself once presented and needs no Cash Book correction, only disclosure in the Bank Reconciliation Statement.

s:
ABC Bank evaluates two companies applying for identical term loans.
Particular | Company X | Company Y Long-term Debt | ₹180 crore | ₹120 crore Shareholders' Funds | ₹90 crore | ₹160 crore Interest Coverage Ratio | 6.5 times | 3.2 times The Credit Officer recommends Company Y solely because its Debt–Equity Ratio is lower. The Senior Credit Manager disagrees. Which statement is most appropriate?
o: Debt--Equity Ratio should be evaluated together with repayment capacity, profitability, cash flows and debt-servicing ability before arriving at a lending decision.
Debt--Equity Ratio and Interest Coverage Ratio measure exactly the same aspect of financial strength.
A lower Debt--Equity Ratio always guarantees lower credit risk.
Debt--Equity Ratio alone is sufficient for every lending decision.
w: A low Debt-Equity Ratio alone does not guarantee creditworthiness; a lender must also assess the borrower's repayment capacity, profitability trends, actual cash flow generation and overall debt-servicing ability before taking a final lending decision, since capital structure ratios capture only one dimension of financial risk.

s:
The Trial Balance of Vertex Industries Ltd. showed a difference of ₹3,42,000, which was temporarily transferred to a Suspense Account. During investigation, the following errors were identified:
1. Cash received from a debtor ₹1,25,000 was correctly entered in the Cash Book but posted to the debtor's account as ₹1,52,000.
2. Sales Book total was undercast by ₹48,000.
3. Purchase Return of ₹36,000 was correctly entered in the journal but omitted from the supplier's account.
4. Salary paid ₹84,000 was posted twice to Salary Account.
The Finance Executive comments: "Every correction involving the Suspense Account ultimately affects the company's profit." Which statement is technically correct?
o: Incorrect, because Suspense Account merely facilitates temporary balancing of one-sided errors; many corrections affect only ledger balances and not profit.
Correct, because every posting error changes the Statement of Profit and Loss.
Correct, because Suspense Account is opened only for revenue-related errors.
Incorrect, because Suspense Account is used only while preparing Bank Reconciliation Statements.
w: The Suspense Account is merely a temporary balancing tool used to make a Trial Balance agree when one-sided errors are discovered; many rectification entries involving the Suspense Account affect only ledger account balances (like correcting a wrongly posted amount) and do not necessarily alter the reported profit figure at all.

s:
A large manufacturing company plans to shift its banking operations to a Neo Banking Platform. The platform offers:
• API integration with ERP.
• Automated vendor payments.
• Virtual corporate debit cards.
• AI-based reconciliation.
• Cash flow analytics.
The CFO asks whether the Neo Bank can independently:
• Accept deposits,
• Lend funds, and
• Maintain CRR/SLR with RBI.
Which statement is correct?
o: Neo Banks may independently accept deposits but cannot provide payment services.
Neo Banks are exempt from RBI regulation because they operate digitally.
Neo Banks generally provide technology-driven banking services through partnerships with licensed banks, while regulated banking activities remain with the partner bank.
Every Neo Bank automatically receives a banking licence after registration.
w: Most Neo Banks function as technology-driven service providers that deliver banking products digitally, but they do so in partnership with an RBI-licensed bank that holds the actual banking licence and carries out the regulated activities (like accepting deposits); Neo Banks themselves typically do not hold an independent licence.

s:
ABC Ltd. has issued ₹60 crore, 9% Debentures, redeemable after 6 years. The Board creates a Sinking Fund by investing fixed annual amounts in Government Securities.
The CFO makes the following observations:
1. A Sinking Fund spreads the financial burden of redemption over several years.
2. Income earned on Sinking Fund investments increases the amount available for redemption.
3. Creation of a Sinking Fund removes the legal obligation to redeem debentures on maturity.
4.
The primary objective is to ensure availability of funds for redemption. Which combination is correct?
o: All four statements
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 4 only
w: A sinking fund sets aside fixed amounts each year and invests them, so the redemption burden is spread (1) and investment income adds to the fund (2); its purpose is to have cash ready at redemption (4). It does not remove the legal obligation to redeem (3 wrong).

s:
Delta Engineering Ltd. purchased machinery costing ₹1.80 crore. Original estimates:
• Useful Life : 10 years
• Residual Value : ₹20 lakh After five years, a revised technical report estimates the residual value at ₹8 lakh, while the remaining useful life remains unchanged. The Accounts Officer proposes recalculating depreciation for all previous years. The Statutory Auditor disagrees. Which accounting treatment is correct?
o: The revision represents a change in accounting estimate and should be applied prospectively over the remaining useful life.
The reduction should be adjusted directly against General Reserve.
Residual value becomes irrelevant after the asset is put to use.
Previous years' depreciation should always be recomputed whenever residual value changes.
w: A change in the estimated salvage (residual) value of an asset is treated as a change in accounting estimate under AS 5, and is applied prospectively — the remaining depreciable amount (cost less revised residual value less accumulated depreciation) is spread over the asset's remaining useful life, without restating depreciation already charged in prior years.

s:
The Trial Balance of Omega Components Ltd. agreed on 31 March 2026. Audit reveals the following independent errors:
• Machinery purchased for ₹9,80,000 debited to Repairs Account.
• Sales Return Book overcast by ₹45,000.
• Credit purchase from Rahul Traders ₹2,10,000 posted to his account as ₹1,20,000.
• Discount Received ₹18,000 credited to Discount Allowed Account.
The Audit Committee asks whether all these errors have identical effects on the financial statements. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Since the Trial Balance agreed, no rectification entry is necessary.
Different errors have different accounting consequences---some affect profit, some affect asset valuation, while others affect only ledger balances.
Every error merely affects classification and therefore does not influence reported profit.
Every error should be rectified through the Suspense Account.
w: Different types of errors have different accounting consequences: some (like errors of omission or errors of principle affecting revenue items) impact reported profit, others (like wrongly capitalising or expensing an item) affect asset valuation, and still others (like errors of posting within the same class of accounts) affect only ledger balances without touching profit — so a uniform assumption about impact would be incorrect.

s:
ABC Bank evaluates a proposal for enhancement of working capital limits. Financial information:
Particulars | FY 2025 | FY 2026 Current Ratio | 2.10 : 1 | 2.08 : 1 Quick Ratio | 1.28 : 1 | 0.82 : 1 Inventory Holding Period | 52 Days | 96 Days
The borrower argues that liquidity has not deteriorated because the Current Ratio has remained almost unchanged. The Credit Manager disagrees. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
o: The sharp decline in Quick Ratio together with increased inventory holding suggests funds are increasingly locked in inventory, requiring further analysis.
Since the Current Ratio exceeds 2:1, liquidity is satisfactory.
Quick Ratio becomes irrelevant once Current Ratio exceeds 2:1.
Inventory has no impact on liquidity because it forms part of Current Assets.
w: A current ratio remaining broadly stable can mask a real decline in liquidity if the composition of current assets shifts towards less liquid items; here, the sharp fall in Quick Ratio combined with a near-doubling of inventory holding period signals that increasing amounts of working capital are getting tied up in slow-moving inventory, which needs closer investigation despite the current ratio appearing steady.

s: Prime Metals Ltd. sells goods exceeding the prescribed threshold under the Income-tax Act. The buyer requests the seller not to collect TCS, arguing that GST has already been charged on the invoice. The Accounts Manager seeks advice. Which statement is technically correct?
o: TCS applies only to export transactions.
Once GST is charged, TCS cannot apply.
TCS can be collected only by Government departments.
Applicability of TCS should be examined independently under the Income- tax Act. GST and TCS operate under different statutes.
w: TCS is governed by the Income-tax Act and GST by the CGST/IGST Acts. Charging GST on an invoice does not remove an Income-tax TCS obligation; each is tested under its own law.

s:
A manufacturing company evaluates two alternatives for acquiring an automated packaging line.
Alternative A Purchase today for ₹1.52 crore Alternative B Lease by paying ₹36 lakh at the end of each year for five years
Additional Information:
• Cost of Capital = 10%
• PVAF (10%, 5 years) = 3.7908
The Finance Executive recommends purchasing because total lease payments amount to ₹1.80 crore. The CFO recommends evaluating the proposal using the Time Value of Money. Which alternative is financially preferable?
o: Lease because the present value of lease payments is lower than the immediate purchase price.
Purchase because the total lease payments exceed the purchase price.
Both alternatives are financially identical.
Time Value of Money should not be considered in lease-versus-purchase decisions.
w: Comparing the present value of the annual lease payments (discounted at the given cost of capital using the PVAF) against the immediate purchase price shows that the present value of leasing is lower than the purchase cost, making the lease option financially preferable in time-value-of- money terms, even though its nominal total (₹1.80 crore) exceeds the purchase price.

s: After the balance sheet date but before approval of accounts, a fire destroys a warehouse (no doubt about going concern). The accountant reduces the year-end stock and assets because "the accounts are not yet approved". The correct treatment is:
o: Do not adjust; disclose the event in the report if it is material
Ignore the event entirely because it happened after year-end
Adjust the year-end figures because the accounts were not yet approved
Adjust only if the loss exceeds 10% of net profit
w: Trap: 'not yet approved' does not make every event adjusting. A fire is a new condition arising after the balance sheet date: non-adjusting under AS 4, disclosed if material.

s: A company received a government grant of ₹10 lakh in cash this year towards a machine with a 10-year life. The accountant credits the full ₹10 lakh to P&L because "cash was received this year". Under AS 12 the grant should be:
o: Credited fully to P&L this year because cash was received
Kept outside the books until the machine is sold
Credited to Share Capital as owners' funds
Reduced from cost or released over the machine's life
w: Trap: receipt of cash ≠ income. AS 12 matches a grant on a depreciable asset with the depreciation, either by reducing cost or as deferred income.

s: Which of the following is TRUE under AS 26?
o: An internally generated brand cannot be recognised as an asset even if it is valuable
All research and development spend can be capitalised once a patent is filed
Staff training on new software can be capitalised as part of the software
Pre-launch advertising can be capitalised if it builds the brand
w: Trap: 'it adds value, so capitalise'. AS 26 bans internally generated brands, mastheads and customer lists, and always expenses advertising, training and research.

s: A related-party question: two companies, X Ltd and Y Ltd, have one director in common and no other link. X sells goods to Y. Under AS 18:
o: No disclosure: a common director alone isn't a link
Disclosure is required only if the sale was at a loss
Disclosure is required only if payment was in cash
Disclosure is required because they share a director
w: Trap: common director = related. AS 18 expressly excludes two companies related only through a common director.

s: Under AS 7, a contract is 25% complete; total estimated cost now exceeds the contract price by ₹8 crore. How much loss is recognised this year?
o: ₹6 crore — the loss on the remaining 75% only
₹8 crore — the full expected loss
Nil — loss is recognised only on completion
₹2 crore — 25% of the expected loss
w: Trap: applying percentage-of-completion to losses. Expected losses are recognised immediately in full (prudence).

s: Under AS 2, which value is used for inventory: cost ₹50,000; NRV ₹46,000; replacement cost ₹44,000?
w: Trap: using replacement cost or the lowest number. AS 2 = lower of cost and NRV → ₹46,000. Replacement cost is relevant only for raw materials when the finished goods' NRV is below cost.

s: Under AS 28, recoverable amount of an asset is:
o: Always the net selling price
The carrying amount less accumulated depreciation
The higher of net selling price and value in use
The lower of net selling price and value in use
w: Trap: 'lower of'. A rational owner would sell or use, whichever gives more, so recoverable amount is the HIGHER figure; impairment arises only if carrying amount exceeds it.

s: A company's long-term investment in shares falls 5% below cost due to a temporary market dip. The accountant writes it down because "AS 13 requires market value". The correct view is:
o: Long-term investments are shown at the lower of cost and market value
The fall must be credited to a revaluation reserve
Long-term investments stay at cost; only a decline other than temporary is provided for
All investments must be shown at market value every year
w: Trap: mixing current and long-term rules. Lower of cost and fair value applies to CURRENT investments; long-term ones are at cost less permanent diminution.

s: Which concept explains why a proprietor's capital is shown as a liability of the business?
o: Dual aspect concept alone
Money measurement concept
Business entity concept
Going concern concept
w: Trap: 'dual aspect'. Because the business is a separate entity from its owner, it owes the capital to the owner, which is why capital appears among liabilities.

s: Closing stock is valued at ₹4.8 lakh (cost) though its market value is ₹5.6 lakh. Which convention is applied?
o: Consistency
Conservatism (prudence)
Materiality
Cost concept
w: Trap: 'cost concept'. Choosing the LOWER of cost and market for stock is conservatism: don't anticipate the unrealised gain.

s: A firm bought a building for ₹50 lakh; it is now worth ₹80 lakh. Keeping it at ₹50 lakh (less depreciation) applies:
o: Money measurement concept
Cost concept, supported by going concern
Realisation concept
Conservatism, because gains are never recorded
w: Trap: confusing with conservatism. Fixed assets stay at historical cost because the business will use them, not sell them (going concern).

s: Which transaction INCREASES total assets but does NOT change capital?
o: Cash sales at a profit
Furniture bought for cash
Owner introducing cash
Goods purchased on credit
w: Trap: furniture for cash (assets unchanged, one up one down). Credit purchase raises stock and creditors equally.

s: Profit for the year is ₹4 lakh; drawings ₹1 lakh; fresh capital ₹2 lakh; closing capital ₹15 lakh. Opening capital was:
o: ₹12 lakh
₹16 lakh
₹10 lakh
₹8 lakh
w: Closing = Opening + Fresh + Profit − Drawings → 15 = O + 2 + 4 − 1 → O = ₹10 lakh. Trap: adding drawings instead of subtracting gives ₹8 lakh.

s: Income received in advance is recorded as a liability mainly because of:
o: The conservatism convention only
The going concern concept only
The cost concept
The accrual concept: it is not yet earned
w: Trap: 'conservatism'. Income is recognised when earned; cash received early is a liability until the service is rendered.

s: Which statement is correct?
o: Consistency means a method can never be changed once adopted
Materiality means every item must be shown separately
Consistency permits a justified change, with disclosure
Conservatism requires creating secret reserves wherever possible
w: Trap words: 'never', 'every', 'wherever possible'. Consistency permits justified change with disclosure; materiality allows insignificant items to be grouped; conservatism does not allow secret reserves.

s: Capital ₹6 lakh; liabilities ₹4 lakh. The firm repays ₹1 lakh of a loan and the owner withdraws ₹50,000. Total assets now are:
o: ₹10 lakh
₹9 lakh
₹8.5 lakh
₹9.5 lakh
w: Assets = 10 lakh at start. Loan repayment: assets −1. Drawings: assets −0.5. 10 − 1.5 = ₹8.5 lakh (liabilities 3, capital 5.5).

s: Discount Allowed is a:
o: Nominal account
Representative personal account
Real account
Personal account
w: Trap: 'personal' because it relates to a debtor. Discount allowed is a loss/expense, so it is nominal.

s: Goodwill purchased is classified as:
o: Artificial personal account
Fictitious asset
Intangible real account
Nominal account
w: Trap: 'nominal' because it is not physical. Goodwill is a (intangible) real account.

s: Salary outstanding is classified as:
o: Nominal account
Real account
Representative personal account
Artificial personal account
w: Trap: 'nominal' because salary is an expense. The outstanding salary account represents the employees to whom it is owed.

s: Office furniture is bought on credit from Modern Furnishers. Debit:
o: Furniture A/c; credit Cash A/c
Purchases A/c; credit Modern Furnishers
Modern Furnishers; credit Furniture A/c
Furniture A/c; credit Modern Furnishers
w: Trap: 'Purchases'. Purchases is only for goods meant for resale; furniture is a fixed asset (real account: debit what comes in).

s: Goods worth ₹5,000 (cost) are distributed as free samples. The entry is:
o: Drawings A/c Dr; To Purchases A/c
Purchases A/c Dr; To Advertisement A/c
Advertisement A/c Dr; To Purchases A/c
Advertisement A/c Dr; To Sales A/c
w: Trap: crediting Sales. Samples are not sold; their cost is removed from purchases and treated as advertisement expense.

s: Cash ₹50,000 withdrawn from bank for office use. In a double-column cash book this is:
o: Recorded only in the cash column
A contra entry in both columns
Recorded only in the journal proper
Recorded in the petty cash book
w: Trap: one-column thinking. Both cash and bank are affected, so it is a contra entry marked 'C'.

s: Under the imprest system, the petty cashier spent ₹3,800 out of a float of ₹5,000. The main cashier will give him:
w: Trap: giving the full float again. Imprest = reimburse exactly what was spent so the float returns to ₹5,000.

s: A credit purchase of a computer for office use is recorded in:
o: Purchases book
Bills payable book
Journal proper
Cash book
w: Trap: 'Purchases book'. The purchases book is only for credit purchases of goods for resale; credit purchase of assets goes to the journal proper.

s: Errors found: (a) Purchases Book undercast by ₹3,000; (b) ₹1,500 paid to Ram debited to Shyam; (c) a sales return of ₹700 from Hari posted to the DEBIT of Hari's account. The Suspense Account was opened with:
o: ₹3,700 on the debit side
₹1,600 on the debit side
₹5,200 on the debit side
₹2,300 on the credit side
w: (a) debit side short 3,000. (b) no effect (two-sided). (c) Hari should be credited 700 but was debited 700 → debit side excess 1,400. Net debit short = 3,000 − 1,400 = 1,600 → suspense debited ₹1,600.

s: For the same errors [(a) purchases book undercast ₹3,000; (b) Ram/Shyam; (c) Hari's account], rectification will change net profit by:
o: Nil, as all are posting errors
w: Only (a) touches a nominal account (purchases up by 3,000 → profit down 3,000). (b) and (c) affect personal accounts only. Trap: equating profit effect with the suspense balance.

s: A credit sale of ₹6,000 to Anil was entered in the Sales Book as ₹600. This error:
o: Is a compensating error
Is an error of principle
Affects the Trial Balance by ₹5,400
Leaves the TB agreeing; both sides understated ₹5,400
w: Trap: thinking every wrong amount disturbs the TB. A wrong amount in the book of original entry is posted wrongly to both sides.

s: Which error must be corrected through the Suspense Account?
o: Purchase from Ravi credited to Ravindra's account
Sales Book overcast by ₹2,000
Repairs debited to Machinery A/c
Credit sale to Mohan omitted completely
w: Only one-sided errors go through suspense. Overcasting a book affects only the sales account. The others are two-sided or complete omissions.

s: ₹2,500 received from Sita was correctly entered in the cash book but posted to the DEBIT of Sita's account. The rectifying entry is:
o: Suspense A/c Dr ₹5,000; To Sita ₹5,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹2,500; To Sita ₹2,500
Sita Dr ₹5,000; To Suspense ₹5,000
Suspense A/c Dr ₹2,500; To Sita ₹2,500
w: Trap: correcting with the single amount. Wrong side means cancel the wrong debit AND record the correct credit: double.

s: Repairs of ₹40,000 to a building were debited to the Building Account. Effect if not corrected:
o: Profit overstated, Trial Balance disagrees by ₹40,000
No effect, since the amount was correctly paid
Profit overstated, assets overstated, Trial Balance agrees
Profit understated, assets overstated, Trial Balance agrees
w: Revenue expenditure capitalised (error of principle): expense missing → profit up; building inflated; both sides posted → TB agrees.

s: A purchase of ₹9,000 from Gopal was entered correctly in the Purchases Book but posted to Gopal's account as ₹900. The error is:
o: An error of principle that does not disturb the Trial Balance
A compensating error
An error of commission that disturbs the Trial Balance
An error of omission that does not disturb the Trial Balance
w: Purchases debited 9,000 but Gopal credited only 900: one-sided posting error → TB credit side short by 8,100.

s: Which statement is correct?
o: A suspense account is opened for errors of principle
A Trial Balance can agree even when errors exist in the books
Compensating errors always cause disagreement of the Trial Balance
Agreement of the Trial Balance proves the accounts are correct
w: Errors of omission, principle and compensating errors don't disturb TB totals.

s: An error discovered after closing the books: sale of an old machine ₹30,000 was credited to Sales last year. The correction this year is:
o: Machinery A/c Dr; To Sales A/c
Suspense A/c Dr; To Machinery A/c
Sales A/c Dr; To Machinery A/c
P&L Adjustment A/c Dr; To Machinery A/c
w: Trap: debiting Sales, which was already closed. Last year's sales were overstated (profit overstated), so the adjustment goes through P&L Adjustment; Machinery is still overstated, so it is credited.

s: A Trial Balance is NOT used to detect which of the following?
o: An error of principle
A casting error in the sales book
Wrong balancing of an account
A one-sided posting error
w: Errors of principle record both sides correctly in amount, so totals still agree. The others are one-sided.

s: Cash book shows an OVERDRAFT of ₹50,000. Cheques deposited but not credited ₹8,000; cheques issued not presented ₹12,000; interest on overdraft ₹1,500 not in the cash book. Overdraft as per pass book is:
w: Treat as −50,000: uncredited deposits −8,000; unpresented cheques +12,000; OD interest −1,500 → −47,500. Trap: using favourable-balance signs gives 52,500.

s: Pass book shows a credit balance of ₹30,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹5,000; a customer's direct deposit of ₹2,000 not in cash book; bank charges ₹300 not in cash book. Balance as per cash book is:
w: From pass book: less unpresented cheques 5,000 (cash book already reduced) = 25,000; less direct deposit 2,000 = 23,000; add bank charges 300 = 23,300. Trap: using cash-book-start signs.

s: Which item requires NO entry in the cash book?
o: A customer's cheque returned dishonoured
A cheque issued but not yet presented
Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest credited by the bank
w: Only timing differences (unpresented / uncollected cheques) need no cash-book entry. Bank-originated items must be recorded.

s: While preparing the BRS starting from a favourable cash-book balance, a dishonoured cheque not yet recorded in the cash book is:
o: Ignored
Deducted
Added
Added and then deducted
w: The bank has already reduced the balance, so the pass book is lower: deduct.

s: The bank wrongly debited ₹4,000 belonging to another customer to our account. The correct action is:
o: Write it off as a bad debt
Show it in the BRS only and ask the bank to reverse it
Record it in the cash book and claim later
Record it in the cash book as a bank charge
w: A bank's error is not our transaction. Our cash book is correct; the item appears only in the BRS.

s: The balance of bank to be shown in the Balance Sheet is:
o: The pass-book balance
The unadjusted cash-book balance
The higher of the two balances
The adjusted cash-book balance
w: After recording bank-originated items, the adjusted cash book shows the true balance. Trap: 'pass book because bank prepares it'.

s: Starting from the pass-book balance, 'cheques deposited but not yet credited' are:
o: Ignored
Added to arrive at the cash-book balance
Deducted to arrive at the cash-book balance
Added only in an overdraft situation
w: The cash book already includes them, the pass book doesn't, so the cash book is higher: add.

s: In the cash book, a deposit of ₹56,000 was wrongly recorded as ₹65,000. Starting from the cash-book balance, this error is:
o: Added by ₹9,000
Ignored as a timing difference
Deducted by ₹9,000, cash book corrected
Deducted by ₹65,000
w: The cash book is overstated by 9,000. Deduct it in the BRS and correct the cash book; it is our error, not a timing difference.

s: Which pair is correctly matched?
o: Overdraft – debit in both cash book and pass book
Favourable balance – debit in cash book, credit in pass book
Favourable balance – credit in cash book, debit in pass book
Overdraft – debit in cash book, credit in pass book
w: Mirror image: our asset (debit) is the bank's liability (credit). An overdraft is the reverse.

s: An insurance premium of ₹6,000 was paid by the bank under standing instructions; not in the cash book. In the adjusted cash book:
o: Debit Bank and credit Insurance
Debit Bank ₹6,000
No entry; show only in the BRS
Credit Bank ₹6,000 (debit Insurance)
w: It is a real payment we have not recorded: insurance expense debit, bank credit.

s: A machine costs ₹1,00,000; freight ₹5,000; installation ₹5,000; residual value ₹10,000; life 5 years; SLM. Annual depreciation is:
w: Depreciable amount = (1,00,000 + 5,000 + 5,000) − 10,000 = 1,00,000 ÷ 5 = 20,000. Traps: ignoring freight/installation (18,000) or residual (22,000).

s: An asset costing ₹2,00,000 is bought on 1 October; WDV 15%; the year ends 31 March. First year's depreciation is:
w: 6 months: 2,00,000 × 15% × 6/12 = 15,000. Trap: charging a full year (30,000).

s: A company changes its depreciation method from SLM to WDV after a review of the pattern of benefits. Under AS 10 this is:
o: Not permitted once a method is adopted
A change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively
A prior period item
A change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively
w: Trap: 'policy, retrospective' (old AS 6 view). Under revised AS 10 a change in depreciation method is a change in estimate.

s: Which statement about depreciation is correct?
o: It is charged only when the asset is actually used
It values the asset at its market price
It is a non-cash charge that reduces profit but does not create cash
It is a source of funds because it is added back in the cash flow statement
w: Trap: 'source of funds'. It is added back only because it was deducted without cash outflow. Depreciation starts when the asset is available for use.

s: ₹6,00,000 asset, WDV 20%. Which is the book value at the end of Year 3?
w: 6,00,000 × 0.8³ = 6,00,000 × 0.512 = 3,07,200. 2,40,000 would be SLM at 20% of cost; 3,84,000 is the value after only 2 years.

s: A machine bought for ₹50 lakh is depreciated by SLM over 10 years (nil residual). After 4 years its remaining life is revised to 3 years. Depreciation from Year 5 is:
o: ₹5 lakh a year
₹16.67 lakh a year
₹10 lakh a year
₹7.14 lakh a year
w: Carrying amount after 4 years = 50 − 20 = 30 lakh. Spread over 3 remaining years = ₹10 lakh. Traps: keeping 5 lakh, or using total cost ÷ 3.

s: Which of the following can reduce an asset's book value to exactly zero?
o: SLM with nil residual value
WDV at any rate
WDV at a very high rate such as 90%
Units of production with a residual value
w: WDV applies a % to a declining balance, so a balance always remains; SLM with nil residual writes off fully.

s: A transport operator's buses earn most in early years and need heavy repairs later. Choose the method:
o: Sinking fund
Annuity
SLM
WDV
w: WDV gives high early charges and lower later charges, balancing rising repairs. Trap: SLM because it is simple.

s: Which is REVENUE expenditure?
o: Lubricants for routine servicing of a machine
Wages to own staff for installing a new machine
Freight paid to bring a new machine to the factory
Overhaul that extends a machine's life by 5 years
w: Trap: 'it relates to machinery, so capital'. Routine servicing maintains; the others bring the asset into use or extend its life.

s: Which is CAPITAL expenditure?
o: Carriage on goods purchased
Annual painting of the office
Repairs to a delivery van
Legal fees paid to buy land
w: Costs to acquire an asset are capitalised. Painting, routine repairs and freight on stock are revenue.

s: GST paid on a machine is ₹1.8 lakh and full ITC is available. It should be:
o: Added to the machine's cost
Added to cost and depreciated over the machine's life
Excluded from the machine's cost and taken as input tax credit
Charged to P&L as an expense
w: Only NON-refundable taxes are part of cost under AS 10. Creditable GST is recovered, so it is not a cost.

s: Insurance claim received for a building destroyed by fire is a:
o: Deferred revenue receipt
Revenue expenditure
Capital receipt
Revenue receipt
w: Claim relating to a fixed asset is capital; for stock it is revenue.

s: Cost of training staff to operate a newly installed machine is:
o: Part of the machine's cost
Revenue expenditure
Capital expenditure
Deferred revenue expenditure to be capitalised
w: AS 10 excludes training costs from the cost of PPE.

s: Replacement of a worn-out roof of a factory with a similar roof (no improvement) is generally:
o: Revenue expenditure (repairs)
Capital expenditure as it is large
Capital loss
Deferred revenue expenditure
w: Size doesn't decide. Restoring the existing condition is maintenance; improving capacity or life would be capital. (Under the component approach a significant separately-identified component may be capitalised with derecognition of the old one.)

s: Interest paid on a loan taken to construct a factory, for the period AFTER the factory started production, is:
o: Part of the factory's cost
Deferred revenue expenditure
Revenue expenditure
Capital expenditure
w: AS 16 stops capitalisation when the asset is ready for use. Interest during construction is capital; after that, revenue.

s: A bill dated 15 March 2026 is payable 60 days after date. Ignoring holidays, its due date is:
w: Exclude the date of drawing: 16–31 Mar = 16 days, April = 30 (46), 14 days of May = 60 → 14 May; + 3 grace days = 17 May. Trap: forgetting grace days (14 May).

s: A bill dated 29 January 2026 is payable one month after date. Its due date is:
o: 1 March 2026
4 March 2026
3 March 2026
28 February 2026
w: February 2026 has no 29th, so take its last day, 28 February, + 3 days of grace = 3 March.

s: Which instrument is NOT entitled to days of grace?
o: A bill payable on demand
A bill payable 60 days after sight
A bill payable 3 months after date
A promissory note payable 90 days after date
w: Days of grace apply only to instruments payable after a fixed period, not to demand or sight instruments or cheques.

s: A bill that the drawer had ENDORSED to his creditor Ram is dishonoured. In the drawer's books:
o: Debit the acceptor; credit Bank
Debit the acceptor; credit Bills Receivable
Debit Ram; credit the acceptor
Debit the acceptor (drawee); credit Ram
w: Trap: crediting B/R. The bill left the drawer's B/R account on endorsement; Ram now has a claim back on the drawer, who in turn charges the acceptor.

s: Rebate allowed on a bill retired before maturity is, for the holder (drawer):
o: Added to the bill's value
An income
An expense (loss)
A capital receipt
w: The holder accepts less than face value for early payment: loss for the holder, income for the acceptor.

s: When a drawer discounts a bill with the bank, the discount is:
o: Added to the cost of goods sold
Credited to Discount A/c as income
A finance cost; sales are not affected
Deducted from Sales A/c
w: The sale was recorded when goods were sold; discounting is a financing act, so the discount is a finance cost.

s: Which statement about an accommodation bill is correct?
o: It cannot be discounted with any bank
It always arises from a genuine sale of goods
It is accepted without consideration, to raise funds
It is void and unenforceable by anyone
w: No trade behind it; but a holder in due course for value can enforce it. Banks avoid it as it is not self-liquidating.

s: In the drawee's books, acceptance of a bill drawn by a creditor is recorded as:
o: Creditor A/c Dr; To Bills Payable A/c
Bills Receivable A/c Dr; To Creditor A/c
Purchases A/c Dr; To Bills Payable A/c
Bills Payable A/c Dr; To Creditor A/c
w: The debt to the creditor is replaced by a bill payable (liability).

s: Which audit in banks is carried out at or near the time of the transaction?
o: RBI inspection
Statutory audit
Concurrent audit
Long Form Audit Report
w: Concurrent audit is the continuous, early-warning part of internal audit. Statutory audit is year-end; RBI inspects periodically; LFAR is a statutory auditor's report.

s: Approval of a bank's statutory auditors by RBI is under which section of the BR Act?
o: Section 29
Section 30
Section 35
Section 17
w: Sec 29 = accounts format; Sec 30 = audit; Sec 35 = inspection; Sec 17 = reserve fund.

s: In bank inter-branch accounts, which balances are the main risk?
o: Entries originated by the head office
Entries reconciled within a week
Long-pending unreconciled DEBIT entries
Long-pending unreconciled credit entries
w: Old unmatched debits can hide frauds or losses; RBI requires 100% provision on net debits outstanding over one year.

s: The Long Form Audit Report is submitted by:
o: Concurrent auditors
RBI inspection team
Statutory central and branch auditors
Internal inspectors of the bank
w: LFAR accompanies the statutory audit report.

s: Risk-Based Internal Audit means:
o: Only loss-making branches are audited
Audit is replaced by branch self-certification
Every branch is audited every month
Audit effort depends on each unit's assessed risk
w: RBIA concentrates audit effort on high-risk branches and activities.

s: In treasury, confirmation and settlement of deals are done by the:
o: Front office (dealers)
Mid office
Branch manager
Back office
w: Dealers deal (front), mid office monitors risk and limits, back office confirms, settles and accounts: separation of duties.

s: Opening stock ₹20,000; purchases ₹80,000; wages ₹6,000; freight inward ₹4,000; freight outward ₹3,000; sales ₹1,50,000; sales returns ₹10,000; closing stock ₹25,000. Gross profit is:
w: COGS = 20 + 80 + 6 + 4 − 25 = 85 (thousand). Net sales = 140. GP = 55. Traps: putting freight outward in COGS (52) or ignoring returns (65).

s: Debtors ₹60,000; further bad debts ₹1,000; provision 5% on debtors; old provision ₹2,000; bad debts in TB ₹1,200. Debtors shown in the Balance Sheet:
Insurance of ₹24,000 paid on 1 January for one year; year ends 31 March. The Balance Sheet shows prepaid insurance of:
w: Only Jan–Mar (3 months = ₹6,000) is this year's expense; 9 months (₹18,000) is prepaid. Trap: showing the expired part as prepaid.

s: Carriage outward is shown in the:
o: Trading Account (debit side)
Profit & Loss Account (debit side)
Balance Sheet as an asset
Trading Account (credit side)
w: Carriage outward is a selling expense; carriage inward is a direct expense for the Trading A/c.

s: Goods costing ₹10,000 taken by the proprietor for personal use are:
o: Added to sales
Ignored, as they are the owner's own goods
Added to closing stock
Deducted from purchases and added to drawings
w: Entry: Drawings Dr; To Purchases (at cost).

s: Interest on a partner's LOAN to the firm is:
o: Debited to the Profit & Loss Account as a charge
Ignored if the firm makes a loss
Credited to the partner's capital as profit share
Debited to the P&L Appropriation Account
w: A partner's loan is like an outsider's loan; its interest is a charge payable even in loss years. Interest on CAPITAL is an appropriation.
