s: Commission received in advance ₹5,000 is shown:
o: Added to commission in P&L and shown as an asset
Deducted from income; shown as a liability
Only in the Trading Account
Only in the Balance Sheet as income
w: Income received in advance is not yet earned: reduce the income and show the liability.

s: Which item appears on the CREDIT side of a partnership's P&L Appropriation Account?
o: Interest on capital
Partner's salary
Interest on drawings
Transfer to reserve
w: Interest on drawings is charged to partners, so it adds to divisible profit; the others are appropriations (debits).

s: Stock costing ₹40,000 was lost in fire; the insurance claim was admitted for ₹25,000 (not yet received). In the final accounts:
o: Only ₹15,000 is debited to the Trading A/c
₹40,000 debited to P&L and nothing else recorded
Trading Cr ₹40,000; P&L Dr ₹15,000; claim ₹25,000 an asset
Closing stock increased by ₹25,000
w: The loss of goods is removed from Trading at cost; the uninsured loss is in P&L; the claim is a receivable.

s: Accrued interest on investments ₹3,000 is shown:
o: Deducted from interest income in P&L
Added to income; shown as a current asset
As a liability
Only in a note to accounts
w: Income earned but not received: add to income and show as receivable.

s: Gross profit is 20% on COST. Sales are ₹1,20,000. Gross profit is:
Closing stock appears in the Trading Account and Balance Sheet. When it also appears INSIDE the Trial Balance it is shown:
o: Only in the Balance Sheet
In the P&L Account
Only in the Trading Account
In both the Trading Account and the Balance Sheet
w: If it is already in the TB (adjusted purchases), it has been accounted through purchases; it goes only to the Balance Sheet.

s: A company offered 50,000 shares; applications 80,000; applications for 10,000 rejected; rest allotted pro-rata. Mr X applied for 1,400 shares. He gets:
o: 1,000 shares
1,120 shares
1,400 shares
875 shares
w: Accepted applications = 70,000 for 50,000 → 5/7. 1,400 × 5/7 = 1,000. Trap: ratio 50/80 gives 875.

s: 500 shares of ₹10 (issued at par): application ₹3, allotment ₹4, call ₹3. Holder paid application and allotment; shares forfeited. Entry:
o: Share Forfeiture Dr ₹3,500; To Share Capital ₹3,500
Share Capital Dr ₹5,000; To Share Forfeiture ₹5,000
Share Capital Dr 5,000; To Calls 1,500; To Forfeiture 3,500
Share Capital Dr ₹3,500; To Share Forfeiture ₹3,500
w: Debit Share Capital with called-up ₹10 × 500; credit unpaid call; credit forfeiture with the amount received (₹7 × 500).

s: Those 500 forfeited shares (forfeiture ₹3,500) are reissued at ₹6 per share fully paid. Capital Reserve:
o: Nil
w: Discount on reissue = ₹4 × 500 = 2,000, adjusted against forfeiture; balance 3,500 − 2,000 = 1,500 → Capital Reserve.

s: Shares can be issued at a discount under the Companies Act, 2013:
o: Only as sweat equity; otherwise void
Never, not even as sweat equity
Freely, with a special resolution
Up to 10% discount with RBI approval
w: Sec 53 prohibits issue at a discount except sweat equity (Sec 54).

s: Interest payable on calls-in-advance (Table F default) is up to:
w: Table F: interest on calls in arrears up to 10%; on calls in advance up to 12%.

s: Preference shareholders get voting rights on ALL resolutions when:
o: The company issues bonus shares
The company makes a loss in any year
They hold more than 10% of total capital
Their dividend is unpaid for 2 years or more
w: Otherwise they vote only on matters affecting their rights.

s: A government company is one in which the government holds at least:
o: 100% of the share capital
26% of the paid-up share capital
74% of the paid-up share capital
51% of the paid-up share capital
w: Sec 2(45): not less than 51% held by Central and/or State Governments.

s: 'Subscribed capital' is that part of issued capital which:
o: Has been called up by the company
Has been paid up by shareholders
Is mentioned in the Memorandum as the maximum
Has been taken up by the public
w: Authorised (maximum) → issued (offered) → subscribed (taken up) → called-up → paid-up.

s: PAT ₹60 lakh; 10 lakh equity shares; bonus 1 : 4 issued during the year. Basic EPS reported for the year is:
w: Bonus shares are treated as outstanding from the beginning: 12.5 lakh shares → 60/12.5 = ₹4.80 (and last year's EPS is restated). Trap: weighting bonus shares from issue date.

s: Rights issue 1 for 3 at ₹120; market price before the issue ₹200. The theoretical ex-rights price is:
Tax depreciation exceeds book depreciation by ₹20 lakh this year; tax rate 25%. Deferred tax:
o: Liability of ₹20 lakh
Asset of ₹5 lakh
Liability of ₹5 lakh
Nil, as depreciation is a non-cash item
w: Higher tax deduction now → lower tax now, more later → DTL = 20 × 25% = ₹5 lakh.

s: A penalty of ₹2 lakh paid for violating pollution law is disallowed for tax. Deferred tax on it is:
o: Recognised only when the penalty is reversed
A deferred tax liability
Nil, because it is a permanent difference
A deferred tax asset
w: Permanent differences never reverse, so no deferred tax.

s: Which reserve CAN be used for issuing fully paid bonus shares?
o: Reserve created on revaluation of land
Revaluation Reserve
Capital Redemption Reserve
Provision for doubtful debts
w: Sec 63: free reserves, securities premium and CRR. Revaluation reserve is barred; a provision is not a reserve.

s: In Schedule III, a security deposit recoverable after three years is shown under:
o: Current investments
Non-current assets
Current assets
Cash and cash equivalents
w: Realisable after 12 months → non-current.

s: Diluted EPS is lower than basic EPS when convertible debentures exist because:
o: Potential shares rise more than the earnings added back
Only the number of shares is adjusted, never earnings
Interest on debentures is deducted twice
Diluted EPS ignores convertible instruments
w: Both numerator and denominator are adjusted; the instrument is dilutive when the incremental EPS is below basic EPS.

s: Which document is part of a company's 'financial statements' under Sec 2(40)?
o: Notice of AGM
Auditor's Report
Statement of changes in equity
Directors' Report
w: Balance sheet, P&L, cash flow statement, SOCE (if applicable) and notes.

s: NPBT ₹25 lakh; depreciation ₹5 lakh; profit on sale of asset ₹2 lakh; decrease in inventory ₹3 lakh; increase in debtors ₹4 lakh; increase in creditors ₹6 lakh; tax paid ₹1.5 lakh. Net cash from operating activities:
o: ₹27.5 lakh
₹33.5 lakh
₹31.5 lakh
₹35.5 lakh
w: 25 + 5 − 2 + 3 − 4 + 6 = 33 cash generated; − 1.5 tax = 31.5. Trap: forgetting tax paid (33.0) or reversing signs.

s: Purchase of machinery ₹12 lakh; sale of old machinery ₹3 lakh; interest received on investments ₹0.5 lakh (non-financial company). Net cash from investing activities:
o: −₹15.5 lakh
−₹8.5 lakh
−₹12 lakh
−₹9 lakh
w: −12 + 3 + 0.5 = −8.5. Interest received is investing for a non-financial company. Trap: leaving it out (−9).

s: Dividend PAID by a manufacturing company is classified as:
o: Investing activity
Financing activity
Not shown in the cash flow statement
Operating activity
w: Payments to owners are financing. Dividend RECEIVED is investing.

s: A company issues shares to a vendor in exchange for land. In the cash flow statement this is:
o: Operating activity
Investing outflow and financing inflow
Excluded, but disclosed as a non-cash transaction
Shown as a financing inflow only
w: No cash moves, so it is not in the statement.

s: Bank overdraft repayable on demand that forms an integral part of cash management is:
o: Shown as an investing activity
Ignored completely
Always shown as a financing inflow
Included in cash and cash equivalents
w: AS 3 allows such overdrafts to be included in cash and cash equivalents.

s: Income tax paid that cannot be specifically identified with investing or financing is classified as:
o: Operating activity
Investing activity
Financing activity
Extraordinary item
w: Taxes on income are operating unless specifically identified otherwise.

s: Under the indirect method, 'loss on sale of machinery' is:
o: Added back to net profit
Deducted from net profit
Shown as an operating outflow
Ignored
w: The loss reduced profit but is not an operating cash outflow; the sale proceeds appear under investing.

s: A 6-month fixed deposit with a bank, made at the start of the year, is:
o: A cash equivalent because it is with a bank
Not a cash equivalent (over 3 months)
Cash on hand
An operating activity
w: Cash equivalents generally mature within three months of acquisition.

s: For a bank, dividend received on investments is classified as:
o: Not shown
Investing activity
Financing activity
Operating activity
w: For financial enterprises, interest and dividend received are operating.

s: Which statement is correct?
o: Depreciation is a cash inflow
Net profit always equals operating cash flow
A profitable company can have negative operating cash flow
Increase in creditors reduces operating cash flow
w: Credit sales, rising stock and receivables can absorb cash despite profits.

s: A loan of ₹20 lakh, doubtful for 4 years (D3), has realisable security of ₹12 lakh. Provision required:
o: ₹12.8 lakh
₹20 lakh
₹14 lakh
₹8 lakh
w: D3 (over 3 years in doubtful): 100% of the secured portion + 100% of the unsecured portion = whole outstanding.

s: A loan of ₹10 lakh has been a sub-standard asset for 8 months (secured). Provision:
w: Sub-standard (NPA up to 12 months) = 15%; unsecured exposure 25%; standard 0.40%.

s: 'Guarantees given on behalf of constituents' appear in a bank's:
o: Other liabilities and provisions (Schedule 5)
Borrowings (Schedule 4)
Advances (Schedule 9)
Contingent liabilities (Schedule 12)
w: Guarantees, LCs, acceptances and forward contracts are contingent liabilities.

s: Commission earned on letters of credit is shown under:
o: Interest expended (Schedule 15)
Other income (Schedule 14)
Interest earned (Schedule 13)
Operating expenses (Schedule 16)
w: Commission, exchange and brokerage are other income; interest/discount on advances and bills is interest earned.

s: Balance held by the bank in its current account with another bank is shown in:
o: Schedule 8 – Investments
Schedule 9 – Advances
Schedule 7 – Balances with banks
Schedule 6 – Cash and balances with RBI
w: Balances with RBI → Sch 6; with other banks → Sch 7.

s: Non-banking assets acquired in satisfaction of claims are shown under:
o: Fixed assets (Schedule 10)
Investments (Schedule 8)
Advances (Schedule 9)
Other assets (Schedule 11)
w: They are listed as a separate item under Other Assets.

s: Printing and stationery expenses of a bank appear in:
o: Operating expenses (Schedule 16)
Interest expended (Schedule 15)
Provisions and contingencies
Other liabilities (Schedule 5)
w: Schedule 16 includes rent, taxes and lighting, printing and stationery, advertisement, depreciation etc.

s: Under Section 17 of the BR Act, and RBI's stricter rule, a scheduled commercial bank transfers to reserve fund at least:
o: 50% of profit
10% of profit
25% of profit (law minimum 20%)
20% only, as RBI has no separate rule
w: BR Act Sec 17 says 20%; RBI requires 25% for SCBs.

s: Bills sent by customers to the bank for collection are shown:
o: Below the balance sheet as a memo item
As advances
As other liabilities
As contingent liabilities
w: The bank is only an agent; no asset or liability arises.

s: Interest on an NPA account that has been charged but not realised is:
o: Credited to the statutory reserve
Taken to income if security is adequate
Not taken to income until realised
Taken to income on accrual basis
w: Income recognition norms: income on NPAs is booked on realisation only.

s: Which error can STILL occur in computerised accounting?
o: Wrong totalling of the ledger
Posting to the wrong side automatically
Trial balance not tallying because of a posting mistake
Entering a transaction with a wrong amount or wrong account
w: Software posts and totals correctly; data-entry errors and errors of principle remain.

s: A speedometer showing continuously varying speed works on the principle of a:
o: Digital computer
Analog computer
Mainframe computer
Supercomputer
w: Continuous physical quantities = analog.

s: Interest application for all savings accounts at month-end in a single run is an example of:
o: Manual processing
Distributed processing by branches
Batch processing
Online real-time processing
w: Transactions collected and processed together = batch.

s: In CBS, 'anywhere banking' is possible mainly because:
o: All branches access a centralised database at the data centre
Customers carry their passbooks to every branch
Each branch keeps a full copy of all customer data
Branches exchange data by courier daily
w: Centralisation makes the customer the bank's, not the branch's.

s: A neo bank in India can:
o: Accept public deposits on its own licence automatically
Maintain CRR/SLR directly with RBI
Offer digital banking services through a partner licensed bank
Issue currency through digital wallets
w: Neo banks have no banking licence of their own; the partner bank does the regulated activities.

s: 'Maker–checker' in bank systems means:
o: The customer checks every entry
The auditor makes all entries
The same officer enters and authorises to save time
One person enters; another verifies and authorises
w: Dual control prevents unauthorised or erroneous entries.

s: Current assets ₹3 lakh, current liabilities ₹1.5 lakh. Goods of ₹50,000 are bought on credit. The current ratio becomes:
o: 2 : 1 (unchanged)
w: (3 + 0.5)/(1.5 + 0.5) = 1.75. Trap: thinking equal additions leave the ratio unchanged. When CR > 1, adding equal amounts to both sides lowers it.

s: Current assets ₹5 lakh include inventory ₹2 lakh and prepaid expenses ₹20,000; current liabilities ₹2.5 lakh. The quick ratio is:
w: Quick assets = 5 − 2 − 0.2 = 2.8; 2.8/2.5 = 1.12. Trap: removing only inventory gives 1.20.

s: COGS ₹60 lakh; opening stock ₹8 lakh; closing stock ₹12 lakh; sales ₹80 lakh. The inventory holding period (365 days) is about:
o: 46 days
55 days
61 days
73 days
w: ITR = 60/10 = 6 → 365/6 ≈ 61 days. Traps: using sales (80/10 = 8 → 46 days) or closing stock only (60/12 = 5 → 73 days).

s: Credit purchases ₹24 lakh; opening creditors ₹3 lakh; closing creditors ₹5 lakh. The average payment period (365 days) is about:
o: 76 days
61 days
91 days
46 days
w: Average creditors = 4; turnover = 24/4 = 6; 365/6 ≈ 61 days. Trap: using closing creditors (5) gives 76 days.

s: For DEBTORS turnover, which figure is used in the numerator?
o: Gross profit
Net credit sales
Cost of goods sold
Total sales including cash sales
w: Only credit sales create debtors. Inventory turnover uses COGS.

s: PAT ₹18 lakh; preference dividend ₹3 lakh; equity shareholders' funds ₹1 crore. Return on equity is:
w: ROE = (18 − 3)/100 = 15%. Trap: not deducting preference dividend (18%).

s: In computing DSCR, which is the correct numerator?
o: PAT + depreciation only
PAT + principal instalment due
EBIT − interest on term loan
PAT + depreciation + interest on term loan
w: Cash available for debt service = profit after tax + non-cash depreciation + interest (added back because it is serviced from the same cash). Denominator = interest + instalment.

s: Which transaction leaves the debt-equity ratio UNCHANGED?
o: Issue of fresh equity for cash
Raising a new term loan
Conversion of debentures into equity
Issue of bonus shares out of general reserve
w: Bonus shares only reclassify reserves into capital; total equity stays the same.

s: A borrower's current ratio rose from 1.6 to 1.9 while quick ratio fell from 1.1 to 0.8. The best inference is:
o: The firm must have repaid its creditors
Liquidity has clearly improved because the current ratio rose
The quick ratio is irrelevant when current ratio is above 1.33
Liquidity may have worsened, with funds getting locked in inventory
w: Current ratio up but quick ratio down means the increase is in inventory. Trap: reading one ratio alone.

s: Which ratio would a supplier giving 30-day credit look at FIRST?
o: Return on equity
Current / quick ratio
Debt Service Coverage Ratio
Price-earnings ratio
w: Short-term creditors care about short-term liquidity. DSCR is for term lenders; P/E and ROE for equity investors.

s: EPS is ₹8 and market price ₹96. Which is correct?
o: P/E = 0.083 and earnings yield = 12%
P/E = 12 and earnings yield = 8.33%
P/E = 8.33 and earnings yield = 12%
P/E = 12 and earnings yield = 12%

s: Proprietary ratio measures:
o: Shareholders' funds to total assets
Debt as a proportion of equity
Current assets to current liabilities
Net profit to sales
w: Proprietary ratio = owners' funds ÷ total assets; the higher it is, the more assets are owner-financed.

s: ₹5,000 invested for 2 years at 8% p.a. compounded QUARTERLY grows to about:
w: 5,000 × 1.02⁸ = 5,858. Traps: annual compounding 5,832; half-yearly 5,849; simple interest 5,800.

s: Rent of ₹1 lakh is payable at the BEGINNING of each year for 4 years. At 10%, its present value is about:
o: ₹3.49 lakh
₹3.17 lakh
₹4.64 lakh
₹4.00 lakh
w: Annuity due PV = 1 × PVAF(10%, 4) × 1.1 = 3.1699 × 1.1 = 3.487. Trap: ordinary annuity (3.17) or no discounting (4.00).

s: A ₹5 lakh loan at 12% p.a. is repaid in 36 equal monthly instalments. The EMI is closest to:
How much must be set aside at the end of each year for 5 years at 8% to accumulate ₹10 lakh (FVAF = 5.8666)?
w: Instalment = 10,00,000 ÷ 5.8666 = 1,70,456. Trap: 10 lakh ÷ 5 ignores interest.

s: What is the present value of a perpetuity of ₹5,000 a year at 8%?
o: Infinite
w: PV = A/r = 5,000/0.08 = 62,500. Trap: 'infinite payments → infinite value'.

s: Using the Rule of 72, at 6% compound interest money doubles in about:
o: 10 years
6 years
16.7 years
12 years
w: 72/6 = 12 years. Trap: simple interest (100/6 = 16.7 years).

s: Which statement on EMIs (reducing balance) is correct?
o: The principal portion falls with each instalment
Interest is charged on the original loan amount throughout
Interest part falls and principal part rises each month
Interest and principal portions remain equal throughout
w: Interest is on the outstanding balance, which reduces every month. Trap: flat-rate thinking.

s: A borrower must choose between 10% compounded annually and 9.6% compounded monthly. The cheaper one is:
o: 9.6% compounded monthly, because its nominal rate is lower
10% compounded annually
Cannot be decided without the loan amount
Both cost exactly the same
w: EAR of 9.6% monthly = (1.008)¹² − 1 ≈ 10.03%, slightly above 10%. So 10% annual is (marginally) cheaper. Trap: comparing nominal rates.

s: In an ORDINARY annuity, payments occur:
o: At the beginning of each period
In the middle of each period
At the end of each period
Only at the end of the whole term
w: Ordinary = end; annuity due = beginning.

s: A bank deducts interest upfront on a 1-year ₹2 lakh loan at 12%. The borrower's effective rate is:
w: Receives 1,76,000, repays 2,00,000: 24,000/1,76,000 = 13.64%. Front-end interest raises the effective cost.

s: Savings bank interest in India is calculated on:
o: The daily closing balance, credited at least quarterly
The minimum balance between the 10th and last day of the month
The opening balance of each quarter
The average annual balance, credited yearly
w: Since 2010 RBI requires interest on daily products. Trap: the old 10th-to-end-of-month minimum balance rule.

s: A ₹1,000 bond carries an 8% annual coupon, 5 years to maturity, and the market yield is also 8%. Its price is:
w: Coupon = yield → price = par. Trap: computing unnecessarily; 681 is just the PV of the redemption alone.

s: A perpetual bond pays a 9% coupon on ₹1,000; the market yield is 12%. Its price is:
w: Perpetuity price = coupon/yield = 90/0.12 = ₹750. Trap: inverting (1,333).

s: A 7% bond (face ₹1,000) is quoted at ₹875. Its current yield is:
w: CY = 70/875 = 8%. Trap: coupon rate (7%).

s: A portfolio has modified duration 6.5. If yields rise by 75 basis points, the value falls by about:
w: %ΔP ≈ −6.5 × 0.75% = −4.875%. Trap: forgetting to multiply by the yield change.

s: Which bond has the LOWEST duration?
o: 10-year zero-coupon bond
10-year bond with a 12% coupon
5-year zero-coupon bond
5-year bond with a 12% coupon
w: Shorter maturity and higher coupon both lower duration. A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity.

s: Market yields FALL by 1%. Which bond gains the MOST in percentage terms?
o: 20-year 12% bond
5-year 6% bond
20-year 6% bond
5-year 12% bond
w: Longest maturity + lowest coupon = most price sensitive.

s: For a bond trading at a PREMIUM, the correct order is:
o: Coupon rate > current yield > YTM
YTM > current yield > coupon rate
Current yield > coupon > YTM
All three are equal
w: Premium means the buyer loses (price − par) at maturity, so YTM is lowest. For a discount bond the order reverses.

s: An investor expects interest rates to RISE. To protect his bond portfolio he should:
o: Buy long-dated zero-coupon bonds
Sell floating-rate bonds and buy fixed-rate bonds
Lengthen the portfolio's duration
Shorten the portfolio's duration
w: Lower duration = smaller loss when rates rise. Floating-rate bonds are the safer ones in rising rates.

s: A bond whose holder can sell it back to the issuer before maturity is a:
o: Convertible bond
Zero-coupon bond
Puttable bond
Callable bond
w: Put = investor's option; call = issuer's option.

s: The duration of a perpetual bond at a yield of 10% is:
o: 1.1 years
Infinite
10 years
11 years
w: Perpetuity duration = (1 + y)/y = 1.1/0.1 = 11 years. Trap: 'infinite' because it never matures.

s: Spot USD/INR 83.10/83.18; 1-month forward margin 25/30 paise. The forward rate quoted to an IMPORTER is:
w: Ascending margin = premium → add. Importer buys USD at the bank's selling rate: 83.18 + 0.30 = 83.48. Trap: 83.35 is the exporter's (buying) rate.

s: A student remits USD 20,000 for fees. Quote USD/INR 83.48/83.56. The rupee amount debited is:
w: Customer buys USD → bank's selling rate 83.56 × 20,000 = 16,71,200. Trap: using 83.48.

s: USD/INR 83.20/83.30 and EUR/USD 1.0850/1.0860. The EUR/INR quote is:
Spot USD/INR 83.00; 6-month forward 82.70. The USD is at an annualised:
o: Discount of about 0.36%
Premium of about 1.45%
Discount of about 0.72%
Premium of about 0.72%
w: (82.70 − 83.00)/83 × 12/6 × 100 = −0.72%. Forward below spot = discount. Trap: forgetting to annualise (0.36%).

s: Which rate does a bank apply when it purchases an export bill (paying the exporter before realisation)?
o: TT selling rate
Bill selling rate
Bill buying rate
TT buying rate
w: Bank buys the bill and pays out before reimbursement: bill buying rate, which is lower than TT buying.

s: A spot deal done on Monday (no holidays) is settled on:
o: Wednesday
Friday
Tuesday
Monday
w: Spot = T+2 working days. Cash = same day; TOM = next day.

s: If Indian interest rates are higher than US rates, by interest rate parity the USD will trade at a:
o: Forward discount against the rupee
Forward premium against the rupee
Spot premium only
Forward rate equal to spot
w: The higher-interest currency (INR) trades at a forward discount; the lower-interest currency (USD) at a premium.

s: An exporter hedged with a forward contract to sell USD at 83.00. On maturity spot is 82.40. Result:
o: He gets 83.00 plus the 0.60 difference
He sells at 83.00, protected from the fall
He must sell at 82.40, the spot rate on maturity
The contract lapses because spot moved against the bank
w: A forward fixes the rate for both sides; here the hedge saved him 60 paise per dollar.

s: In India, the quotation 'USD/INR 83.25' is an example of a:
o: Cross rate
Indirect quote
Forward quote
Direct quote
w: Home currency per unit of foreign currency = direct quote, used in India since 1993.

s: Our bank's US dollar account maintained with Citibank, New York, is our:
o: Vostro account
Nostro account
Mirror account
Loro account
w: Nostro = 'ours with you'. Our internal record of it is the mirror account.

s: Equity 60% at 14%; debt 40% at 9% pre-tax; tax 30%. WACC is:
12% irredeemable debentures are issued at ₹96 (face ₹100); tax 25%. The after-tax cost of debt is:
10% preference shares (face ₹100) are issued at ₹95; tax rate 30%. The cost of preference capital is:
w: Kp = 10/95 = 10.53%. Trap: applying a tax shield (preference dividend is not tax-deductible).

s: Rf = 7%, Rm = 15%, β = 0.8. Required return by CAPM is:
A stock with beta 0.6 is best described as:
o: Aggressive: it moves more than the market
Risk-free, since beta is below 1
Negatively correlated with the market
Defensive: it tends to move less than the market
w: β < 1 = defensive; β > 1 = aggressive; β = 0 risk-free; only a negative β moves opposite to the market.

s: Which is FALSE about retained earnings?
o: They save floatation costs compared with a new equity issue
Their cost is generally taken close to the cost of equity
Their cost is broadly the shareholders' opportunity cost
They have no cost because no fresh money is raised
w: Retained earnings belong to shareholders who could invest elsewhere: they have an opportunity cost.

s: EBIT ₹40 lakh; interest ₹10 lakh; preference dividend ₹4.5 lakh; tax 25%. The degree of financial leverage is:
w: DFL = EBIT/[EBIT − I − Pref div/(1 − t)] = 40/(40 − 10 − 6) = 40/24 = 1.67. Trap: ignoring preference dividend (1.33).

s: Operating leverage arises from:
o: Preference dividend
Fixed interest charges
Variable selling costs
Fixed operating costs
w: Operating leverage = fixed operating costs (DOL = contribution/EBIT). Financial leverage = fixed financing costs.

s: Under the Net Income approach, increasing debt in the capital structure:
o: First reduces then increases WACC
Reduces WACC and increases firm value
Leaves WACC and firm value unchanged
Increases WACC and reduces firm value
w: NI: debt helps. NOI/MM (no tax): irrelevant. Traditional: U-shaped WACC with an optimum.

s: Which is an EXTERNAL factor affecting WACC?
o: Investment policy
Tax rate
Dividend policy
Capital-structure policy
w: Interest rates, tax rates and market risk premium are outside the firm's control.

s: Project cost ₹100 lakh; inflows ₹30 lakh a year for 5 years; k = 12% (PVAF 3.6048). NPV is about:
o: ₹−8.14 lakh
₹8.14 lakh
₹30 lakh
₹50 lakh
w: PV = 30 × 3.6048 = 108.14; NPV = 8.14. Trap: undiscounted surplus 150 − 100 = 50.

s: For the same project (₹100 lakh outlay, ₹30 lakh a year for 5 years), payback period and PI at 12% are:
o: 3.33 years and 1.08
3 years and 0.92
5 years and 1.08
3.33 years and 1.50
w: Payback = 100/30 = 3.33 years; PI = 108.14/100 = 1.08. 1.50 is undiscounted.

s: Which method ignores the time value of money?
o: Payback period
Net present value
Internal rate of return
Profitability index
w: Payback (and ARR) don't discount cash flows. Discounted payback does.

s: ARR is calculated using:
o: Cash flows before depreciation
Average profit after depreciation
The IRR of the project
Discounted cash inflows
w: ARR = average profit ÷ average (or initial) investment. Trap: using cash flows.

s: A project's NPV at the firm's cost of capital is negative. Then:
o: Its IRR is below the cost of capital
Its payback must be longer than its life
Its IRR is above the cost of capital
Its PI is above 1
w: NPV < 0 ⇔ IRR < k ⇔ PI < 1.

s: Which should be EXCLUDED from project cash flows?
o: Interest on the project loan
Depreciation tax shield
Salvage value of the plant
Working capital released at the end
w: Financing costs are reflected in the discount rate; including interest would double-count.

s: Two mutually exclusive projects rank differently by NPV and IRR. Choose by:
o: NPV
IRR
Whichever has the higher initial investment
Payback period
w: NPV measures the absolute increase in wealth and assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital.

s: A project has cash flows −100, +250, −160. A problem with using IRR here is:
o: There may be more than one IRR because the cash flows change sign twice
IRR cannot be computed for projects longer than one year
The IRR will always be zero
NPV cannot be computed for such cash flows
w: Non-conventional cash flows (sign changes more than once) can produce multiple IRRs; NPV still works.

s: Under a Deferred Payment Guarantee, the bank guarantees:
o: Instalments payable to the machinery supplier
Payment of customs duty on imports
Repayment of a cash credit limit
Performance of a contract by the borrower
w: DPG supports purchase of machinery on deferred credit; appraised like a term loan.

s: Lease rentals of ₹15 lakh are payable at the BEGINNING of each year for 4 years; discount rate 10% (PVAF 4 yrs = 3.1699). PV of rentals is about:
o: ₹52.30 lakh
₹60.00 lakh
₹43.23 lakh
₹47.55 lakh
w: Annuity due: 15 × 3.1699 × 1.1 = 52.30. Trap: ordinary annuity 47.55.

s: In which lease does the lessor bear the risk of obsolescence?
o: Sale and leaseback treated as a finance lease
Leveraged lease
Finance lease
Operating lease
w: Operating leases are short, cancellable, and the lessor keeps the risks and rewards.

s: A dry lease of an aircraft means:
o: Aircraft only; lessee arranges crew and upkeep
The aircraft is leased without fuel only
The aircraft is leased with crew, maintenance and insurance
The lessor buys the aircraft back at the end of the lease
w: Dry = aircraft only; wet = ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance, insurance).

s: Under Ind AS 116, a 9-month lease of office equipment may be:
o: Shown only as a contingent liability
Expensed on a straight-line basis using the short-term lease exemption
Capitalised only if ownership passes
Must be recognised as a right-of-use asset in all cases
w: Leases of 12 months or less (and low-value assets) can be exempted.

s: Three parties — lessor, lessee and a lender who finances most of the asset's cost — are involved in a:
o: Operating lease
Leveraged lease
Sale and leaseback
Direct lease
w: The lessor 'leverages' its investment by borrowing from the lender.

s: Which is a feature of hire purchase but NOT of a lease?
o: The user gets possession immediately
Ownership passes on the last instalment
The owner can repossess on default
Payments are made periodically
w: In a lease ownership stays with the lessor; in hire purchase it passes to the hirer at the end.

s: Total lease rentals are ₹60 lakh against a cash price of ₹50 lakh. The correct conclusion is:
o: Lease, because payments are spread over time
The two are equal over the asset's life
Cannot decide until rentals are discounted
Buy, because ₹60 lakh exceeds ₹50 lakh
w: Lease-vs-buy compares present values, never undiscounted totals.

s: CA ₹500 lakh; current liabilities other than bank borrowings ₹150 lakh. Under Tandon Method II, MPBF is:
o: ₹350 lakh
₹375 lakh
₹262.5 lakh
₹225 lakh
w: Method II: 75% of CA − other CL = 375 − 150 = 225. Trap: Method I = 75% of WCG (350) = 262.5.

s: Projected turnover ₹4 crore (MSE). Under the Nayak Committee method, minimum bank finance is:
o: ₹1 crore
₹80 lakh
₹20 lakh
₹60 lakh
w: WC need = 25% (₹1 crore); bank finance = 20% of turnover = ₹80 lakh; margin 5% = ₹20 lakh.

s: Raw material 30 days, WIP 10 days, finished goods 20 days, debtors 45 days, creditors 40 days. Net operating cycle:
o: 145 days
65 days
105 days
25 days
w: 30 + 10 + 20 + 45 − 40 = 65 days. Trap: not deducting creditors (105).

s: Which REDUCES working-capital requirement?
o: Longer credit period from suppliers
Longer production cycle
Longer credit period to customers
Rapid growth in sales
w: Supplier credit finances current assets; the others lengthen the cycle or raise current assets.

s: Commercial Paper is issued:
o: By banks to raise short-term deposits
At par with a fixed coupon, secured by stock
For a minimum tenor of one year
At a discount to face value, as an unsecured instrument
w: CP: unsecured, discounted, 7 days to 1 year, ₹5 lakh multiples; banks issue CDs instead.

s: Which is TRUE of forfaiting?
o: It is a short-term domestic service including sales-ledger management
It is identical to factoring
It is without recourse and usually finances 100% of an export receivable
It is with recourse and finances 80% of domestic receivables
w: Forfaiting: export, medium-term, without recourse, 100%. Factoring: ongoing, short-term, with/without recourse, 75–90%, plus services.

s: Tandon Method II implies a minimum current ratio of:
w: Borrower funds 25% of CA from long-term sources → CL at most 75% of CA → CR = 1/0.75 = 1.33.

s: Permanent (core) working capital should ideally be financed by:
o: Long-term funds
Trade credit only
Short-term bank overdraft
Commercial paper rolled over every week
w: The core never goes away, so match it with long-term sources; seasonal needs with short-term funds.

s: Under TReDS, MSME invoices are financed:
o: Only by the buyer's bank
With full recourse to the MSME seller
Only after the buyer pays
Without recourse to the MSME seller
w: TReDS platforms let multiple financiers discount MSME receivables on large buyers without recourse to the MSME.

s: Which derivative has NO counterparty default risk for the participants because a clearing corporation guarantees it?
o: Exchange-traded futures
Forward rate agreements
Forward contracts
OTC interest rate swaps
w: Exchange-traded contracts are novated to the clearing corporation; OTC contracts carry counterparty risk.

s: The writer of a call option:
o: Receives the premium and must sell if the buyer exercises
Can lose at most the premium
Pays the premium and has the right to buy
Has no obligation once the premium is received
w: The writer is obliged; the buyer has the right. A call writer's loss can be unlimited.

s: A put option is 'in the money' when:
o: Spot equals strike
The premium exceeds the strike price
Spot price is above the strike price
Spot price is below the strike price
w: A put lets you sell at the strike; it has value when the market price is lower.

s: In a currency swap, unlike an interest rate swap:
o: No cash flows are exchanged
Only interest on a notional amount is exchanged
Principal in two currencies is exchanged
The contract is always exchange-traded
w: IRS: notional never exchanged. Currency swap: principal exchanged.

s: A borrower worried about RISING rates on a future loan should:
o: Receive fixed in an interest rate swap
Buy an FRA
Write a put option on bonds
Sell an FRA
w: Buying an FRA locks the borrowing rate; if rates rise, the FRA pays the difference.

s: Exchange-traded currency futures in India are regulated by:
o: FEDAI
SEBI
Only RBI
IRDAI
w: ETDs are SEBI-regulated; OTC forex and interest-rate derivatives are under RBI.

s: Which is a feature of a FORWARD contract?
o: It is marked to market daily
It is customised and settled on maturity
It is standardised by the exchange
The buyer has a right but no obligation
w: Forwards: OTC, customised, one settlement, obligation on both sides.

s: Which form of organisation gives limited liability WITHOUT share capital?
o: Limited Liability Partnership
Partnership firm
Hindu Undivided Family business (for the Karta)
Sole proprietorship
w: LLPs have no share capital requirement but offer limited liability; partners and the Karta have unlimited liability.

s: A company had net profit of ₹6 crore last year (turnover ₹300 crore, net worth ₹200 crore). Average net profit of the last 3 years is ₹4 crore. CSR obligation:
o: Applies; minimum spend ₹12 lakh
Does not apply, as turnover is below ₹1,000 crore
Applies; minimum spend ₹8 lakh
Does not apply, as average profit is below ₹5 crore
w: Any one trigger (net profit ≥ ₹5 crore in the preceding year) applies. Spend 2% of the 3-year average: 2% × 4 crore = ₹8 lakh. Traps: 2% of last year (12 lakh) or testing the average against ₹5 crore.

s: Which is NOT an agency cost?
o: Cost of audit to monitor managers
Interest paid on bank loans
Loss from managers' value-reducing decisions
Cost of independent directors
w: Agency costs: monitoring, bonding, residual loss. Interest is a financing cost.

s: The maximum number of members in a private company (excluding employee members) is:
o: No limit
w: Private company: 200. Partnership firm: 50 (rules).

s: Wealth maximisation is preferred over profit maximisation because it:
o: Focuses on this year's accounting profit
Considers the timing and risk of returns
Ignores risk to keep decisions simple
Maximises dividends every year
w: Profit maximisation ignores time value and risk.

s: Which CSR spending qualifies under Schedule VII?
o: Funding a skill-training centre for unemployed youth
Sponsoring a cricket match to advertise the company's brand
Bonus paid to the company's own employees
Donation to a political party
w: Brand promotion, employee benefits and political contributions are excluded.

s: Interest of ₹9,000 on a savings account and ₹40,000 on FDs is earned by a 45-year-old (old regime). Deduction under 80TTA:
w: 80TTA covers savings-account interest only, up to ₹10,000; here actual is ₹9,000. FD interest gets nothing. Trap: 80TTB (₹50,000) is for seniors.

s: A disabled DEPENDANT of the taxpayer is maintained by him. The deduction is under:
o: Section 80DD
Section 80D
Section 80U
Section 80DDB
w: 80DD = dependant with disability; 80U = the taxpayer himself; 80D = health insurance; 80DDB = treatment of specified diseases.

s: An author earns ₹4 lakh royalty on a book. Deduction under 80QQB is limited to:
o: ₹4 lakh
₹1.5 lakh
₹3 lakh
w: 80QQB (and 80RRB for patents) cap the deduction at ₹3 lakh.

s: Under the NEW tax regime for FY 2025-26, which deduction is still available to a salaried employee?
o: Section 80D for health insurance
Section 80C up to ₹1.5 lakh
Standard deduction of ₹75,000
Section 80TTA for savings interest
w: The new regime removes most Chapter VI-A deductions; standard deduction (₹75,000) and employer NPS (80CCD(2)) remain.

s: Health insurance premium of ₹20,000 paid in CASH for self:
o: Is fully deductible under 80D
Is not deductible under 80D
Is deductible up to ₹5,000 only
Is deductible under 80C
w: 80D needs a non-cash mode; only preventive check-up (up to ₹5,000) may be paid in cash.

s: Rent received by an individual from letting out a house is taxed under:
o: Income from other sources
Profits and gains of business
Capital gains
Income from house property
w: Annual value of house property is a separate head.

s: A bank pays FD interest of ₹60,000 in a year to a 50-year-old customer who has submitted PAN. TDS under 194A:
o: Is never deductible on FD interest
Is deductible at 20%
Is deductible at 10%, as interest exceeds ₹50,000
Is not deductible, as the limit is ₹1 lakh
w: Threshold ₹50,000 for non-seniors (₹1 lakh for seniors) from 1 April 2025; rate 10% with PAN, 20% without.

s: Form 15H is submitted by:
o: A non-resident depositor
Any person below 60 years with nil tax
A company with losses
A resident senior citizen with nil tax
w: 15H = senior citizens; 15G = others (individuals below 60, HUFs) with nil tax.

s: For a charitable trust to keep its exemption, it must apply to its objects at least:
o: 15% of its income
85% of its income
50% of its income
100% of its income every year
w: 15% can be accumulated freely; the rest must be applied or accumulated under Form 10 conditions.

s: Which of the following is NOT a blocked credit under GST?
o: Food and beverages for staff
Machinery purchased for use in the factory
Steel used to build the factory building
Motor car for the Managing Director
w: Capital goods like plant and machinery get ITC; the others are blocked under Sec 17(5).

s: A trader in Rajasthan supplies only services. GST registration is mandatory when aggregate turnover exceeds:
o: ₹40 lakh
₹1.5 crore
₹20 lakh
₹10 lakh
w: ₹40 lakh applies to exclusive suppliers of GOODS; services ₹20 lakh (₹10 lakh in some special-category States).

s: A supplier gives a post-sale discount that reduces the taxable value. He should issue a:
o: Credit note
Fresh tax invoice
Payment voucher
Debit note
w: Credit note reduces value/tax; debit note increases it.

s: Invoice-wise details of outward supplies are furnished in:
o: GSTR-1
GSTR-2B
GSTR-9
GSTR-3B
w: GSTR-1 = outward supplies; GSTR-3B = summary + payment; GSTR-2B = auto ITC statement; GSTR-9 = annual.

s: A composition dealer:
o: Can make inter-State outward supplies freely
Can neither collect GST nor claim ITC
Pays GST at 18% on turnover
Can claim ITC on all purchases
w: Composition: low flat rate, no ITC, no tax collection, no inter-State outward supply.

s: Interest on delayed payment of GST is charged at:
o: 24% per annum
12% per annum
2% per month
18% per annum
w: Sec 50: 18% p.a. on tax paid late.

s: The GST Council is constituted under:
o: Article 246A of the Constitution
Section 22 of the CGST Act
Article 279A of the Constitution
Article 280 of the Constitution
w: 279A = GST Council; 246A = concurrent power to levy GST; 280 = Finance Commission.

s: For GOODS, the time of supply is generally:
o: The end of the month of supply
The date payment is received
The later of invoice date and delivery date
Earlier of invoice date and due invoice date
w: Sec 12; GST on advances for goods is not payable since 2017.

s: 2,000 units enter a process at total cost ₹1,64,000; normal loss 10% with scrap value ₹10 per unit; actual output 1,850 units. Abnormal gain is valued at:
w: Normal cost per unit = (1,64,000 − 200 × 10)/1,800 = ₹90. Normal output 1,800; actual 1,850 → gain 50 units × 90 = ₹4,500 (net of scrap forgone ₹500, Costing P&L gets ₹4,000).

s: A hospital computes cost per patient-day. This is:
o: Process costing
Job costing
Service costing
Batch costing
w: Services use composite cost units like passenger-km, patient-day, kWh.

s: A sugar mill produces sugar (main) and molasses (minor). Molasses is a:
o: Scrap
By-product
Joint product
Abnormal gain
w: Joint products are of comparable value; a by-product has small relative value.

s: Which method suits a shipbuilder constructing a vessel over three years at a customer's site?
o: Process costing
Batch costing
Unit costing
Contract costing
w: Large, long, site-based work = contract costing.

s: In process costing, abnormal LOSS is:
o: Valued at scrap value only
Ignored as it is unavoidable
Absorbed by good units
Valued like good units; to Costing P&L
w: Abnormal loss is controllable; it shouldn't burden good output.

s: Which statement is correct?
o: Marginal costing replaces job and process costing
Batch costing cannot be used with standard costing
Standard costing is a method only for job shops
Marginal costing can be used along with process costing
w: Techniques (marginal, standard) are used with methods (job, process, batch).

s: Prime cost consists of:
o: Works cost + office overheads
Direct material + direct labour + direct expenses
Prime cost + factory overheads
Cost of production + selling overheads
w: Prime → works (+ factory OH) → cost of production (+ office OH) → cost of sales (+ selling OH).

s: A fixed cost per unit, as output rises:
o: Rises
Falls
Stays constant
Becomes variable
w: Total fixed cost is constant, spread over more units.

s: Escalation clause in a contract allows:
o: The contractee to withhold retention money
The contractor to stop work without notice
Profit to be recognised only on completion
A price rise if input costs rise
w: It protects the contractor from price rises during long contracts.

s: SP ₹50; VC ₹30; fixed cost ₹60,000. BEP in units and sales:
Same data (SP 50, VC 30, FC 60,000). If fixed costs rise by 10%, the new BEP is:
o: 3,300 units
2,727 units
3,000 units
3,600 units
w: 66,000/20 = 3,300. BEP rises in proportion to fixed cost.

s: Sales ₹2,00,000; BEP sales ₹1,50,000; P/V ratio 40%. Profit is:
w: Profit = MoS × P/V = 50,000 × 40% = 20,000. Trap: MoS itself (50,000) is not profit.

s: With SP ₹50, VC ₹30 and FC ₹60,000, units needed for profit of ₹40,000 are:
A component can be made at variable cost ₹46 plus allocated fixed overhead ₹10 (which continues anyway), or bought at ₹52. Decision:
o: Indifferent
Buy, since ₹52 is below ₹56
Make, since the relevant cost is ₹46
Buy, since buying is always cheaper
w: Unavoidable fixed overhead is irrelevant. Compare 46 vs 52 → make.

s: If variable cost per unit rises while SP is unchanged, the P/V ratio:
o: Stays the same
Rises and BEP falls
Falls and BEP rises
Falls and BEP falls
w: Lower contribution per unit → lower P/V → more units needed to break even.

s: When closing stock is HIGHER than opening stock, profit under absorption costing compared with marginal costing is:
o: Lower
Always zero
Higher
Equal
w: Part of fixed overhead is carried forward in the higher closing stock.

s: Margin of safety can be improved by:
o: Increasing fixed costs
Reducing sales volume
Increasing variable cost per unit
Raising price or cutting fixed costs
w: Anything that lowers BEP or raises sales widens MoS.

s: At break-even point:
o: Contribution equals variable cost
Profit equals fixed cost
Sales equal fixed cost
Contribution equals fixed cost
w: Profit = contribution − fixed cost = 0.

s: P/V ratio is 25% and fixed costs are ₹1,00,000. Sales required to break even:
w: BEP sales = FC/P/V = 1,00,000/0.25.

s: Which is a LIMITATION of marginal costing?
o: It helps in make-or-buy decisions
Semi-variable costs are hard to split
It avoids carrying fixed cost in stock
It shows the effect of volume on profit
w: The other options are advantages.

s: Standard: 5,000 kg at ₹20. Actual: 4,800 kg at ₹22 (for the same output). Material price variance:
o: ₹10,000 Adverse
₹4,000 Favourable
₹9,600 Adverse
₹9,600 Favourable
w: MPV = (SP − AP) × AQ = (20 − 22) × 4,800 = −9,600 (adverse). Trap: using standard quantity (10,000).

s: Same data (std 5,000 kg at ₹20; actual 4,800 kg at ₹22). Material usage variance:
o: ₹4,000 Adverse
₹5,600 Adverse
₹4,400 Favourable
₹4,000 Favourable
w: MUV = (SQ − AQ) × SP = (5,000 − 4,800) × 20 = +4,000 (favourable). Trap: valuing at actual price (4,400).

s: Material cost variance in the same case is:
o: ₹5,600 Favourable
₹4,000 Favourable
₹13,600 Adverse
₹5,600 Adverse

s: The purchase department is usually responsible for:
o: Labour efficiency variance
Material price variance
Fixed overhead volume variance
Material usage variance
w: Price → purchasing; usage and efficiency → production.

s: Labour rate variance is calculated on:
o: Idle hours only
Budgeted hours
Actual hours paid
Standard hours for actual output
w: Rate variance = (SR − AR) × AH; efficiency = (SH − AH) × SR.

s: 'Standard quantity' in variance analysis refers to:
o: Average quantity used in the last year
Quantity purchased during the period
Quantity budgeted for the budgeted output
Quantity allowed for the actual output
w: Variances compare actual input with what the actual output should have consumed.

s: Which statement is correct?
o: Standard costing cannot be used with budgetary control
Variances are analysed to find causes and fix responsibility
A favourable variance always indicates efficiency
Only adverse variances need to be reported
w: Large favourable variances may also signal poor standards or quality problems.

s: A standard that can be achieved under efficient operating conditions, allowing normal losses, is:
o: Historical standard
Ideal standard
Basic standard
Attainable standard
w: Ideal = perfect; basic = unchanged base; attainable = realistic and most used.

s: Std labour 1,000 hours at ₹50; actual 1,100 hours at ₹48 for the same output. Labour cost variance:
o: ₹2,800 Favourable
₹2,200 Favourable
₹5,000 Adverse
₹2,800 Adverse

s: At 15,000 units: variable cost ₹8 per unit; fixed cost ₹90,000. A flexible budget at 15,000 units allows total cost of:
Which budget is the summary of all functional budgets?
o: Master budget
Sales budget
Cash budget
Flexible budget
w: The master budget includes budgeted P&L and balance sheet.

s: A budget that is continuously updated by adding one more period as each period ends is a:
o: Zero-based budget
Fixed budget
Rolling budget
Performance budget
w: Also called continuous budget.

s: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of zero-based budgeting?
o: It links spending to objectives
It is time-consuming and paper-heavy
It questions every activity's need
It removes wasteful spending
w: The other options are advantages.

s: Performance budgeting focuses on:
o: Last year's budget plus inflation
Only the amount spent by each department
Cash receipts and payments
Outputs and results achieved for the money spent
w: It links inputs (money) to physical outputs/outcomes.

s: The 'principal budget factor' is:
o: The cash balance at the year-end
The factor that limits activity
The largest item of expenditure
The total of all budgets
w: Usually sales demand; sometimes capacity or materials.

s: A fixed (static) budget is unsuitable for control when:
o: The budget period is one year
Actual output differs widely from budget
Output is exactly as budgeted
All costs are fixed
w: Flexible budgets adjust cost allowances to actual activity.

s: Budgetary control involves:
o: Only recording actual costs
Auditing the financial statements
Only preparing budgets
Setting budgets, comparing actuals and acting
w: Planning + comparison + corrective action.

s:
Kaveri Textiles Ltd. closes its books on 31 March 2026; the Board approves the accounts on 22 May 2026. Between these dates:
1. A major customer owing ₹3.5 crore is admitted into insolvency on 12 April; its losses had been mounting since November 2025.
2. A court finalises damages of ₹1.2 crore in a suit filed against the company in 2024.
3. A flood on 2 May destroys raw material worth ₹80 lakh.
4. The Board proposes a final dividend of ₹2 per share on 22 May.
The Finance Manager adjusts all four events in the 2025-26 accounts, arguing that "anything known before approval must be adjusted". Which treatment is technically correct under AS 4?
o: Adjust only event 2, since only a court decree gives conclusive evidence of a condition at year-end
Adjust all four, since every event occurred before the Board approved the accounts
Adjust 1 and 2; disclose 3 if material; disclose 4 without a liability
Adjust events 1, 2 and 4; ignore event 3 since it relates to the next year
w: AS 4 distinguishes adjusting events (more evidence of conditions existing at the balance sheet date: the customer's insolvency rooted in losses since November, and settlement of a suit already pending) from non-adjusting events (the flood, a new condition). A dividend proposed after the balance sheet date is not a liability at that date; it is disclosed.

s:
Metro Infra Ltd. has a fixed-price flyover contract:
• Contract price: ₹220 crore
• Estimated total cost: ₹180 crore
• Cost incurred till 31 March: ₹72 crore (stage of completion measured by cost)
• Outcome can be estimated reliably
The Project Accountant wants to show no revenue until the final bill is raised. Applying AS 7, what revenue and profit should be recognised this year?
o: Revenue ₹72 crore and nil profit, recognising revenue only to the extent of cost
Revenue ₹88 crore and profit ₹40 crore, as total expected profit is assured
Revenue ₹88 crore and profit ₹16 crore, by reference to 40% completion
Nil revenue and nil profit until completion, as no bill has been raised
w: Stage of completion = 72/180 = 40%. Revenue = 40% × 220 = ₹88 crore; profit = 88 − 72 = ₹16 crore (40% of the expected ₹40 crore). Recognising revenue only up to cost applies when the outcome CANNOT be estimated reliably.

s: GreenPower Equipments installed pollution-control machinery costing ₹12 crore (life 10 years). The State Government sanctioned a capital subsidy of ₹3 crore specifically for this machinery, received after commissioning. Separately, it received ₹2 crore under a scheme computed as 10% of total project investment, with no repayment obligation. The executive credits ₹5 crore to Other Income. Which treatment is most appropriate under AS 12?
o: ₹3 crore: reduce asset cost or defer over 10 years; ₹2 crore: capital reserve
₹3 crore to capital reserve; ₹2 crore to Other Income because it is not linked to any asset
Credit the entire ₹5 crore to Other Income because cash has been received this year
Credit the entire ₹5 crore to capital reserve because both grants are capital receipts
w: A grant tied to a depreciable asset is matched with depreciation (deduction from cost or deferred income). A grant in the nature of promoters' contribution, linked to total investment and not repayable, is credited to capital reserve as part of shareholders' funds.

s:
Alpha Biotech incurs, while developing a new drug:
• Laboratory research on molecules – ₹6 crore
• Development after technical feasibility, intention, resources and market are established – ₹9 crore
• Patent registration fees – ₹40 lakh
• Pre-launch advertising – ₹2 crore
• Training of medical representatives – ₹60 lakh
The Finance Manager proposes capitalising ₹18 crore "because every rupee builds future profit". What amount does AS 26 allow to be recognised as an intangible asset?
o: ₹9.40 crore
₹18 crore
₹11.40 crore
₹15.40 crore
w: Research (₹6 crore), advertising (₹2 crore) and training (₹0.6 crore) are always expensed under AS 26. Qualifying development cost (₹9 crore) plus directly attributable patent fees (₹0.4 crore) = ₹9.40 crore.

s: Orion Ltd. holds: (a) shares of a listed company bought 2 months ago to sell within the year, cost ₹50 lakh, market value ₹44 lakh; (b) shares of a supplier held for 5 years as a strategic long-term investment, cost ₹80 lakh, market value ₹74 lakh owing to a temporary market correction. The accountant writes down both to market value. Which is correct under AS 13?
o: Keep both at cost, since no investment has been sold during the year
Write down both, since all investments must be shown at market value
Write down (a) to ₹44 lakh; keep (b) at ₹80 lakh, as its fall is temporary
Keep (a) at cost and write down (b), since long-term holdings carry more risk
w: Current investments: lower of cost and fair value. Long-term investments: cost, less provision only for a decline other than temporary.

s:
Vardhan Ltd. and its related entities had the following transactions:
1. Sales to its wholly owned subsidiary.
2. Interest-free loan to the Managing Director's spouse.
3. Rent paid to a firm in which a director is a partner.
4. Purchases from Delta Ltd., which merely has one director in common with Vardhan.
The Finance Manager proposes to disclose only item 1. Which items require disclosure under AS 18?
o: 1 and 4 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3 only
w: Subsidiaries, relatives of KMP and enterprises in which a director has significant influence (as partner) are related parties; disclosure is needed even if no price (interest) is charged. A common director alone does not make Delta a related party.

s: Sterling Ltd. revises the estimated useful life of its plant from 12 to 8 years after a technical report, and separately discovers that depreciation of ₹40 lakh was omitted in last year's accounts due to a clerical mistake. The CFO wants to treat both as prior period items. Which statement correctly applies AS 5?
o: The life revision is a change in accounting policy requiring retrospective restatement
The life revision is a change in estimate (prospective); only the omitted ₹40 lakh is a prior period item
Both are prior period items and must be shown separately in the current P&L
Both are changes in accounting estimate applied from the current year onwards
w: Prior period items arise from errors or omissions in earlier years' accounts. A revised useful life is a new estimate, applied prospectively.

s: An Indian company imported machinery for USD 2,00,000 when the rate was ₹82; the supplier is still unpaid at year-end when the rate is ₹84. It also holds an export receivable of USD 50,000 booked at ₹83. Under AS 11, what is the net exchange difference recognised in the P&L for the year?
o: Net loss of ₹4,00,000
No exchange difference, since both items are recorded at historical rates
Net loss of ₹3,50,000
Net gain of ₹50,000
w: Monetary items are restated at the closing rate. Payable: 2,00,000 × (84 − 82) = ₹4,00,000 loss. Receivable: 50,000 × (84 − 83) = ₹50,000 gain. Net loss ₹3,50,000, charged to P&L.

s:
Consider these statements on Indian Accounting Standards:
1. Ind AS are notified by the Central Government under the Companies Act after recommendation of NFRA.
2. Scheduled commercial banks follow Ind AS from FY 2018-19 under RBI directions.
3. A company that has adopted Ind AS cannot revert to the earlier AS.
4. US GAAP permits LIFO for inventory, whereas IFRS and Ind AS do not.
Which are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
w: RBI has deferred Ind AS for scheduled commercial banks until further notice (2 wrong). The rest are correct.

s: Under AS 28, Nova Ltd.'s plant has a carrying amount of ₹90 lakh. Its net selling price is ₹62 lakh and the present value of future cash flows from continued use is ₹74 lakh. The Finance Manager books an impairment loss of ₹28 lakh "on a prudent basis". Which is correct?
o: Impairment loss is ₹22 lakh, being the average of the two shortfalls
No impairment is needed, because value in use is positive
Impairment loss is ₹28 lakh, because prudence requires the lower figure
Impairment loss is ₹16 lakh, because recoverable amount is the higher figure of ₹74 lakh
w: Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use = ₹74 lakh. Impairment = 90 − 74 = ₹16 lakh.

s: Ganga Ltd. borrowed ₹50 crore on 1 April specifically to build a new plant (expected to take 20 months). Work stopped for 4 months due to a dispute with the contractor; the plant was substantially ready on 31 January the following year but production began only on 1 April. The accountant capitalises all interest up to 1 April. Which is correct under AS 16?
o: Interest is capitalised only for the dispute period, since work was interrupted
Interest for the dispute period and for the period after the plant was substantially ready must be expensed
All interest till production begins is capitalised, since the plant was not producing
No interest can be capitalised, since the plant was financed by a loan
w: Capitalisation is suspended during extended interruption of active development and ceases when the asset is substantially ready for its intended use, even if production starts later.

s: ABC India Pvt. Ltd. buys components from its UK parent at prices 25% above those charged by unrelated suppliers, cutting Indian taxable profit. The CFO argues group policy is binding and customs authorities have already accepted the invoice value. Which statement is correct?
o: Transfer pricing applies only to transactions between two Indian companies, so no adjustment
Customs acceptance of the invoice value automatically fixes it for income-tax too
The TPO can adjust income to arm's length price; group policy and customs value don't bind
Group policy prevails because the parent and subsidiary are under common control
w: Sections 92–92F require international transactions between associated enterprises to be at arm's length price (CUP, resale price, cost plus, profit split, TNMM).

s:
Mr Raj, a sole proprietor, during the year:
• Paid his personal life-insurance premium from the business bank account.
• Brought office furniture worth ₹60,000 from home for the shop.
• Withdrew ₹15 lakh to build his residence.
• Paid business loan instalments from the business account.
The accountant books the first and third items as business expenses because "the owner and the business are one in law". Which concept is violated and what is the correct effect?
o: Money measurement concept; the furniture brought from home is not recorded at all
Matching concept; the premium is a prepaid expense to be spread over the policy term
Going concern concept; all four items are business expenses of the year
Business entity; premium and withdrawal are drawings, furniture adds to capital
w: Accounting treats the business as separate from the owner. Personal payments are drawings (reduce capital); assets the owner brings in add to capital.

s:
A consulting firm on cash basis reports March profit of ₹2.4 lakh. It has:
• Fees earned in March but unpaid – ₹1.6 lakh
• April rent paid in March – ₹40,000
• March electricity unpaid – ₹15,000
• Advance received in March for April work – ₹50,000 (included in cash receipts)
What would March profit be under accrual accounting?
o: ₹4.75 lakh
₹3.75 lakh
₹4.25 lakh
₹2.85 lakh
w: Accrual: 2.40 + 1.60 (fees earned) + 0.40 (April rent removed) − 0.15 (electricity) − 0.50 (advance not earned) = ₹3.75 lakh.

s: The Finance Manager states: "Whenever a company earns profit, its liabilities must increase because the profit belongs to someone." The Chief Accountant examines profit that is (i) retained, (ii) declared as dividend, (iii) used to repay a bank loan, (iv) invested in machinery. Which statement is sound?
o: Profit always increases liabilities, because the whole of it is owed to shareholders
Profit always reduces liabilities because it is used to repay creditors
Profit affects only the Statement of Profit and Loss and never the Balance Sheet
Profit raises equity; it becomes a liability only when a dividend is declared
w: Retained profit sits in reserves (equity). Declaring dividend moves it to a liability; repaying a loan reduces liabilities; buying machinery changes only the asset mix.

s:
Consider these statements about accounting concepts:
1. Showing assets at cost less depreciation rather than at forced-sale value rests on the going concern assumption.
2. Recording a building at ₹50 lakh though its market value is ₹80 lakh reflects conservatism.
3. Treating capital as a liability of the business reflects the business entity concept.
4. Expensing a ₹400 calculator that lasts 3 years reflects materiality.
Which are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
w: Keeping a fixed asset at cost despite a higher market value is the cost concept (supported by going concern), not conservatism. The others are correct.

s: A business shows: Cash ₹60,000; Debtors ₹1,40,000; Stock ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹4,00,000; Prepaid insurance ₹20,000; Creditors ₹1,80,000; Bank overdraft ₹70,000; Outstanding wages ₹30,000; Long-term loan ₹2,00,000. During the year the owner introduced ₹1,00,000 and withdrew ₹60,000; opening capital was ₹2,40,000. What was the profit for the year?
w: Assets = 8,20,000; liabilities = 4,80,000; closing capital = 3,40,000. Profit = Closing − Opening − Fresh capital + Drawings = 3,40,000 − 2,40,000 − 1,00,000 + 60,000 = ₹60,000. Traps: forgetting fresh capital (1,60,000) or ignoring drawings.

s: At year-end, Delta Traders values closing stock (cost ₹9 lakh, NRV ₹7.5 lakh) at ₹7.5 lakh, creates a 5% provision for doubtful debts, but refuses to create a provision for discount on creditors. A partner objects that the treatment is "inconsistent". Which explanation is correct?
o: Stock should be at cost, as the cost concept overrides conservatism
Provision for doubtful debts violates the accrual concept
The discount on creditors must also be provided for, to be consistent
All three follow conservatism: anticipate losses, but do not anticipate gains
w: Prudence provides for probable losses (stock below cost, doubtful debts) but does not recognise expected gains (discount from creditors).

s: A company converts ₹50 lakh of its equity share capital into a long-term loan from the promoter, and on the same day repays a ₹20 lakh bank loan in cash. What is the combined effect on the accounting equation?
o: Assets −₹20 lakh; liabilities −₹20 lakh; capital unchanged
Assets +₹30 lakh; liabilities +₹30 lakh; capital unchanged
Assets −₹20 lakh; liabilities +₹30 lakh; capital −₹50 lakh
Assets unchanged; liabilities +₹50 lakh; capital −₹50 lakh
w: Conversion: liabilities +50, capital −50, assets unchanged. Repayment: assets −20, liabilities −20. Net: assets −20, liabilities +30, capital −50.

s: Under AS 1, which statement is correct?
o: Fundamental assumptions apply only to companies listed on a stock exchange
Every accounting policy must be disclosed only when it differs from the previous year
Going concern, consistency and accrual are fundamental assumptions; disclosure is needed only if they are not followed
Prudence, substance over form and materiality are fundamental assumptions that must always be disclosed
w: AS 1 names three fundamental assumptions; prudence, substance over form and materiality guide the selection of policies.

s:
Vertex Manufacturing had these transactions:
1. Purchased machinery through bank.
2. Paid installation wages for the new machine.
3. Bought lubricants for routine servicing.
4. Received an insurance claim for damage to a machine.
The Accounts Executive debits Machinery Account in all four cases, arguing "Machinery is a real account – debit what comes in". Which statement is technically correct?
o: Only 1 is correct; installation wages are always charged to Wages Account
Only 1 and 2 are debited to Machinery; 3 is a revenue expense and 4 debits Bank and credits the claim/loss account
1, 2 and 3 are correct; only the insurance claim is wrongly recorded
All four are correct, because every transaction involving machinery is a real-account debit
w: Golden rules decide the side; capital-vs-revenue decides the account. Installation is part of cost; routine servicing is revenue; a claim received is a receipt (Dr Bank).

s: A trainee classifies: Factory building – Real; Bank loan – Personal; Outstanding salary – Nominal; Goodwill – Nominal; Drawings – Personal; Discount allowed – Nominal. How many classifications are WRONG under the traditional approach?
o: Three
Four
Two
One
w: Outstanding salary is a representative personal account, and goodwill is an intangible real account. The other four are correct.

s:
The following independent transactions are recorded by a trainee:
1. Furniture bought on credit – Purchases A/c Dr; To Supplier.
2. Goods worth ₹8,000 (cost) taken by the proprietor – Drawings A/c Dr; To Sales A/c.
3. Free samples distributed (cost ₹5,000) – Advertisement A/c Dr; To Purchases A/c.
4. Bad debt written off last year now recovered – Cash A/c Dr; To Debtor's A/c.
Which entries are correct?
o: 3 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
1 and 3 only
w: Furniture → Furniture A/c (not Purchases). Goods taken by owner → credit Purchases (not Sales). Recovery of written-off debt → credit Bad Debts Recovered (the debtor's account is closed). Only 3 is correct.

s: A shop keeps a petty-cash float of ₹10,000 on the imprest system. This week the petty cashier spent ₹2,400 on postage, ₹3,100 on conveyance and ₹1,700 on stationery. The main cashier proposes to give him ₹10,000 'to restart the week'. Which is correct?
o: Reimburse ₹7,200 by debiting Petty Cash A/c, restoring the float to ₹10,000
Give ₹10,000 by debiting the three expense accounts directly
Give ₹10,000 and credit the expense accounts with ₹7,200
Give ₹2,800, the balance left with the petty cashier
w: Under the imprest system the petty cashier is reimbursed exactly the amount spent (2,400 + 3,100 + 1,700 = 7,200), so the float returns to ₹10,000.

s: Which entry correctly records 'Goods costing ₹60,000 destroyed by fire; insurance company admits a claim of ₹45,000'?
o: Insurance Company A/c Dr ₹60,000; To Purchases A/c ₹60,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹45,000; Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Sales A/c ₹60,000
Insurance Claim A/c Dr ₹45,000; Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Purchases A/c ₹60,000
Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹60,000; To Stock A/c ₹60,000
w: Goods lost are removed from purchases at cost; the admitted claim is a receivable and the balance is a loss. Cash is debited only when the claim is actually received.

s: In a triple-column cash book, the accountant: (i) records ₹50,000 cash deposited into bank only in the bank column; (ii) balances the discount columns and carries forward the balances; (iii) records a trade discount of ₹2,000 in the discount column. Which of these are errors?
o: (i) and (iii) only
(ii) and (iii) only
(i) only
All three
w: A deposit of cash is a contra entry affecting both cash and bank columns; discount columns are totalled (not balanced) and posted; trade discount is never recorded.

s: Machinery worth ₹5 lakh is bought from Vikas Ltd., which accepts 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each in settlement. Which pair of entries is correct?
o: Purchases Dr; To Vikas Ltd ₹5 lakh, and then Vikas Ltd Dr; To Share Capital ₹5 lakh
Machinery Dr; To Bank ₹5 lakh, and then Bank Dr; To Equity Share Capital ₹5 lakh
Equity Share Capital Dr; To Machinery ₹5 lakh only
Machinery Dr; To Vikas Ltd ₹5 lakh, and then Vikas Ltd Dr; To Equity Share Capital ₹5 lakh
w: The asset is debited and the vendor credited; the vendor's claim is then settled by issuing shares. No cash is involved; Purchases is only for goods dealt in.

s:
Consider these statements:
1. Credit purchase of goods for resale is recorded in the Purchases Book.
2. Credit purchase of a computer for office use is recorded in the Purchases Book.
3. Goods returned to a supplier are supported by a debit note and recorded in the Purchase Returns Book.
4. Opening and rectification entries are recorded in the Journal Proper.
Which are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
w: The Purchases Book is only for credit purchases of goods dealt in; a computer for office use goes to the Journal Proper.

s: Under the modern (accounting-equation) approach, a trainee lists normal balances: Drawings – Credit; Prepaid rent – Debit; Income received in advance – Debit; Provision for depreciation – Credit. Which are correctly stated?
o: Prepaid rent and Provision for depreciation only
Drawings and Prepaid rent only
Income received in advance and Provision for depreciation only
All four
w: Drawings reduce capital → debit balance. Income received in advance is a liability → credit balance. Prepaid rent (asset) is debit; provision for depreciation is credit.

s: Cash ₹19,600 received from a debtor in full settlement of ₹20,000 is posted by the trainee as: Cash Dr ₹19,600; To Debtor ₹19,600. The senior says the debtor's account will show a false balance. Which correction is needed?
o: Discount Allowed A/c Dr ₹400; To Debtor ₹400
No correction, since cash received is correctly recorded
Debtor Dr ₹400; To Discount Received ₹400
Discount Received A/c Dr ₹400; To Cash ₹400
w: Full settlement means ₹400 was allowed as discount (a loss). The debtor must be credited with the full ₹20,000.

s:
The Trial Balance of Indus Ltd. agreed. During audit:
1. A machine costing ₹12 lakh bought on 1 October on credit was entered in the Purchases Book (supplier correctly credited). Depreciation is 10% p.a. SLM.
2. Repairs of ₹2 lakh to the office were debited to Building Account.
What is the combined effect on net profit before rectification?
o: Profit understated by ₹11.40 lakh
Profit understated by ₹10 lakh
Profit overstated by ₹2 lakh
Profit understated by ₹9.40 lakh
w: Error 1: purchases overstated by 12 lakh, depreciation of 0.60 lakh (6 months) not charged → profit understated by 11.40. Error 2: repairs capitalised → profit overstated by 2.00. Net understatement = ₹9.40 lakh. Both are errors of principle, so the TB agreed.

s:
A Trial Balance did not agree and the difference was put to Suspense. Found later:
(a) Sales Book undercast by ₹12,000.
(b) Cash ₹8,000 received from Mohan posted to the debit of his account.
(c) Purchase of furniture ₹25,000 debited to Purchases.
(d) Discount received ₹1,500 posted to the debit of Discount Allowed.
The Suspense Account originally had a balance of:
o: ₹22,000 credit
₹56,000 credit
₹31,000 credit
₹31,000 debit
w: Debits exceed credits by: (a) 12,000 (sales under-credited); (b) 16,000 (Mohan debited 8,000 instead of credited 8,000); (c) nil (two-sided); (d) 3,000 (debit 1,500 wrongly made, credit 1,500 missing). Total 31,000 excess debit, so Suspense is opened on the CREDIT side with ₹31,000.

s: Which group contains ONLY errors that will NOT affect the agreement of the Trial Balance?
o: Error of principle; complete omission; wrong amount in the Sales Book; posting to Ram instead of Shyam (same side)
Wrong balancing of Wages Account; error of principle; complete omission; compensating error
Posting to the wrong side; wrong amount in the Sales Book; error of principle; complete omission
Error of principle; undercasting of Purchases Book; complete omission; compensating error
w: Undercasting a book, wrong balancing and posting to the wrong side are one-sided errors that disturb the TB. Principle, complete omission, wrong amount in a book of original entry and posting to a wrong account of the same class do not.

s: Credit sale of ₹4,80,000 (cost ₹3,20,000) was completely omitted from the Sales Book; the goods left the warehouse and were excluded from closing stock; the customer confirms the balance. The Finance Manager says "net profit is unaffected because both sale and cost are missing". Which is correct?
o: The TB will disagree, because debtors are understated by ₹4.8 lakh
Profit and debtors understated by ₹4.8 lakh; the TB still agrees
Profit understated by only ₹1.6 lakh (the margin); the TB agrees
Net profit is unaffected because sale and cost are both missing
w: Cost of the goods is already reflected (lower closing stock); only the sale is missing, so the whole ₹4.8 lakh is understated. Complete omission does not disturb the TB.

s:
The Audit Committee reviews four errors found after the TB agreed:
1. Purchase of machinery ₹9.8 lakh debited to Repairs.
2. Credit purchase from Rahul ₹2,10,000 entered in the Purchases Book as ₹1,20,000.
3. Goods sold to Ravi ₹15,000 posted to Ravindra's account.
4. Rent ₹6,000 paid debited to the landlord's personal account.
Which errors affect reported profit?
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
w: 1: expense overstated (profit understated). 2: purchases understated by 90,000 (profit overstated). 4: rent expense missing (profit overstated). 3 affects only personal accounts.

s: An error discovered next year after the books were closed: an old machine sold for ₹40,000 (book value ₹35,000) had been credited to Sales Account. The accountant proposes 'Sales A/c Dr ₹40,000; To Machinery A/c ₹40,000' this year. The auditor disagrees. The correct rectification is:
o: No entry is needed because last year's books are closed
Machinery A/c Dr ₹40,000; To Suspense A/c ₹40,000
P&L Adjustment A/c Dr ₹35,000; To Machinery A/c ₹35,000
Sales A/c Dr ₹40,000; To Machinery A/c ₹40,000, as proposed
w: After closing, last year's Sales (nominal) is no longer open; its effect on profit is corrected through P&L Adjustment. Last year: Sales was credited 40,000, but only a profit of 5,000 should have reached P&L, so profit was overstated by 35,000; Machinery is still carried at its book value of 35,000. Both are corrected by one entry.

s:
Rectification entries passed through a Suspense Account at Bharat Ltd. are:
1. Suspense Dr; To Sales ₹10,000 (sales book undercast).
2. Arun Dr; To Suspense ₹6,000 (sale not posted to Arun).
3. Suspense Dr; To Purchase Returns ₹4,000 (returns book undercast).
4. Mohan Dr ₹2,000; To Suspense (wrong posting in Mohan's account).
What is the net effect on profit?
o: Increase of ₹22,000
No effect, as suspense entries only balance the TB
Increase of ₹6,000
Increase of ₹14,000
w: Only nominal accounts change profit: Sales +10,000 and Purchase Returns +4,000 → +14,000. Arun and Mohan are personal accounts.

s: Before rectification, Sun Ltd.'s TB showed debit ₹8,45,000 and credit ₹8,62,000. The only error is that the Purchases Book was overcast. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Impossible: an overcast Purchases Book would raise the debit total
The suspense account should be credited with ₹17,000
The Purchases Book was overcast by ₹17,000, the full difference
The Purchases Book was overcast by ₹8,500, half of the difference
w: Overcasting purchases inflates the debit side. Here the debit side is ₹17,000 SHORT, so the single error must reduce debits (e.g. undercasting purchases or overcasting a credit-side book).

s: Which statement about the Suspense Account is technically correct?
o: It is for one-sided errors; any year-end balance goes to the Balance Sheet
It must always be closed before the Trial Balance can be drawn up
Every rectification passed through it changes the profit of the year
It is opened for every error, including errors of principle, to reach a correct profit
w: Two-sided errors are rectified directly. Many suspense corrections touch only personal or real accounts. An unresolved balance is carried in the Balance Sheet.

s: A credit sale of ₹4,500 was recorded in the Sales Book as ₹5,400 and posted from there. The trainee rectifies with 'Suspense Dr ₹900; To Sales ₹900'. The auditor objects. Why?
o: Sales Dr, To Suspense ₹1,800, double the difference
Two-sided error: Sales Dr, To Customer ₹900, no suspense
The entry is correct but must be passed in the next year
Customer Dr, To Sales ₹900, with no suspense
w: An error in the book of original entry is carried to both sides, so the TB agreed and no suspense exists. Both accounts are overstated by ₹900.

s:
Year-end adjusting entries are required for which of these, even though the Trial Balance has agreed?
1. Salary for March unpaid.
2. Insurance paid for the next year.
3. Interest accrued on investments but not due.
4. Depreciation on plant.
5. A cheque from a customer received and banked on 31 March.
o: 1 and 4 only
1, 2, 3 and 4 only
4 only
w: Accrual accounting needs adjustments for outstanding, prepaid and accrued items and depreciation. A banked cheque is an ordinary transaction already recorded.

s:
On 31 March, Sagar Traders' cash book shows a debit balance of ₹3,60,000. Analysis reveals:
• Cheques issued but not presented – ₹72,000
• Cheques deposited but not credited – ₹41,000
• Bank charges not in cash book – ₹1,800
• NEFT receipt from a customer not in cash book – ₹25,000
• A cheque issued for ₹14,600 was entered in the cash book as ₹16,400
What are the adjusted cash-book balance and the pass-book balance?
o: Adjusted cash book ₹3,85,000; pass book ₹4,16,000
Adjusted cash book ₹3,85,000; pass book ₹3,54,000
Adjusted cash book ₹3,60,000; pass book ₹4,16,000
Adjusted cash book ₹3,83,200; pass book ₹4,14,200

s: The cash book of Ravi & Co. shows an overdraft of ₹1,20,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹30,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹45,000; interest on overdraft debited by bank ₹4,500; a customer paid ₹20,000 directly into the bank. The trainee calculates the pass-book overdraft as ₹1,49,500. The correct figure is:
w: Treat overdraft as −1,20,000: +30,000 (unpresented) − 45,000 (uncredited) − 4,500 (interest) + 20,000 (direct deposit) = −1,19,500. The trainee reversed the signs of the unpresented cheques and direct deposit.

s:
While reconciling, Nova Enterprises finds:
1. A cheque received ₹1,80,000 recorded in the cash book as ₹18,000.
2. A dividend of ₹95,000 collected and credited by the bank.
3. A cheque of ₹42,000 issued remains unpresented.
4. The bank debited ₹12,000 belonging to another customer.
5. Insurance premium ₹48,000 paid under standing instructions.
Which items need an entry in the cash book?
o: 1, 2 and 5 only
2 and 5 only
1, 2, 4 and 5 only
All five
w: Our own error (1) and bank-originated items we have not recorded (2, 5) need cash-book entries. The unpresented cheque is a timing difference; the bank's wrong debit is shown in the BRS and the bank asked to reverse it.

s: Pass book shows a credit balance of ₹2,40,000. Cheques deposited but not credited ₹36,000; cheques issued not presented ₹58,000; bank charges ₹2,000 and interest credited ₹6,500, neither in the cash book. Balance as per cash book is:
w: From PB: + 36,000 (cash book already has the deposit) − 58,000 (cash book already reduced) + 2,000 (charges not yet in CB) − 6,500 (interest not yet in CB) = 2,13,500.
